rules.name: PI Collection Via Third-Party Authentication Without VPC
rules.description: Social login (Google, Facebook, Twitter) without age gating is prohibited for child-directed apps
rules.fix_suggestion: Wrap the auth call in a conditional check for user.age >= 13 or use signInWithParentEmail() for children
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects third-party authentication integrations (Google Sign-In, Facebook Login, Apple Sign In, Discord OAuth, GitHub OAuth) in child-directed applications that lack a verifiable parental consent (VPC) flow. Social login inherently involves collecting personal information — the child's name, email, and profile data are transmitted from the identity provider to the application. Under COPPA §312.5, operators must obtain VPC before collecting children's PI. The 2025 amendments add a requirement for separate VPC when personal information is disclosed to third parties (§312.5(a)(2)), which social login triggers by design since it shares data with the identity provider.
tp_criteria: Third-party OAuth/social login SDK initialization (GoogleSignIn, FacebookLogin, AppleSignIn, etc.) in a child-directed app with no VPC flow anywhere in the authentication chain — no age gate, no parental consent screen, no consent verification before or after login
Social login callback handler processes authentication and creates user account without any parental consent verification step — child can complete registration with one click
OAuth flow requests scopes that include PI (email, profile, contacts) from the identity provider without prior VPC
fp_criteria: Social login is wrapped in a VPC flow — age gate checks before login is offered, or parental consent is required after authentication before account activation
Social login is only available in parent/admin/teacher portal, not in child-facing UI
Application uses social login but requests only non-PI scopes (e.g., authentication-only, no email or profile data)
Application is general audience with age screening that redirects under-13 users to a parental consent flow before social login is accessible
rule_logic: The violation is collecting PI without VPC — NOT the use of social login itself. Social login behind proper VPC is fully COPPA-compliant.
Do NOT use the term 'age verification' — the COPPA requirement is 'verifiable parental consent' (VPC), which is a legally distinct and more stringent standard.
The 2025 amendment requiring separate VPC for third-party disclosure (§312.5(a)(2)) makes this rule MORE important — social login inherently discloses PI to the identity provider.
Upstream provider age restrictions (e.g., Google's 13+ requirement) do NOT substitute for the operator's VPC obligation. The operator must independently verify consent.

tp_examples.explanation: TP: TutorAI's LEARNER login page (used by students/children) implements Facebook, Google, and GitHub social login via Firebase signInWithPopup with no age gate or verifiable parental consent (VPC) flow. Social login providers share PII (email, name, profile photo) with the app. The component name 'learner/login' indicates this is for students, not administrators. Per 16 CFR 312.5(b)(1), operators must obtain VPC before collecting PI from children, and social auth inherently collects PI from the OAuth provider.

TP: Oppia (a child-directed educational platform) implements Google OAuth sign-in with explicit email scope request. The signInWithRedirect method sends users to Google's auth flow which shares their email with Oppia. While Oppia is designed for learners of all ages, the platform is frequently used by minors and there is no visible VPC or age-gating mechanism in the auth service itself. Per 16 CFR 312.5(b)(1), collecting email via Google OAuth from potential child users requires VPC.

TP (borderline): TutorAI's parent login also uses social auth (Facebook, Google, GitHub) via Firebase. While this is the parent/guardian portal (navigates to '/parent'), the same social auth SDK is used without any verification that the person logging in is actually a parent/guardian vs. a child. The identical code pattern across learner and parent components suggests no differentiation in auth flow. A child could use the parent login to bypass any learner restrictions.

fp_examples.explanation: FP (contextual): The parent login component routes to '/parent' portal, indicating it is designed for adult guardians, not children. Social auth in an explicitly parent-facing portal is less concerning since COPPA VPC requirements apply to PI collection FROM children, not from their parents. The component name 'guardian/parent-login' signals the intended audience is adults.

FP: TutorAI's instructor login uses the same social auth pattern but is explicitly for adult instructors/teachers (routes to '/instructor'). The component is under the 'guide' module and named 'instructor-login', clearly indicating an adult-facing portal. Social auth for teacher/admin accounts does not trigger COPPA VPC requirements since the PI is collected from adults, not children.

FP: Oppia's DevAuthServiceImpl is a development-only auth implementation (used when firebaseEmulatorIsEnabled). The signInWithRedirectAsync is a no-op and getRedirectResultAsync returns null. This demonstrates that Oppia has environment-specific auth handling and the social login only activates in production (ProdAuthServiceImpl), not in development/test environments.

knowledge.regulatory_source: 16 CFR §312.5(b) — VPC required before collecting children's PI. §312.5(a)(2) (2025) — Separate VPC for third-party disclosure. §312.2 — Personal information definition includes name, email, profile data transmitted via social login.

rules.name: PII Collection in URL Parameters
rules.description: Email, name, DOB, or phone in GET request URLs exposes PII in logs
rules.fix_suggestion: Switch to POST method and move PII to request body
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects personally identifiable information (email, name, date of birth, phone) being transmitted in GET request URL parameters. URL parameters are logged by servers, proxies, and CDNs, exposing PII to unauthorized access and violating COPPA data security requirements.
tp_criteria: Code constructs GET request URL with email, phone, name, or DOB as query parameters (e.g., 'GET /api/register?email=child@email.com&dob=01011995')
PII is appended to URL string without encryption or obfuscation before transmission
API call uses query parameters to pass PII instead of request body (POST with body encryption)
fp_criteria: Code demonstrates URL construction in documentation, comments, or test cases without actual implementation
PII parameters are present only in POST request body or encrypted payload, not in URL itself
Code is in a vendor library or third-party dependency file not under app control
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS POST request body transmission or uses encrypted request payloads for PII, it's FP.
If PII appears concatenated directly into URL strings in GET requests, it's TP.
If URL parameters contain only anonymized tokens or session IDs (not raw PII), it's FP.

rules.name: Third-Party Ad Trackers
rules.description: Facebook Pixel, Google Analytics, or other ad trackers without child_directed_treatment flag
rules.fix_suggestion: Add "child_directed_treatment": true or "restrictDataProcessing": true to SDK initialization
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects integration of ad tracking SDKs (Facebook Pixel, Google Analytics, Mixpanel) without the child-directed treatment flag. Ad trackers create behavioral profiles and enable targeted advertising, which COPPA prohibits for children unless the child_directed flag is set to disable ad targeting.
tp_criteria: Code initializes Facebook Pixel (fbq('init')), Google Analytics (gtag or ga), or similar tracker without setting child_directed or consent parameter to true
Tracker SDK is configured to collect behavioral data (page views, clicks, conversions) without disabling ad personalization for children
Code passes user identifiers or PII to ad tracker SDKs without first verifying age or obtaining parental consent
fp_criteria: Code initializes tracker with child_directed flag explicitly set (e.g., 'gtag('consent', 'update', {'ad_personalization': 'denied'})' or 'fbq('dataProcessingOptions', [0])')
Tracker code is in a test file, mock library, or documentation example
Ad tracker is only loaded after age verification confirms user is 13+ and outside COPPA scope
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS child_directed flag or disables ad personalization for children, it's FP.
If tracker SDK initialization appears without any child-directed consent or flag setting, it's TP.
If tracker is conditionally loaded only after age gate confirmation (if userAge >= 13), it's FP.

rules.name: Precise Geolocation Collection
rules.description: High-accuracy geolocation without parental consent is prohibited
rules.fix_suggestion: Downgrade accuracy to kCLLocationAccuracyThreeKilometers or require parental consent
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects collection of precise geolocation data (GPS coordinates, cell tower triangulation) without parental consent. High-accuracy location data can enable tracking and physical targeting of children, violating COPPA privacy requirements.
tp_criteria: Code requests geolocation permission and uses coordinates with accuracy < 1km (e.g., navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition() without consent check)
GPS or high-precision location is collected and transmitted to server without prior parental consent verification
Location data is stored in user profiles or databases without encryption and without documented retention/deletion policy
fp_criteria: Code only uses coarse location (city/state level) or IP-based geolocation for non-tracking purposes (e.g., language selection)
Geolocation request includes consent prompt that requires parental email confirmation before data is collected
Geolocation code is in a parent/admin app section or behind age verification confirming 13+ status
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS parental consent verification before requesting geolocation, it's FP.
If geolocation is collected with high precision (GPS) without consent checks, it's TP.
If geolocation data is only used for coarse location purposes (city selection) and not transmitted to servers, it's FP.

Minified/bundled code containing geolocation API references (navigator.geolocation, getCurrentPosition, watchPosition, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION) is TP by default — if the minified code references geolocation, the unminified source uses it. Do NOT dismiss geolocation findings in minified code as 'unreadable' or 'infrastructure.' Exception: vendor mapping libraries (OpenLayers, Leaflet, Google Maps SDK) that reference geolocation internally but don't expose it to the app.

rules.name: Missing Data Lifecycle Management
rules.description: COPPA 2025 explicitly prohibits indefinite retention of children's PI. Operators must retain data only as long as reasonably necessary for the purpose collected. Schemas with PII fields must define retention periods, deletion mechanisms, and purpose limitation.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add explicit retention period (retentionDays, expiresAt, or TTL index), deleted_at column, and document the purpose limitation for data collection per COPPA 2025 § 312.10
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation (COPPA 2025 indefinite retention prohibition)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects child-directed applications that collect personally identifiable information but show no evidence of data lifecycle management — no deletion endpoints, no data purge mechanisms, no retention configuration, and no soft-delete patterns. COPPA Section 312.10 requires operators to retain children's personal information only as long as reasonably necessary to fulfill the purpose for which it was collected, and to delete it using reasonable measures. The 2025 amendments strengthen this with explicit retention limitation requirements.
tp_criteria: Application has database models storing children's PII (name, email, DOB) with created_at timestamps but NO deletion mechanism — no delete endpoint, no soft-delete column (deleted_at), no data purge/cleanup script, no retention configuration
Application collects children's PII and stores it indefinitely with no evidence of any data lifecycle management (no TTL, no archival, no scheduled cleanup, no admin delete functionality)
Application has user registration collecting children's information but the codebase contains zero file or function references to data deletion, purging, or retention policies
fp_criteria: Application implements any form of data deletion — soft delete (deleted_at column), hard delete endpoint, admin purge tool, scheduled cleanup job, or retention configuration
Application uses a framework or platform that provides built-in data lifecycle management (e.g., Firebase auto-delete rules, Supabase RLS with TTL)
Code is in a test file, migration script, or seed data that doesn't represent production data handling
rule_logic: The rule detects ABSENCE of deletion infrastructure, not PRESENCE of specific schema fields. A User model with email is not itself a violation — a User model with email and NO way to ever delete it is the concern.
If ANY deletion mechanism exists in the codebase (delete endpoint, purge script, soft-delete pattern), the rule should NOT fire.
This is a heuristic detector. It cannot determine whether an organization HAS a documented retention policy — only whether the code shows evidence of data lifecycle management.

rules.name: Unencrypted PII Transmission
rules.description: HTTP transmission of PII exposes data in transit. All API endpoints handling personal information must use HTTPS.
rules.fix_suggestion: Replace http:// with https:// for all API endpoints and resources
rules.penalty: Security breach liability + COPPA penalties

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects HTTP transmission of PII, which exposes data in transit to interception attacks. All API endpoints handling children's personal information must use HTTPS with TLS encryption to protect data confidentiality.
tp_criteria: API endpoint handling PII (email, password, phone, DOB) uses http:// protocol instead of https:// (e.g., 'http://api.example.com/register')
Code transmits authentication tokens or session cookies over HTTP without TLS encryption
Third-party API calls to send PII use unencrypted HTTP connection
fp_criteria: All PII transmission URLs use https:// protocol with valid TLS certificates
Code is in a local development environment (localhost) or test configuration that explicitly allows HTTP for testing only
API endpoint only receives non-PII data (e.g., anonymized analytics) over HTTP
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS or enforces HTTPS for all PII endpoints, it's FP.
If any PII is transmitted over HTTP without encryption, it's TP.
If HTTP is only used in test/development config and production config requires HTTPS, it's FP.

rules.name: Unauthorized Audio Recording
rules.description: Audio recording without explicit user consent is prohibited. COPPA 2.0 clarifies voice prints as biometric data.
rules.fix_suggestion: Wrap audio recording in click handler and add parental consent check
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects unauthorized audio recording without explicit user consent. COPPA 2.0 clarifies that voice prints and audio data are biometric information, and recording audio from children requires documented parental consent before activation.

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects forms and data collection flows that gather personally identifiable information from users in contexts likely directed at children, without evidence of a verifiable parental consent (VPC) flow. COPPA Section 312.5 requires operators to obtain VPC before collecting, using, or disclosing children's personal information. VPC methods include: signed consent form, credit card transaction, government ID verification, video conference, knowledge-based authentication, facial recognition, and email-plus (email to parent plus additional verification step).
tp_criteria: Registration or data collection form collects PII (email, name, DOB, phone) in an application directed to children under 13, with no evidence of a VPC flow (no parental consent screen, no age gate, no consent verification API call) anywhere in the codebase

Sign-up flow collects child's information and proceeds directly to account creation without any intermediate parental consent or notification step

Form is behind an age gate that blocks users under 13 or redirects them to a parental consent flow

Form is in an admin, teacher, or parent portal (not child-facing)

Do NOT require 'parent email in same form' as the only valid consent mechanism. COPPA allows 7+ VPC methods.
The school consent exception (§312.5(c)(3)) allows schools to consent on behalf of parents for educational purposes only. This is a valid FP.

rules.name: Biometric Data Collection
rules.description: COPPA 2025 explicitly adds biometric identifiers to the definition of PI. Face recognition, voice prints, gait analysis, behavioral biometrics (keystroke dynamics, mouse movement patterns), iris/pupil scanning, and health biometric APIs all require verifiable parental consent.
rules.fix_suggestion: Ensure biometric data remains local-only (on-device) or obtain verifiable parental consent per COPPA 2025. Do not transmit biometric identifiers to servers without separate parental consent.
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: COPPA 2025 expanded the definition of personal information to include biometric identifiers. This rule detects collection of face recognition, voice prints, gait analysis, keystroke dynamics, mouse movement patterns, iris scanning, or health biometric APIs without documented verifiable parental consent. Biometric data is permanent and cannot be changed like passwords, making it critical to protect.
tp_criteria: Code calls biometric APIs (FaceAPI, tf.js face detection, voice.js, keystroke dynamics, fingerprint.js) and processes the output without explicit parental consent check
Biometric data (face vectors, voice embeddings, keystroke patterns, gait signatures) is stored in database or sent to third-party service
No conditional logic gates the biometric collection behind a parental consent flag (e.g., consentStatus === 'parental_approved')
fp_criteria: Biometric code is in documentation, README, or comment-only examples (not executable)
Code imports a biometric library but never calls any collection/processing method (import FaceAPI from 'face-api' with no usage)
Biometric feature is behind a strict 13+ age gate that prevents any user under 13 from reaching the code path
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS parental consent verification before any biometric processing (e.g., if (!user.parentalConsent) return), it's FP
Keystroke dynamics, mouse tracking, and behavioral biometrics used only for fraud detection on adult-only payment flows (age >= 18) are FP; same patterns in child-facing views are TP
Health biometric APIs (heart rate, fitness trackers, medical device SDKs) without parental consent are TP even if intended for wellness features

rules.name: Manipulative Push Notification Patterns
rules.description: FTC declined to codify push notification restrictions in the 2025 final rule but stated it 'remains concerned about push notifications and other engagement techniques.' Best practice: gate push subscriptions behind parental consent. Maps to NGL Labs and Sendit enforcement patterns.
rules.fix_suggestion: Gate push notification subscription behind parental dashboard setting
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects push notification patterns that may be manipulative or deceptive when used in child-directed applications. While push notifications are not explicitly prohibited by COPPA, the FTC has taken enforcement action against manipulative notification practices targeting minors (NGL Labs, 2024 — $5M settlement for sending fake notifications to drive engagement). Push notification tokens may qualify as persistent identifiers under §312.2, but the §312.5(c)(7) internal operations exception covers functional notifications (e.g., app updates, security alerts). This rule flags notification patterns that appear designed to manipulate engagement rather than serve a functional purpose.
tp_criteria: Push notification content is dynamically generated to create false urgency or social pressure (e.g., fake friend requests, fake messages, countdown timers for limited offers)
Push notification scheduling uses engagement-maximizing patterns targeting children (e.g., notifications during school hours, escalating frequency when user hasn't opened app)
Push notification registration occurs without any user awareness or opt-in mechanism, and the app is directed at children
fp_criteria: Push notifications are functional — app updates, security alerts, assignment reminders in educational apps, parental notifications
Push notification registration includes clear opt-in UI with description of what notifications will contain
Notification frequency is reasonable and content is non-manipulative (e.g., daily digest, weekly summary)
rule_logic: Push notifications are NOT per se prohibited by COPPA. The legal concern is MANIPULATIVE use targeting children, not notification functionality itself.
The §312.5(c)(7) internal operations exception covers push tokens used for functional purposes (site maintenance, contextual advertising, frequency capping).
This is an ETHICAL best practice rule, not a hard COPPA compliance requirement. Severity should be LOW.

knowledge.regulatory_source: No direct COPPA provision. FTC enforcement precedent: NGL Labs consent order (2024). §312.2 persistent identifier definition may apply to push tokens. §312.5(c)(7) internal operations exception covers functional use.

rules.name: Missing Cookie Notice
rules.description: Cookies or localStorage storing tracking data or PII requires a consent banner
rules.fix_suggestion: Add a cookie consent banner component before setting tracking or PII cookies
rules.penalty: Compliance warning

knowledge.plain_description: Cookies or localStorage storing tracking data, analytics IDs, or PII must be disclosed in a privacy notice and consent banner. COPPA and GDPR both require transparent communication about tracking. Even 'essential' cookies should be documented if they store identifiable information like user IDs or timestamps linked to a profile.
tp_criteria: Code calls document.cookie, localStorage.setItem(), or sessionStorage.setItem() to store data (user ID, email, session token, advertising ID) without a preceding consent check
Tracking cookies (e.g., _ga, _fbp, analytics token) are set on page load before any user consent interaction
A cookie consent banner or privacy notice exists elsewhere in the codebase but is not checked before the cookie/storage write

Code calls a consent check function (if (!user.cookieConsent) return) before any document.cookie or localStorage write
Cookie/localStorage code is in test mocks, vendor SDK documentation, or dead code only
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a consent gate (e.g., if (consentManager.hasConsent('cookies')) before setItem()), it's FP
Cookies marked as 'HttpOnly' and 'Secure' used only for session management with no tracking or PII may be FP; any tracking or PII-bearing cookie without consent notice is TP
localStorage.setItem() in child-app context without consent check is TP; same code in adult-app context (age >= 18 verified) is FP

In a children's app, ANY direct cookie/localStorage manipulation (document.cookie =, localStorage.setItem) without an adjacent consent check is TP — even if the code looks like a generic utility. The violation is the ABSENCE of consent, not the presence of tracking. Exception: if the code IS a consent implementation (cookie-law, cookieconsent library) or sets auth/CSRF tokens, it's FP.

rules.name: Missing External Link Warning (Best Practice)
rules.description: External links in child-facing views should trigger a "You are leaving..." modal
rules.fix_suggestion: Wrap external links in SafeLink component with warning modal
rules.penalty: Warning

knowledge.plain_description: External links in child-facing views should warn children they are leaving the safe environment. This is a best practice recommended by CARU Self-Regulatory Guidelines and the kidSAFE Seal Program. It is NOT required by COPPA (16 CFR Part 312) or any federal regulation. Apps seeking CARU or kidSAFE certification should implement transition warnings; apps seeking only COPPA compliance are not required to do so.
tp_criteria: Child-facing UI contains hyperlinks or buttons that navigate to external domains without any transition warning or interstitial
App targets children under 13 AND is pursuing CARU or kidSAFE certification AND lacks exit warnings
External link opens in the same webview without any indication the child has left the app's controlled environment
fp_criteria: App is not directed to children under 13
External link opens in system browser (provides natural transition break)
App implements any form of transition warning, even minimal (e.g., 'You are leaving [App Name]')
rule_logic: This is a VOLUNTARY best practice, not a legal requirement. Severity should always be LOW.
If the app is not seeking CARU or kidSAFE certification, this is purely advisory.
The absence of exit warnings is NOT a COPPA violation under any interpretation.
