rules.name: Mapping PII to Analytics User IDs
rules.description: Passing email, name, or phone to analytics.identify() exposes PII to third parties
rules.fix_suggestion: Hash user ID and omit email/name from analytics payload
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: Passing email, full name, phone number, or other PII to analytics.identify() or segment.track() exposes that PII to third-party analytics vendors. Under COPPA, even if parental consent exists, PII should not be shared with third parties for behavioral analytics. This rule flags code that sends identifying information to analytics platforms.
tp_criteria: Code calls analytics.identify(), segment.identify(), mixpanel.identify(), or similar with a user ID parameter that includes email, phone, or full name as the identifier or in traits
User PII (email, name, phone) is passed as properties in analytics.track() or event() calls without anonymization or hashing
A condition checks for parental consent but does not prevent PII from being sent to analytics (e.g., consent gate exists but PII is still in identify() call)
fp_criteria: Code passes only an anonymized user ID (UUID, internal user_id integer) to analytics, not email or name
Code implements a check (if (user.parentalConsent === false) return) before calling analytics.identify() with any PII
Analytics code is in test mocks, documentation, or dead code only; not called in production
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS PII hashing or anonymization before analytics.identify() (e.g., identify(sha256(email))), it's FP
Passing userId (internal numeric ID) to analytics is FP; passing email as identifier is TP
If the code IMPLEMENTS a feature flag that disables analytics.identify() in child-app builds, it's FP

tp_examples.explanation: TP: Open edX CMS directly maps user email and username to Segment analytics.identify() call. This sends PII (email address, username) to a third-party analytics platform (Segment) as user traits linked to the user ID. Open edX is used for educational platforms including those serving minors. Per 16 CFR 312.2, email addresses are personal information, and mapping them to analytics user IDs enables cross-site tracking of children.

tp_examples.code:
traits = {
                'email': user.email,
                'username': user.username,
                'name': profile.name,
                'age': profile.age or -1,
                'yearOfBirth': profile.year_of_birth or datetime.now(ZoneInfo("UTC")).year,
                'education': profile.level_of_education_display,
                'address': profile.mailing_address,
                'gender': profile.gender_display,
                'country': str(profile.country),
                'is_marketable': False
            }
            # .. pii: Many pieces of PII are sent to Segment here.
            # .. pii_types: email_address, username
            # .. pii_retirement: third_party
            segment.identify(user.id, traits)
tp_examples.explanation: TP: Open edX backend sends extensive PII to Segment analytics including email, username, full name, age, year of birth, mailing address, gender, and country. The code's own comments acknowledge this is PII ('pii_types: email_address, username'). Year of birth and age are particularly sensitive for COPPA as they can identify children under 13. Per 16 CFR 312.2 and 312.3, this constitutes collection of personal information from children when the platform serves minors.

tp_examples.code:
const trialRequestIdentifyData = _.pick(
            this.trialRequest.attributes.properties,
            ['siteOrigin', 'marketingReferrer', 'referrer', 'notes',
             'numStudentsTotal', 'numStudents', 'purchaserRole', 'role',
             'phoneNumber', 'country', 'state', 'city', 'district',
             'organization', 'nces_students', 'nces_name', 'nces_id',
             'nces_phone', 'nces_district_students',
             'nces_district_schools', 'nces_district_id', 'nces_district']
          )
          application.tracker.identifyAfterNextPageLoad()
          return globalVar.application.tracker.identify(trialRequestIdentifyData)
tp_examples.explanation: TP: CodeCombat's teacher signup sends PII including phone number, city, state, district, and organization name to analytics via tracker.identify(). While this is for teacher accounts (not students), the data includes school district identifiers (nces_id, nces_phone) that could indirectly identify student populations. Per 16 CFR 312.3(c), operators of child-directed sites must provide notice of all data collection including from adult users when it relates to children's educational services.

fp_examples.explanation: FP: CodeCombat's student auth module calls tracker.identify() without passing any PII arguments. The identify call with no arguments typically syncs the current anonymous user state without mapping email or name to the analytics ID. The isSmokeTestUser check also shows awareness of test data exclusion. No PII is directly passed in this call.

FP: CodeCombat's BasicInfoView calls tracker.identify() without explicit PII parameters. The identify() call with no arguments relies on the tracker's internal state rather than directly passing email/name. Additionally, smoke test users are explicitly excluded. The PII (email) is used only for the isSmokeTestUser check, not passed to the tracker.

FP: Element Web's Posthog analytics uses an anonymous analytics_id string (not PII like email or name) for user identification. The identifier is generated via a callback function that returns an opaque string, not mapped to any personal information. This is the COPPA-compliant pattern of using anonymous/hashed identifiers for analytics.

knowledge.regulatory_source: 16 CFR §312.5(a)(2) — Separate VPC when PI disclosed to third parties for analytics/advertising.

legal_council.method: 3-perspective legal council (FTC Enforcer + Compliance Officer + Defense Counsel)

rules.name: Missing Teacher/School Verification
rules.description: Teacher accounts using generic email (@gmail.com) bypass "School Official" consent exception
rules.fix_suggestion: Restrict teacher sign-ups to verified EDU domains or require manual approval
rules.penalty: Loss of School Official consent status

knowledge.plain_description: Teacher accounts using generic email domains (@gmail.com, @yahoo.com, @outlook.com) cannot benefit from the COPPA 'School Official' exception, which allows schools to collect parental consent. Only accounts with school-issued domain emails (@schoolname.edu) or verified by school administrator records qualify as 'School Officials.' Generic email teacher accounts may be adults collecting data on children without proper authorization.
tp_criteria: Code creates teacher or school official accounts and accepts any email domain without domain verification (@gmail.com, @yahoo.com accounts accepted)
Teacher role is assigned based on email alone without checking against a school domain whitelist or admin verification
No verification mechanism (OAuth with school directory, admin approval queue) validates that the teacher is actually employed by the school
fp_criteria: Code implements email domain verification (e.g., if (!email.endsWith('@school.edu')) reject) before approving teacher accounts
Teacher accounts require admin approval from a verified school account before activation
Code uses OAuth or SAML login with a school directory service (Google Workspace, Clever, ClassLink) that auto-verifies school affiliation
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a whitelist of approved school domains (ALLOWED_DOMAINS = ['school.edu', 'district.edu']) and rejects other domains, it's FP
If teacher role requires admin verification (role !== 'teacher' until admin approves), it's FP; auto-approval of any @gmail teacher is TP
Teacher accounts with optional domain verification (verification suggested but not required) are TP; same with required verification are FP

tp_examples.explanation: TP: Teacher role panel accepts self-declared role and numStudents without any institutional verification. A user simply selects 'teacher' from a dropdown and enters student count to gain teacher privileges. No school email verification, no SSO through Clever/ClassLink, no DPA signature required. Under COPPA 16 CFR 312.5(b)(4), school context requires verified institutional authorization.

TP: CreateTeacherAccountView allows anyone to create a teacher account via a simple signup form. The TrialRequest model captures self-reported school data (district, NCES fields) but these are used for CRM purposes, not verification. No school admin approval, no institutional email domain check, no signed DPA required before gaining access to student management features.

tp_examples.code:
const getDefaultState = () => {
  return {
    trialRequestProperties: _.assign(ncesData, {
      organization: '',
      district: '',
      city: '',
      state: '',
      country: '',
      role: '',
      purchaserRole: '',
      numStudents: '',
      numStudentsTotal: '',
      notes: '',
      referrer: '',
      marketingReferrer: '',
      siteOrigin: 'create teacher',
    }),
tp_examples.explanation: TP: The teacher signup store captures organization, district, and role as free-text self-declared fields. NCES school data (district_id, district_schools) is used for auto-complete suggestions but not for verification. A user can type any organization name and claim any role to access the teacher dashboard and student management, without institutional verification required by COPPA for school-context data access.

fp_examples.explanation: FP: CodeCombat/Ozaria supports Clever SSO for student signup. Clever is a verified institutional identity provider that requires school districts to sign Data Processing Agreements before enabling SSO. Students authenticated through Clever have verified school context, satisfying COPPA's school verification requirement under 16 CFR 312.5(b)(4).

FP: CodeCombat integrates ClassLink SSO, another verified institutional identity provider used by K-12 school districts. ClassLink integration requires district-level administrative setup and data sharing agreements, providing verified school context that satisfies COPPA's requirement for institutional authorization.

FP: The User schema stores cleverID and edLinkID (ClassLink) as verified institutional identity fields alongside generic OAuth identities. When these fields are populated, the user was authenticated through a verified school SSO provider with a signed DPA, providing the institutional verification COPPA requires for school-context access.

knowledge.regulatory_source: COPPA applies alongside FERPA in ed-tech. FTC enforcement: Edmodo (2023). FTC Ed-Tech Policy Statement (2022). .edu domain check is factually wrong for K-12.

legal_council.method: 3-perspective legal council (FTC Enforcer + Compliance Officer + Defense Counsel)

rules.name: Default Public Profile Visibility
rules.description: Default profile visibility must be private. COPPA 2.0 requires privacy by design.
rules.fix_suggestion: Change default visibility to "private" or false
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation

knowledge.plain_description: COPPA 2.0 mandates privacy by design: user profiles must default to private visibility, not public. A public default profile exposes child information (name, photo, location hints, friend lists) to strangers and search engines. Changing default visibility to private ensures children cannot accidentally share sensitive information before understanding the consequences.
tp_criteria: Code initializes new user profiles with visibility: 'public' or does not set visibility, leaving it public by database default
Profile visibility is not checked or enforced at profile creation; public visibility is the database schema default
A privacy setting exists in the UI to change profile visibility but defaults to public if not explicitly changed
fp_criteria: Code explicitly sets visibility: 'private' on all new profile creation (e.g., profiles.visibility = 'private')
Database schema defines visibility with a default value of 'private' in the table definition
Profile visibility is enforced by a middleware or guard function that blocks public rendering unless visibility === 'public'
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a profile creation function that sets visibility = 'private' before INSERT, it's FP
If the database schema includes DEFAULT 'private' in the visibility column definition, it's FP; DEFAULT 'public' is TP
If profile rendering includes a check (if (profile.visibility !== 'public') return 404) before showing profile to non-owner users, it's FP; absence of this check with public default is TP

tp_examples.code:
ACCOUNT_VISIBILITY_CONFIGURATION = {
    # Default visibility level for accounts without a specified value
    # The value is one of: 'all_users', 'private'
    "default_visibility": "all_users",

    # The list of account fields that are always public
    "public_fields": [
        'account_privacy',
        'profile_image',
        'username',
    ],
}
tp_examples.explanation: TP: Open edX sets default_visibility to 'all_users' meaning all user profiles (including potential minors in educational contexts) are visible to all other users by default. Profile image and username are always public with no consent check. Per COPPA 2.0 (16 CFR 312.2), making a child's profile image and username publicly visible by default constitutes disclosure of personal information without parental consent. The default should be 'private' in child-directed educational platforms.

tp_examples.code:
ACCOUNT_VISIBILITY_CONFIGURATION["bulk_shareable_fields"] = (
    ACCOUNT_VISIBILITY_CONFIGURATION["public_fields"] + [
        'bio',
        'course_certificates',
        'country',
        'date_joined',
        'language_proficiencies',
        "level_of_education",
        'social_links',
        'time_zone',
    ]
)
tp_examples.explanation: TP: When Open edX's default 'all_users' visibility is active, these additional fields become visible to all users: bio, country, date_joined, level_of_education, and social_links. Country and level of education combined with username can identify children. Social links exposure is particularly concerning as it can reveal a child's presence on other platforms. Per 16 CFR 312.4(b), the operator must provide notice of what PI is made public.

tp_examples.code:
course_visibility = String(
        display_name=_("Course Visibility For Unenrolled Learners"),
        help=_(
            "Defines the access permissions for unenrolled learners. This can be set to one of three values: "
            "'private' (default visibility, only allowed for enrolled students), 'public_outline' "
            "(allow access to course outline) and 'public' (allow access to both outline and course content)."
        ),
        default=COURSE_VISIBILITY_PRIVATE,
        scope=Scope.settings,
    )
tp_examples.explanation: FP: Open edX's course visibility defaults to PRIVATE — unenrolled learners cannot see course content by default. This is the correct privacy-by-default approach per 16 CFR 312.8 (data minimization). Course administrators must explicitly choose 'public' or 'public_outline' to make content visible. This contrasts with the account visibility setting which defaults to 'all_users'.

fp_examples.explanation: FP: The client-side UserPreferencesModel in Open edX defaults account_privacy to 'private'. This shows the frontend model's default is privacy-protective. However, this is overridden by the server-side ACCOUNT_VISIBILITY_CONFIGURATION which sets default_visibility to 'all_users'. The client default of 'private' is the correct COPPA-compliant pattern, even though it's overridden server-side.

fp_examples.code:
course_visibility = String(
        default=COURSE_VISIBILITY_PRIVATE,
        scope=Scope.settings,
        values=[
            {"display_name": "private", "value": COURSE_VISIBILITY_PRIVATE},
            {"display_name": "public_outline", "value": COURSE_VISIBILITY_PUBLIC_OUTLINE},
            {"display_name": "public", "value": COURSE_VISIBILITY_PUBLIC},
        ],
    )
fp_examples.explanation: FP: Open edX course visibility defaults to PRIVATE and provides explicit visibility controls with three clearly labeled options. Administrators must actively choose to make courses public. This is a privacy-by-design pattern with explicit visibility selection and consent, compliant with 16 CFR 312.8's requirement that default settings minimize data exposure.

fp_examples.code:
ACCOUNT_VISIBILITY_PREF_KEY = 'account_privacy'

ALL_USERS_VISIBILITY = 'all_users'
PRIVATE_VISIBILITY = 'private'
CUSTOM_VISIBILITY = 'custom'

VISIBILITY_PREFIX = 'visibility.'
fp_examples.explanation: FP: Open edX defines three visibility levels (all_users, private, custom) with a custom option allowing granular field-level control. The existence of PRIVATE_VISIBILITY and CUSTOM_VISIBILITY constants shows the platform supports privacy-protective profile settings. Users can choose per-field visibility, which is the gold standard for COPPA compliance. The issue is only that the server default is 'all_users' rather than 'private'.

knowledge.regulatory_source: 16 CFR §312.3 — Unfair/deceptive practices. No 'privacy by design' mandate in COPPA. Public profile defaults may constitute unauthorized disclosure under §312.5.

legal_council.method: 3-perspective legal council (FTC Enforcer + Compliance Officer + Defense Counsel)

rules.name: Targeted Advertising Without Separate Consent
rules.description: COPPA 2025 requires separate, specific opt-in consent before collecting children's PI for targeted advertising. Marketing consent cannot be bundled with general terms acceptance. Ad SDK initialization without a distinct consent flow is a violation.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement a separate, specific opt-in consent flow for advertising before initializing ad SDKs. Marketing consent must NOT be bundled with general terms acceptance. Use age-gated ad experiences or contextual-only advertising for children under 13.
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation (COPPA 2025 separate advertising consent requirement)

knowledge.plain_description: COPPA 2025 requires separate, explicit opt-in consent before collecting children's personal information for targeted advertising purposes. This rule detects when ad SDKs are initialized or ad targeting is configured without a distinct consent flow that is separate from general terms acceptance. Bundling ad targeting consent into blanket acceptance or initializing ad tracking without any consent mechanism violates COPPA requirements.
tp_criteria: Ad SDK (Google Ads, Facebook Ads, etc.) is initialized with user targeting parameters (age, interests, location) before any consent dialog is shown or without checking for separate ad-specific consent flag
Code sets advertising-related parameters (setUserId, setUserData, custom audiences) without first confirming a distinct ad-targeting consent has been obtained
Ad network targeting is enabled through the same consent mechanism as general ToS acceptance, with no separate step for advertising-specific consent
fp_criteria: Ad SDK is imported or declared but not initialized with targeting data, or initialization is wrapped in a conditional that checks for explicit ad-targeting consent flag
Code is in a test file, mock implementation, or documentation example (e.g., commented code showing 'how NOT to do it')
Ad SDK is configured with child_directed_treatment=true or equivalent flag that explicitly disables all targeting before any user data is passed
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a separate consent dialog specifically for targeted advertising (distinct from general ToS) and gates all ad personalization behind this consent check, it's FP
If ad SDKs are initialized with ANY targeting parameters (custom user IDs, audiences, behavioral data) without prior consent verification, it's TP
If the code uses a blanket 'Accept All' pattern that includes marketing consent without a separate ad-targeting consent step, it's TP

tp_examples.explanation: TP: Facebook Pixel SDK initialized in a child-directed coding platform (CodeCombat). While students are excluded via isStudent check, the platform is child-directed overall and the exclusion is role-based rather than age-verified parental consent. No separate verifiable parental consent (VPC) mechanism for behavioral advertising under 16 CFR 312.5(a)(2). The fbq('init') call enables behavioral tracking before any consent verification.

tp_examples.code:
export default class Tracker2 extends BaseTracker {
  constructor (store) {
    super()
    this.store = store
    this.cookieConsentTracker = new CookieConsentTracker(this.store)
    this.internalTracker = new InternalTracker(this.store)
    this.googleAnalyticsTracker = new GoogleAnalyticsTracker(this.store)
    this.fullStoryTracker = new FullStoryTracker(this.store, this)
    this.facebookPixelTracker = new FacebookPixelTracker(this.store)
    this.twitterPixelTracker = new TwitterPixelTracker(this.store)
    this.zendeskTracker = new ZendeskTracker(this.store)
    this.superflowTracker = new SuperflowTracker(this.store)
tp_examples.explanation: TP: CodeCombat initializes multiple ad/behavioral tracking SDKs (Facebook Pixel, Google Analytics, FullStory session replay, Twitter Pixel) as a bundle in its top-level tracker. These enable behavioral profiling across a child-directed educational platform. While China users are excluded, there is no separate parental consent mechanism for behavioral advertising per 16 CFR 312.5(a)(2). FullStory session replay is particularly concerning as it records all user interactions.

TP: Google Analytics 4 initialized on Code.org, a platform explicitly directed at children (K-12 education). GA4 is configured with userAnalyticsDimensions which may include user-level data. While GA4 can be configured for COPPA compliance, no child_directed_treatment flag or consent check is visible in this initialization. Per 16 CFR 312.5(a)(2), behavioral analytics on child-directed sites require separate verifiable parental consent.

fp_examples.explanation: FP (borderline): The same FacebookPixelTracker explicitly disables tracking for students (isStudent check) and removes the tracking script entirely for student users. This demonstrates a role-based consent gate that prevents behavioral advertising for the student population. The script removal is a strong privacy protection. However, note this is FP only in the context of the student-exclusion branch — the overall file is still a TP when considering the init path.

FP: The trackEvent method respects doNotTrack and disableAllTracking flags before sending any data to Facebook. It also strips PII (email, name) from properties before sending via mapToFbProperties. The consent revocation mechanism (fbq('consent', 'revoke')) provides user-level opt-out. These are privacy-protective measures that reduce COPPA risk.

FP (borderline): The trackEvent method passes only category and action names to GA4 without directly including PII. The event tracking pattern (tracking UI actions like button clicks) is standard non-behavioral analytics. Code.org uses OneTrust consent management (visible in their codebase) which provides cookie consent gating before GA4 loads, making this a weaker finding.

knowledge.regulatory_source: 16 CFR §312.5(a)(2) (2025) — Separate VPC for targeted advertising. FTC stated ad disclosures are 'never integral to the purpose for which information was collected.'

legal_council.method: 3-perspective legal council (FTC Enforcer + Compliance Officer + Defense Counsel)

rules.name: Infinite Scroll / Endless Feed
rules.description: Infinite scroll exploits lack of impulse control. Children spend 2-3x longer on infinite feeds.
rules.fix_suggestion: Replace infinite scroll with pagination or "Load More" buttons to create natural stopping points. Suppress with .haloignore for admin/internal dashboards.
rules.penalty: Ethical Design Violation

knowledge.plain_description: Infinite scroll and endless feeds exploit children's developing impulse control by removing natural stopping points, causing them to spend 2-3x longer in the app. This rule detects pagination mechanisms that automatically load and append content without requiring explicit user action to fetch more. This is particularly harmful in children's applications where cognitive self-regulation is still developing.
tp_criteria: Feed/list implements auto-pagination that loads and renders additional content when user scrolls near the bottom, without requiring explicit button click or page navigation
Scroll event listener triggers data fetching and content rendering in an infinite loop without any max-item limit or 'end of feed' indicator
Content stream uses intersection observer or similar technique to detect viewport position and automatically load more items as user scrolls
fp_criteria: Pagination requires explicit user action (e.g., 'Load More' button that must be clicked) before new content is fetched
Code is in a test file or mock data demonstration for pagination components
App implements a hard stop with 'End of Results' message and prevents further loading after a reasonable content limit is reached
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS explicit 'Load More' buttons or pagination controls that require user action, it's FP even if infinite scroll is commented or disabled
If scroll-based content loading happens automatically as user approaches the end of current content, it's TP
Lazy loading for performance (loading images below the fold) is different from infinite feed pagination—flag only if new content items are added to the feed automatically

rules.name: Streak Pressure Mechanics
rules.description: Streak mechanics use loss aversion to manufacture daily compulsive usage
rules.fix_suggestion: Remove streak loss penalties. Frame progress as cumulative (e.g., "15 days practiced") rather than consecutive.
rules.penalty: Ethical Design Violation

knowledge.plain_description: Streak mechanics use loss aversion psychology to manufacture daily compulsive usage by punishing breaks in consecutive-day patterns. This rule detects systems that track consecutive user engagement (login streaks, daily challenges) and apply negative consequences for missing days. Children are particularly vulnerable to loss aversion, making this pattern manipulative.
tp_criteria: Code tracks consecutive-day engagement (login_streak, day_count, consecutive_sessions) and applies negative consequences (streak resets, point loss, badge removal) when user misses a day
UI prominently displays streak count and includes countdown or reminder notifications pushing users to maintain the streak
Code implements streak-preservation mechanics (e.g., 'use a streak freeze') only as a paid feature, making the punishment for missing days a monetization lever
fp_criteria: Code implements optional daily challenges or rewards but does NOT penalize users for missing days (e.g., rewards accumulate but don't reset)
Streak tracking exists but is purely informational (displayed only in profile stats) with no game mechanics tied to maintaining the streak
Code is in a test file or implements streak logic as a commented example for documentation purposes
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS streak rewards that accumulate without penalty for breaks (e.g., login each day for bonus points, but points don't reset), it's FP
If streak tracking directly causes gameplay consequences (stat resets, ability lockouts, progress loss) on missed days, it's TP
Distinguish between optional daily bonus programs (FP) and required-to-progress streaks that punish absence (TP)

rules.name: Variable Ratio Rewards (Loot Boxes)
rules.description: Randomized rewards (loot boxes, gacha) exploit gambling psychology in developing brains
rules.fix_suggestion: Replace random rewards with transparent, effort-based rewards. Disclosure of odds is a minimum requirement.
rules.penalty: Ethical Design Violation

knowledge.plain_description: Randomized reward systems (loot boxes, gacha mechanics, surprise rewards) exploit gambling psychology and variable-ratio reinforcement in developing brains. This rule detects code that implements probabilistic reward drops or randomized loot mechanics. Variable-ratio schedules are the most addictive behavioral pattern and are especially harmful to children whose impulse control and risk assessment are underdeveloped.
tp_criteria: Code implements randomized reward drops using Math.random(), probability checks, or weighted tables to determine if/what item user receives from an action
Gacha or loot box mechanics allow repeated pulls with randomized outcomes, with no guaranteed reward timeline (e.g., no pity system or guaranteed rarity increase)
Reward probabilities are hidden from users or only shown in small-print odds disclosures, with code containing internal probability tables not exposed in UI
fp_criteria: Rewards are deterministic and guaranteed (e.g., 'complete task X, always get reward Y') with no randomization involved
Code is in a test file or example implementation showing 'how reward randomization works' without actual game integration
Randomization applies only to cosmetic/non-gameplay elements (e.g., random colors or decorative items), not to gameplay progression or power mechanics
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS guaranteed progression systems with no randomness (e.g., 'pull 10 times, guaranteed 5-star on pull 10'), it's FP
If reward outcomes depend on random number generation with hidden or opaque probabilities, it's TP
Variable-ratio reinforcement (random rewards on random attempts) is the pattern to flag—fixed reward systems without randomization are FP

rules.name: Manipulative Notification Language
rules.description: User-facing strings using urgency language ("Hurry!", "Missing out") manipulate children's fear of social exclusion. Only flags text inside string literals or JSX content.
rules.fix_suggestion: Use neutral, informational language. Avoid FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out) triggers.
rules.penalty: Ethical Design Violation

knowledge.plain_description: Manipulative notification and UI text using urgency language ('Hurry!', 'Don't miss out!', 'Limited time!') exploits children's fear of social exclusion and missing out. This rule flags user-facing strings (in string literals, JSX text, localization keys) that use psychological manipulation tactics. Only text visible to users is flagged, not comments or internal variable names.
tp_criteria: Notification or UI text contains urgency/scarcity language (e.g., 'Hurry! Only 2 spots left!', 'Don't miss out on this amazing deal', 'Limited time offer ending soon') in string literals or JSX content
FOMO-triggering language references friends/social exclusion (e.g., 'Your friends are playing now!', 'Everyone else is getting this reward', 'See what you're missing') in user-visible text
Countdown timers are paired with manipulative copy (e.g., 'Offer expires in 2 hours—act now!') designed to pressure impulsive decisions
fp_criteria: Text is in code comments, documentation, or variable/function names (not user-visible)
Language is informational and factual (e.g., 'Sale ends on Friday') without urgency manipulation or emotional appeals
Code is in a test file or shows manipulative text as an example of 'what to avoid' with clear anti-patterns
rule_logic: If the manipulative text is ONLY in comments or variable names, not displayed to users, it's FP
If user-facing strings use urgency words (hurry, rush, limited, don't miss, act now, expires soon) paired with scarcity or social proof triggers, it's TP
Distinguish between informational copy ('Sale ends Friday') and manipulative copy ('Hurry! Offer expires in 2 hours—don't miss out!')

rules.name: Artificial Scarcity / Countdowns
rules.description: Fake scarcity ("Only 2 left!") and countdown timers pressure children into impulsive decisions
rules.fix_suggestion: Remove artificial urgency. If an offer expires, state the date calmly without countdown pressure. Suppress with .haloignore for non-commerce timers (quizzes, sessions, deploys).
rules.penalty: Ethical Design Violation

knowledge.plain_description: Artificial scarcity and countdown timers ('Only 2 left!', fake inventory counts, time-pressure mechanics) push children into impulsive purchasing or engagement decisions by exploiting time pressure and fear of losing out. This rule detects code that implements false or exaggerated scarcity claims and countdown timers tied to purchasing/reward mechanics. Children's impulse control makes them especially vulnerable.
tp_criteria: Code displays item stock/availability counts that are either fake (hardcoded), dynamically inflated, or intentionally misrepresented (e.g., 'Only 3 left!' resets hourly regardless of actual sales)
Countdown timers are tied to purchasing/reward claims (e.g., 'Offer expires in 1 hour') with no actual backend enforcement or expiration
Scarcity messaging uses comparative language (e.g., 'Only 2 of 100 remaining!') to create false urgency, with code showing the denominator is arbitrary or inflated
fp_criteria: Inventory counts reflect actual backend stock levels and are updated in real-time based on actual sales/availability
Countdown timers are informational only and don't pressure purchase decisions (e.g., 'Event starts in 2 hours' without sales copy)
Code is in a test or demo file showing scarcity mechanics as an educational/anti-pattern example
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS real inventory tracking and scarcity claims are backed by actual stock data, it's FP
If scarcity claims (stock counts, expiration times) are hardcoded, reset repeatedly, or not validated against real inventory, it's TP
Countdown timers paired with sales/purchase pressure are the target pattern—timers for informational events (game starts in X hours) are FP

rules.name: Placeholder Analytics Script
rules.description: AI-generated code frequently includes placeholder analytics (UA-XXXXX, G-XXXXXX, fbq) copied from training data. These may activate real tracking without child_directed_treatment flags.
rules.fix_suggestion: Remove placeholder analytics IDs. If analytics are needed, use a COPPA-compliant provider with child_directed_treatment: true.
rules.penalty: AI-generated compliance risk

knowledge.plain_description: AI-generated code frequently includes placeholder analytics tracking IDs (Google UA-XXXXX, GA4 G-XXXXXX, Facebook fbq) copied from training data patterns. These placeholders may be replaced with real tracking IDs in production without proper consent flows or child_directed_treatment flags, creating compliance gaps. This is particularly risky in children's apps where tracking consent is legally required.
tp_criteria: Code contains placeholder analytics ID patterns (UA-XXXXXXX, G-XXXXXXX, fbq('init') with no tracking ID, or obvious example IDs like 'UA-123456') that match common boilerplate
Analytics initialization code is present but uses generic/example configuration without child_directed_treatment flag or consent checks
Analytics script tags or initialization code are formatted exactly as they appear in AI training examples (e.g., generic Google Analytics boilerplate), suggesting copy-paste from training data
fp_criteria: Analytics IDs are real, environment-specific values (pulled from .env, config files, or build parameters) not placeholder patterns
Code includes explicit child_directed_treatment=true flag or consent check before analytics initialization
Analytics code is in a test/demo file with clear comments indicating it's a placeholder example
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS proper consent flow or uses child_directed_treatment flags before analytics initialization, the placeholder ID is still a risk (TP) but the consent layer mitigates it
If analytics IDs match training-data patterns (UA-123456, generic G-XXXXX) or are obvious placeholders (GA-placeholder), it's TP
Real tracking IDs that are environment-configured are FP—the issue is PLACEHOLDER IDs that may never be replaced

rules.name: AI-Generated Hardcoded Secrets
rules.description: AI coding assistants frequently generate placeholder API keys, tokens, and secrets inline. These may be committed to version control and exposed.
rules.fix_suggestion: Move all secrets to environment variables. Use process.env.API_KEY or a secrets manager. Never hardcode credentials.
rules.penalty: Security exposure — credentials in source code

knowledge.plain_description: AI coding assistants frequently generate placeholder API keys, tokens, and authentication secrets inline in code. These hardcoded secrets may be committed to version control and exposed if the code is published without review. In children's apps, exposed secrets could lead to unauthorized API access and data breaches of sensitive user information.
tp_criteria: Code contains hardcoded API key, token, or secret values (even if obviously fake) embedded as string literals (e.g., const apiKey = 'sk-XXXXXXXXXXXXX')
Secrets are generated with placeholder patterns (e.g., bearer tokens formatted as 'Bearer eyJhbGc...' or obvious fake values like 'super_secret_key_123')
Authentication credentials are defined inline in code files (not in environment variables, config files, or secrets management systems)
fp_criteria: Secrets are loaded from environment variables, .env files, or secrets management systems (e.g., process.env.API_KEY, config.getSecret())
Code is in documentation or example files with clear comments indicating these are placeholders for educational purposes
Hardcoded values are non-sensitive strings (e.g., API endpoints like 'https://api.example.com') not authentication credentials
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS environment variable loading or secrets management for credentials, it's FP
If any authentication token, API key, or password is hardcoded as a string literal, it's TP regardless of whether it looks 'fake'
Placeholder-looking secrets (obviously fake values) are STILL TP because they indicate AI copy-paste without proper security review

rules.name: Hallucinated/Placeholder API URLs
rules.description: AI models often generate fake API endpoints (api.example.com, jsonplaceholder, reqres.in) that may be replaced with real endpoints without proper review.
rules.fix_suggestion: Replace placeholder URLs with actual endpoints from environment variables. Review all API calls for COPPA data handling compliance.
rules.penalty: AI-generated placeholder risk

knowledge.plain_description: AI models frequently generate fake or hallucinated API endpoints (api.example.com, jsonplaceholder.typicode.com, reqres.in) that serve as placeholders in training data. When developers replace these with real endpoints, they may inadvertently skip security reviews or consent implementations. In children's apps, unvetted API endpoints could expose user data to third parties.
tp_criteria: Code references fake/placeholder API domains (jsonplaceholder.typicode.com, reqres.in, api.example.com, example.api.com) in fetch/axios/HTTP calls
API endpoints are hardcoded as string literals with no configuration or environment variables, suggesting they may never be replaced
Code fetches from 'example' or 'demo' domains that are obviously placeholders, with no production URL in comments or configuration
fp_criteria: API endpoints are loaded from environment variables or configuration files (not hardcoded), allowing for environment-specific URLs
Code is in a test file or has clear comments indicating it's a demo/placeholder (e.g., '// TODO: replace with real API endpoint')
Domains are legitimate first-party APIs (company's own domain) or well-known production services, not example/placeholder domains
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS environment-based endpoint configuration, even with placeholder defaults, it's lower risk (FP)
If hallucinated/placeholder API domains are hardcoded as the only endpoint reference, it's TP—this indicates unvetted third-party data flows
Example domains (.example.com, .test) and known placeholder services (jsonplaceholder, reqres) are the primary patterns to flag

rules.name: Copy-Paste Tracking Boilerplate
rules.description: AI assistants reproduce common analytics setup patterns from training data. These often include user identification, event tracking, and session recording without consent flows.
rules.fix_suggestion: Remove session recording and analytics initialization unless COPPA consent is obtained. These tools capture keystrokes, mouse movements, and user behavior — all PII for children.
rules.penalty: Third-party data collection without consent

knowledge.plain_description: AI assistants reproduce common analytics setup patterns from training data, including user identification, event tracking, session recording, and pixel firing. These boilerplate implementations often lack consent flows, child_directed_treatment flags, or privacy considerations. The code may activate real tracking systems without proper legal gating, creating COPPA/GDPR violations in children's apps.
tp_criteria: Code implements analytics event tracking (analytics.track(), gtag('event', ...), mixpanel.track()) with user identification (setUserId, setUserData) without prior consent checks
Session recording or heatmap tracking (Hotjar, Clarity, Session Replay) is initialized without checking for user consent or child_directed_treatment
Boilerplate analytics code includes multiple tracking platforms (GA, Facebook Pixel, custom event tracking) set up in standard patterns from AI training data, all firing without consent gates
fp_criteria: Analytics initialization is wrapped in consent checks (e.g., if (userConsent.analytics) { initializeAnalytics() }) or uses child_directed_treatment=true flag
Code is in a test/demo file with clear comments indicating it's a template or example
Tracking is limited to non-PII events (e.g., page views, feature usage) without user identification or personal data collection
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS consent checks before ANY analytics initialization (event tracking, user ID setting, session recording), it's FP
If analytics/tracking code runs without checking for user consent or COPPA flags, it's TP regardless of whether it's actual AI boilerplate
Multiple tracking platforms initialized together without consent gating is a strong signal of copy-paste boilerplate (TP)

rules.name: AI-Generated Insecure Defaults
rules.description: AI models commonly generate code with insecure default configurations: CORS *, disabled SSL verification, permissive CSP, or open CORS origins.
rules.fix_suggestion: Replace wildcard CORS with specific allowed origins. Enable SSL verification. Use restrictive CSP. Set secure cookies.
rules.penalty: Security misconfiguration

knowledge.plain_description: AI models often generate code with insecure default configurations like CORS set to accept all origins (*), disabled SSL/TLS verification, overly permissive Content Security Policy headers, or unrestricted CORS settings. This matters because these defaults expose applications to cross-site attacks, man-in-the-middle threats, and unauthorized data access if not explicitly hardened.
tp_criteria: Code explicitly sets CORS origins to '*' or equivalent wildcard without conditional logic based on environment
SSL/TLS certificate verification is actively disabled (e.g., rejectUnauthorized: false, verify: false) in production-path code
CSP headers are defined with unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval, or * for script-src/style-src without environment-conditional overrides
fp_criteria: Configuration is inside test files, fixtures, or mock server setup (*.test.js, *.spec.js, /tests/, /mocks/)
Insecure defaults are wrapped in explicit environment checks (if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development')) that prevent production deployment
Code is in documentation, comments, or configuration examples marked as 'example only' or 'do not use in production'
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS environment-aware configuration that uses secure defaults in production and relaxed settings only for local development, it's FP.
If the insecure default is set inside a conditional block that explicitly prevents it from reaching production (e.g., development-only middleware), it's FP.

rules.name: Unresolved Compliance TODOs
rules.description: AI-generated code often includes TODO/FIXME comments for compliance-related features (consent, age verification, privacy policy) that may ship unimplemented.
rules.fix_suggestion: Resolve all compliance-related TODOs before shipping. Each unresolved TODO is a potential COPPA violation in production.
rules.penalty: Unimplemented compliance requirement

knowledge.plain_description: AI-generated code frequently includes TODO or FIXME comments for unimplemented compliance features like age verification gates, consent flows, privacy policy displays, or parental controls. This matters because unresolved compliance TODOs can ship to production with critical safety or regulatory features missing, creating liability and user harm.
tp_criteria: A TODO/FIXME comment references a compliance feature (age verification, consent, privacy policy, parental control) in code that is not commented out and appears to be in main execution path
The referenced compliance feature is absent from the codebase — searching related modules/functions shows no implementation of the stated requirement
The TODO is on a line or block that handles user data, account creation, or feature access without the stated guard in place
fp_criteria: The TODO/FIXME is inside a fully commented-out code block or dead code section
The compliance feature referenced in the TODO is already implemented elsewhere in the codebase (e.g., 'TODO: add age check' but age checking exists in a different module that's called)
The TODO is in test code, documentation, or a template file marked as non-executable example
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS the compliance feature mentioned in the TODO (even if not yet integrated), it's FP — verify the feature exists before flagging.
If the TODO is in commented-out or test-only code, it's FP; only flag TODOs in active execution paths.

rules.name: Default Public Profile Visibility
rules.description: User profiles default to public or visible. AU Safety by Design requires privacy-by-default for minors — profiles should be private until explicitly changed by the user or a verified parent.
rules.fix_suggestion: Set profile visibility to "private" by default. Require explicit user action (or parental consent for children) to make profiles public. AU SbD Principle 1: safety as a fundamental design consideration.
rules.penalty: Default public exposure of minor profiles

knowledge.plain_description: User profiles are configured to be publicly visible or discoverable by default, without requiring explicit opt-in from the user or parent. AU Safety by Design requires privacy-by-default, especially for minors — profiles should start as private and only become public if the user actively changes their privacy settings.
tp_criteria: User profile visibility is set to 'public' or 'visible' in the database schema default value or account creation function without checking user age or parental status
Profile data (name, avatar, bio, follower list) is returned in API endpoints accessible to unauthenticated users by default, with no age gate or privacy check
Profile discovery features (search, recommendations, directory listings) include profiles of minor accounts without a privacy setting override or age-gating mechanism
fp_criteria: Profile visibility defaults to 'private' in the schema and requires explicit user action to change to public
Code is in a test fixture or seed script marked as development-only
The code implements age detection and applies 'private-by-default' only to minor accounts while allowing adults' public defaults
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-aware defaults where minors' profiles default to private and adults' can default to public, it's FP.
If profile visibility is explicitly set to private in schema defaults and requires user confirmation to become public, it's FP.

rules.name: Social Features Without Report/Block
rules.description: Social interaction features (comments, posts, messaging) detected without corresponding report or block mechanisms. AU SbD Principle 2 requires users to have tools to protect themselves from harmful interactions. Excludes window.postMessage (IPC) and admin/internal contexts.

patterns.pattern: (?!.*(?:interface |type |implements |extends |PropTypes|\.d\.ts|@types\/|declare |abstract |readonly |generic |<T>|<T,))(?!.*(?:\?: |: string|: number|: boolean|: any|: void|: never|: unknown|Promise<|Array<|Record<|Partial<|Required<))(?:addComment|postComment|submitComment|createComment|commentCreate)\s*(?:=|:|\()

(?!.*(?:interface |type |implements |extends |PropTypes|\.d\.ts|@types\/|declare |abstract |readonly |generic |<T>|<T,))(?!.*(?:\?: |: string|: number|: boolean|: any|: void|: never|: unknown|Promise<|Array<|Record<|Partial<|Required<))(?<!window\.)(?:sendMessage|createMessage|submitMessage|messageCreate)\s*(?:=|:|\()

(?!.*(?:interface |type |implements |extends |PropTypes|\.d\.ts|@types\/|declare |abstract |readonly |generic |<T>|<T,))(?!.*(?:\?: |: string|: number|: boolean|: any|: void|: never|: unknown|Promise<|Array<|Record<|Partial<|Required<))(?:createPost|submitPost|publishPost|addPost|postCreate)\s*(?:=|:|\()

(?!.*(?:interface |type |implements |extends |PropTypes|\.d\.ts|@types\/|declare |abstract |readonly |generic |<T>|<T,))(?!.*(?:\?: |: string|: number|: boolean|: any|: void|: never|: unknown|Promise<|Array<|Record<|Partial<|Required<))(?:addReview|submitReview|createReview|postReview|reviewCreate)\s*(?:=|:|\()

(?!.*(?:interface |type |implements |extends |PropTypes|\.d\.ts|@types\/|declare |abstract |readonly |generic |<T>|<T,))(?!.*(?:\?: |: string|: number|: boolean|: any|: void|: never|: unknown|Promise<|Array<|Record<|Partial<|Required<))(?:shareContent|createShare|submitShare)\s*(?:=|:|\()

rules.fix_suggestion: Implement report and block mechanisms alongside every social feature. Users must be able to report harmful content and block abusive accounts. AU SbD Principle 2: user empowerment and autonomy.
rules.penalty: Social features without safety controls

knowledge.plain_description: Social interaction features (comments, posts, direct messaging, reactions) are implemented without corresponding moderation or safety tools like report and block mechanisms. AU Safety by Design Principle 2 requires users to have tools to protect themselves from harmful interactions. Excluding window.postMessage (inter-process communication) and admin/internal-only contexts.
tp_criteria: User-to-user interaction features (comments, posts, messages) exist in code but lack associated report or block endpoints/UI components
Interactions are stored and surfaced to other users with no mechanism to filter, hide, or report problematic content or users
The code handles social interactions outside of admin-only or internal-use-only contexts without safety controls (no permission checks limiting to staff)
fp_criteria: Code is in admin or staff-only modules (authenticated with admin role, within /admin/ path, or wrapped in admin permission checks)
The report/block mechanism is implemented in a separate module that is called or integrated by the interaction feature
Code is window.postMessage or other inter-process communication (IPC) without user-facing social interaction intent
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS report or block mechanisms for the social feature (even if in a separate module), it's FP — verify integration before flagging.
If the social feature is admin-only or internal-only (permission-gated), it's FP; only flag user-facing social features without safety tools.

rules.name: Unrestricted Direct Messaging for Minors
rules.description: Direct messaging or chat functionality without safety controls (contact restrictions, message filtering, or parental oversight). The AU Online Safety Act requires platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent child exploitation in private communications.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add safety controls to messaging: restrict contacts to approved friends, implement message filtering, enable parental oversight, and log communications for safety review. AU Online Safety Act 2021 s.45-46.
rules.penalty: Unrestricted private communication channel

knowledge.plain_description: Direct messaging or chat functionality allows unrestricted communication without safety controls like contact verification, message filtering, or parental oversight capabilities. The AU Online Safety Act requires platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent child exploitation in private communications, making controls essential for children's apps.
tp_criteria: Direct messaging or chat feature allows any authenticated user to initiate contact with any other user, including minors, without contact request review or parental notification
Messages are delivered and displayed without content filtering, keyword detection, or abuse flagging (no safety scanning)
Code implements messaging for minors without parental access, message history oversight, or contact restriction settings (no way for parents to limit who can message their child)
fp_criteria: Code implements contact approval workflows where recipients must accept contact requests before messaging is enabled
Messaging is restricted to verified mutual connections (e.g., friends must be added bidirectionally first)
Code implements message content filtering, known-exploit keyword detection, or automated abuse reporting for minor accounts
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS contact restriction, message filtering, or parental oversight for minor users, it's FP — verify all three are absent before flagging.
If the code requires bidirectional friend/contact verification before messaging is enabled, it's FP.

rules.name: Recommendation Algorithm Without Safety Guardrails
rules.description: Content recommendation or feed algorithms detected without safety filtering, content classification, or age-appropriate guardrails. AU SbD requires platforms to assess and mitigate algorithmic harms, particularly for young users.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add age-appropriate content filters to recommendation algorithms. Classify content before serving, implement safety guardrails, and provide transparency on how content is selected. AU SbD Principle 3: transparency and accountability.
rules.penalty: Unfiltered algorithmic content delivery

knowledge.plain_description: Content recommendation or algorithmic feed features serve content to users without safety filtering, age-appropriate content classification, or guardrails to prevent algorithmic harms. AU Safety by Design requires platforms to assess and mitigate algorithmic harms, particularly for young users who may be exposed to inappropriate or addictive content.
tp_criteria: Recommendation algorithm or feed logic selects and ranks content for display without content category checks, age-appropriateness filtering, or safety scoring
Algorithm serves identical content recommendations to minor and adult users without age-based content classification or filtering
Code includes engagement maximization (viral/trending ranking) without corresponding safety guardrails or content quality/safety thresholds
fp_criteria: Algorithm implements content classification (e.g., maturity labels, category tags) and filters recommendations based on user age or safety tier
Code includes explicit rules to exclude or demote harmful, explicit, or age-inappropriate content from recommendations
Recommendation logic is admin-only or test-only (test data, seed scripts, or internal tools with permission restrictions)
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-based content filtering or safety classification for recommendations, it's FP.
If the algorithm includes explicit guardrails to exclude harmful content categories (e.g., violent, sexual, hateful), it's FP — verify these are active for all users.

rules.name: Engagement Features Without Time Awareness
rules.description: High-engagement features (autoplay, continuous scrolling, notifications) detected without corresponding digital wellbeing controls (screen time limits, break reminders, usage dashboards). AU SbD encourages platforms to build in digital wellbeing tools.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement digital wellbeing features: screen time dashboards, break reminders after sustained use, and configurable usage limits (especially for accounts under 18). AU SbD: promote healthy technology use.
rules.penalty: Engagement-maximizing features without wellbeing controls

knowledge.plain_description: High-engagement features (autoplay, infinite/continuous scrolling, push notifications, gamification) are implemented without corresponding digital wellbeing controls like session time limits, break reminders, usage dashboards, or engagement throttling. AU Safety by Design encourages platforms to mitigate addictive design, especially for young users.
tp_criteria: Autoplay, continuous scrolling, or infinite-load features are enabled by default without user toggles, session limits, or throttling mechanisms
Push notification system sends notifications without frequency caps, quiet hours, or user-configurable limits (notifications can fire continuously)
App/site includes gamification (streaks, achievements, level progression) without break reminders, daily usage caps, or digital wellbeing dashboards
fp_criteria: Code implements user-configurable controls to disable autoplay, limit scrolling sessions, or cap notification frequency
Engagement features include break reminders, daily usage limits, or time-aware throttling (e.g., reduced notifications after 30 min usage)
Code is in test fixtures or mock implementations not exposed to real users
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS screen time limits, break reminders, or engagement throttling for high-engagement features, it's FP.
If engagement features are user-configurable or have built-in limits, it's FP — verify controls are actually active and not just suggested.

rules.name: Location Data Without Explicit Consent
rules.description: Location data collection or sharing enabled without explicit, informed opt-in. AU SbD and the Privacy Act 1988 require data minimization, especially for children's geolocation data — location should never be collected by default.
rules.fix_suggestion: Require explicit opt-in for any location data collection. Never enable location sharing by default. For minors, require parental consent before any geolocation access. AU Privacy Act 1988 APP 3.2.
rules.penalty: Default location data exposure

knowledge.plain_description: Location data is collected, stored, or shared without explicit, informed opt-in consent. AU Safety by Design and the Privacy Act 1988 require data minimization, especially for children's geolocation data — location should never be collected by default and requires clear, granular user consent.
tp_criteria: Location data (GPS, IP-based geolocation, or location history) is collected or accessed in background without prompting for explicit user consent first
Location data defaults to 'enabled' or 'shared' in user settings; users must actively opt out rather than opt in
Location data is shared with third parties (analytics, advertisers, other services) without separate explicit consent or disclosure of sharing
fp_criteria: Code prompts user for explicit opt-in permission before requesting location access (e.g., 'Allow location?' with clear yes/no options)
Location data collection is disabled by default; users must explicitly enable it in settings
Code is in a test or admin context with explicit permission gates, not user-facing
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS explicit opt-in consent flow for location access, it's FP.
If location is disabled by default and requires user action to enable, it's FP — verify the default is truly off and not overridden elsewhere.

rules.name: Minor Account Creation Without Age Assurance
rules.description: Utah SB 142 requires an age assurance system with at least 95% accuracy to identify minor account holders (under 18). Account creation flows that lack age verification gates violate this requirement. Excludes test factories and seed scripts.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add an age assurance step (date-of-birth collection, age estimation, or ID verification) before account creation. If the user is under 18, flag the account as a minor account and require parental consent before activation. See Utah SB 142 §13-72-201.
rules.penalty: Up to $2,500 per violation; private right of action for parents

knowledge.plain_description: Utah SB 142 requires social media platforms and app distributors to implement age assurance systems with at least 95% accuracy to identify minor account holders (users under 18). Account creation flows that lack this age verification gate or allow accounts to be created without age checking violate the statute. Excludes test factories and seed scripts.
tp_criteria: Account creation endpoint or flow does not call or implement an age assurance/verification function before account activation
Age verification is optional or can be skipped — users can complete signup without proving their age, even if an age gate UI exists
Age data is collected (e.g., birthdate input) but not validated against a 95%+ accuracy age assurance system (e.g., only client-side validation, no ID verification, no third-party age service)
fp_criteria: Code is in a test factory, test seed script, or development-only fixture marked as @test or in /tests/, /factories/, /seeds/
Account creation flow calls an age assurance verification function that requires proof of age (ID verification, knowledge-based questions, third-party service) before account is activated
Code implements a documented, auditable age assurance system that meets or exceeds 95% accuracy (e.g., integration with Prove, Socure, or similar certified provider)
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a call to a 95%+ accuracy age assurance service during account creation, it's FP — verify the verification is required, not optional.
If the code is a test factory or seed script (marked @test or in test paths), it's FP; only flag production account creation flows.

rules.name: Missing Parental Consent for Minor Account
rules.description: Utah SB 142 requires verifiable parental consent before a minor (under 18) can use a social media platform or download apps. Code that activates minor accounts without a parental consent verification step violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Before activating any minor account, implement a verifiable parental consent flow: send a verification email/SMS to a parent-linked account, require parental ID verification, or integrate with a COPPA-safe consent provider. See Utah SB 142 §13-72-202.
rules.penalty: Up to $2,500 per violation; private right of action for parents

knowledge.plain_description: Utah SB 142 requires verifiable parental consent before a minor (under 18) can use a social media platform or download apps. Account activation for minors must include a parental consent verification step. Code that activates minor accounts without this consent verification step violates the statute.
tp_criteria: Account creation flow activates a minor account (identified via age assurance or age input) without requiring parental consent verification
Parental consent is collected (e.g., parent email input) but not verified — code does not confirm the parent actually consented (no confirmation email, no callback, no attestation)
Minor account is given full access to the platform before parental consent is obtained, verified, or documented
fp_criteria: Code implements a parental consent verification flow that requires confirmed consent (e.g., parent email confirmation, SMS verification, ID verification) before minor account activation
Minor account access is restricted or limited until parental consent is verified (e.g., 'pending parent approval' state)
Code is in a test factory or development context, not in production account activation logic
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS verifiable parental consent before activating minor accounts, it's FP — verify the consent is actually confirmed, not just collected.
If minor account activation is blocked or restricted until parental consent is verified, it's FP.

rules.name: Default DM Access Open for Minors
rules.description: Utah SB 142 requires that direct messaging for minor accounts be restricted to connected accounts only by default. Code that enables open or unrestricted DM access for all users (including minors) violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Set default DM permissions for minor accounts to 'connected-only' or 'friends-only'. Only allow messaging between mutually connected accounts. Provide parental controls to further restrict messaging. See Utah SB 142 §13-72-301.
rules.penalty: Up to $2,500 per violation; private right of action for parents

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when a social platform allows minors to send direct messages to any user without connection requirements. Utah SB 142 requires DM access be restricted to pre-approved connections only, protecting minors from unsolicited contact by strangers.
tp_criteria: Code implements a DM send function that checks user age and allows messaging without verifying recipient is a connected/approved contact
Minor account DM settings default to 'accept from anyone' rather than 'connected accounts only'
Application logic permits minors to initiate DMs to arbitrary user IDs without connection validation
fp_criteria: Code is in a test suite simulating DM restrictions or connection validation
DM logic includes age-gating that restricts open DMs specifically for users under 18
Codebase is for an adult-only platform with no minor account support
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS recipient connection validation before allowing minors to send messages, it's FP
If the code CHECKS for age and applies stricter DM rules to minors, it's FP
If open DM access is only available to adult-classified accounts, it's FP

rules.name: Missing Parental Supervisory Tools
rules.description: Utah SB 142 requires platforms to offer parents supervisory tools: time limits, mandatory break scheduling, usage data viewing, connected account lists, and setting-change notifications. Applications that provide user accounts for minors without implementing or referencing a parental dashboard violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement a parental supervisory dashboard that allows parents to: set daily time limits, schedule mandatory breaks, view usage data and connected account lists, and receive notifications when account settings change. See Utah SB 142 §13-72-302.
rules.penalty: Up to $2,500 per violation; private right of action for parents

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects applications that support minor user accounts but lack parental oversight features. Utah SB 142 mandates parental dashboards with time limits, break scheduling, usage analytics, connection lists, and change notifications to give guardians control over their child's usage.
tp_criteria: Application creates minor accounts but has no parental dashboard or parent-accessible admin interface
Code defines minor account features (profiles, messaging, content) without any parent supervision mechanism referenced or implemented
System lacks features for time limits, break enforcement, usage reporting, or activity notifications that parents could access
fp_criteria: Code implements or references a parent/guardian dashboard with configurable time limits and usage reports
Application is adult-only with no minor account support pathway
Codebase is documentation or type definitions for a parental control API, not the main application
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a parent dashboard, supervisory APIs, or time-limit enforcement, it's FP
If parental oversight features are documented as planned or integrated via third-party service, it's FP
If the application explicitly excludes minors from using core features, it's FP

rules.name: Minor Profile Visible to Search Engines
rules.description: Utah SB 142 requires that minor accounts have search engine indexing disabled by default and account visibility restricted to connected users only. Code that allows public profile indexing or unrestricted profile visibility for all users violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Default minor accounts to non-indexable (noindex, nofollow) and restrict profile visibility to connected/approved users only. Add a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header that blocks search engine crawling for minor profiles. See Utah SB 142 §13-72-301.
rules.penalty: Up to $2,500 per violation; private right of action for parents

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when minor user profiles are publicly searchable or visible by default. Utah SB 142 requires minor profiles be hidden from search engines and visible only to connected users unless the minor actively changes privacy settings.
tp_criteria: Code sets SEO/robot meta tags to 'index' or 'follow' for minor accounts, or lacks robot.txt exclusion for minor profile URLs
Profile visibility logic defaults to 'public' or 'visible to all' for users identified as minors without explicit opt-in
Application does not implement search engine blocking (robots.txt, noindex meta) for minor profile pages
fp_criteria: Code implements noindex meta tags or robots.txt rules that block search engine indexing of minor profiles
Privacy settings default to 'private' or 'connected-only' visibility for minor accounts
Application is adult-only or does not support public profiles for any user type
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS search engine blocking or restricted visibility for minors by default, it's FP
If profile visibility is set to 'connected-only' or 'private' for all underage users, it's FP
If the codebase is a documentation or configuration file showing privacy defaults, not the enforcement code, review context before flagging

rules.name: Biometric Identifier Collection Without VPC
rules.description: COPPA 2.0 expands 'personal information' to include biometric identifiers: fingerprints, voiceprints, facial geometry, gait patterns. Collection requires Verifiable Parental Consent (VPC) before any data capture.
rules.fix_suggestion: Obtain Verifiable Parental Consent (VPC) before collecting any biometric identifiers. Under COPPA 2.0, biometric data is 'personal information' requiring the highest consent standard. Keep biometric processing local-only where possible.
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation (FTC Final Rule effective April 22, 2026)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects collection of biometric data from children without verified parental consent. COPPA 2.0 expanded the definition of personal information to include fingerprints, voiceprints, facial recognition geometry, and gait patterns. Any collection requires Verifiable Parental Consent before capture.
tp_criteria: Code collects biometric data (fingerprint scan, face geometry, voiceprint, gait analysis) from users without calling or checking a VPC mechanism first
Biometric capture function does not verify parental consent status or age-gate before initiating data collection
Application transmits or stores biometric identifiers without evidence of prior consent validation in the data flow
fp_criteria: Code implements VPC validation before biometric capture is triggered
Biometric functionality is gated behind an age-check that restricts it to adult users only
Code is in a consent management library or VPC handler, not the biometric capture implementation itself
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS parental consent verification before biometric collection, it's FP
If biometric features are restricted to users 18+ or require proof of consent before execution, it's FP
If the code references biometric data in comments or type definitions but doesn't actually collect it, context matters—review for implementation

tp_examples.explanation: TP (borderline/weak): Scratch-GUI accesses the device camera via getUserMedia in a child-directed platform. While the video stream is used for 'video sensing' blocks (motion detection) and processed client-side, the raw video data could potentially capture facial features of children. Per COPPA 2.0 expanded definition of biometric identifiers (16 CFR 312.2), camera access that captures a child's likeness creates potential for biometric data collection. However, since data stays local, this is a weak TP — the concern is the camera access pattern itself in a child-directed context without explicit consent.

FP: Microsoft MakeCode (PXT) defines age group categories including 'MinorWithoutParentalConsent' and 'MinorWithParentalConsent' for its feedback system. This demonstrates COPPA-aware design — the system explicitly models consent states for minors before collecting any data. The presence of these categories shows the platform gates features based on age and consent status, which is the correct approach for handling biometric or sensitive data collection.

FP: The companion function requestDisableVideo shows Scratch-GUI provides explicit camera shutdown capability. The video stream is managed via a reference-counted stack, and when all consumers release the stream, it is fully disabled. This demonstrates privacy-by-design: the camera access is temporary, managed, and explicitly releasable. Data stays on-device for motion sensing blocks.

fp_examples.explanation: FP: Scratch-GUI's camera access is for device-local video sensing (motion detection in Scratch blocks), not biometric identification. The video stream stays entirely on-device and is processed by Scratch's rendering engine for motion/direction detection. No facial recognition, no biometric templates are created, and no data is transmitted to any server. This is analogous to device-local Face ID (Secure Enclave) — the camera data never leaves the device.

FP: Microsoft MakeCode's green screen experiment uses webcam purely as a visual backdrop behind code, not for biometric identification. It is an opt-in experimental feature that displays the video stream locally. No face detection, recognition, or biometric processing occurs. The video stays on the device as a UI element.

FP: MakeCode explicitly models consent states for different age groups before any data collection. The 'MinorWithoutParentalConsent' and 'MinorWithParentalConsent' categories demonstrate the platform gates functionality based on verified consent status. This is the COPPA-compliant pattern for handling any sensitive collection including biometric data.

knowledge.regulatory_source: 16 CFR §312.2 (2025) — Biometric identifiers added to PI definition in adopted final rule.
