rules.name: Push Notification Token Without Parental Opt-In
rules.description: COPPA 2.0 classifies device push notification tokens as 'online contact information'. Subscribing a child's device to push notifications requires prior parental consent and an opt-out mechanism.
rules.fix_suggestion: Gate push notification token registration behind a parental consent check. Under COPPA 2.0, push tokens are 'online contact information' — parents must explicitly opt in, and you must provide an opt-out mechanism accessible from a parental dashboard.
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation (FTC Final Rule effective April 22, 2026)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when a child's device is subscribed to push notifications without prior parental consent. COPPA 2.0 classifies push notification tokens as online contact information requiring opt-in consent and an active opt-out mechanism.
tp_criteria: Code subscribes a child's device to push notifications (Firebase token, APNs registration) without checking parental consent status first
Push notification subscription logic does not verify age or consent before registering a notification token
Application lacks an opt-out mechanism or unsubscribe path for push notifications
fp_criteria: Code implements consent verification before subscribing to push notifications
Push notification registration is gated behind age-check or parental consent confirmation
Application provides clear opt-out/unsubscribe functionality for push notifications
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS parental consent checking before push token registration, it's FP
If push notifications are only enabled after explicit parental opt-in, it's FP
If the code is a notification consent UI or API handler (not the subscription logic), verify it's actually enforced in the calling code
knowledge.regulatory_source: NONE — Provision proposed in 2023 NPRM but explicitly rejected in 2025 final rule.

legal_council.method: 3-perspective legal council (FTC Enforcer + Compliance Officer + Defense Counsel)

knowledge.deprecation_reason: DEPRECATED. This rule previously claimed push notification tokens are classified as online contact information under COPPA 2.0. The FTC explicitly declined to adopt this provision in the 2025 final rule. Push notification concerns are addressed by coppa-notif-013 (reframed as ethical best practice).

rules.name: Ed-Tech Data Use Beyond Educational Purpose
rules.description: COPPA 2.0 restricts ed-tech providers operating under the 'school official' exception: student data may only be used for the educational purpose authorized by the school. No advertising, profiling, or secondary data use.
rules.fix_suggestion: Ensure ed-tech data collected under the 'school official' exception is used exclusively for the authorized educational purpose. Remove any analytics, advertising, or profiling code paths that touch student data. COPPA 2.0 makes this an explicit prohibition.
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation (FTC Final Rule effective April 22, 2026)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects ed-tech applications that use student data beyond the educational purpose authorized by the school. COPPA 2.0 restricts 'school official' exception use: data must only be used for education, with no advertising, behavioral profiling, or secondary market use.
tp_criteria: Code uses student data collected for classroom purposes (grades, assignments, participation) in advertising targeting or personalization
Application implements behavioral profiling, predictive analytics, or interest-based segmentation using educational data
Ed-tech system shares or licenses student data to third parties for non-educational purposes (marketing, data brokers, behavioral research)
fp_criteria: Code restricts data use to educational contexts only with documented purpose limitation
Application implements data minimization that excludes student data from marketing or profiling systems
Codebase is an adult learning platform or non-classroom ed-tech without school authority framework
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code RESTRICTS student data to educational purposes only and excludes it from marketing/profiling pipelines, it's FP
If the application implements purpose-limiting controls that prevent secondary use of classroom data, it's FP
If the system is not operating under a 'school official' exception (e.g., consumer ed-tech), evaluate COPPA general rules instead

tp_examples.code:
export default class Tracker2 extends BaseTracker {
  constructor (store) {
    super()
    this.store = store
    this.cookieConsentTracker = new CookieConsentTracker(this.store)
    this.internalTracker = new InternalTracker(this.store)
    this.googleAnalyticsTracker = new GoogleAnalyticsTracker(this.store)
    this.fullStoryTracker = new FullStoryTracker(this.store, this)
    this.facebookPixelTracker = new FacebookPixelTracker(this.store)
    this.twitterPixelTracker = new TwitterPixelTracker(this.store)
    this.zendeskTracker = new ZendeskTracker(this.store)
    this.superflowTracker = new SuperflowTracker(this.store)
tp_examples.explanation: TP: CodeCombat initializes FullStory (session recording), Facebook Pixel (ad tracking), Twitter Pixel (ad conversion), and Google Analytics for ALL users including students. Under COPPA 16 CFR 312.2, student data from an ed-tech platform must be used solely for educational purposes. FullStory records entire user sessions, and Facebook/Twitter pixels enable ad retargeting — both clearly non-educational uses of student data.

TP: Student gameplay events (level loads, capstone progress) are sent to Google Analytics with session IDs that can be linked back to individual students. This sends identifiable student behavioral data to a third-party advertising company for purposes beyond education, violating COPPA's ed-tech data limitation under 16 CFR 312.2.

TP: Teacher signup events fire Google AdWords conversion tracking (gtag) with a specific conversion ID, linking educator registration to advertising campaigns. When teachers create accounts in an ed-tech context, this data may include school information that flows to Google's ad network beyond educational purpose, per COPPA 16 CFR 312.2.

fp_examples.explanation: FP: Moodle's H5P xAPI handler only processes 'answered' and 'completed' verbs — strictly educational assessment events. The data stays within Moodle's first-party system for grading purposes only. No data is sent to external analytics or advertising services, satisfying COPPA's educational purpose limitation.

FP: Open edX's event tracking uses a NameWhitelistProcessor with an empty whitelist by default, meaning NO events are forwarded to Segment unless explicitly configured. Login/credential URLs are explicitly excluded from tracking. This privacy-by-default configuration satisfies COPPA's data minimization requirements.

fp_examples.explanation: FP: Open edX sets GOOGLE_ANALYTICS_ACCOUNT to None by default, meaning Google Analytics is disabled unless explicitly configured by the deployer. This privacy-by-default approach ensures no student data flows to Google's advertising infrastructure without deliberate opt-in, consistent with COPPA's educational purpose limitation.

rules.name: Data Retention Beyond Reasonable Necessity
rules.description: COPPA 2.0 strengthens data retention requirements: operators must delete children's personal information when it is no longer reasonably necessary for the purpose for which it was collected. Indefinite retention or missing deletion mechanisms violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement automatic data deletion policies for children's personal information. Set reasonable TTLs based on the purpose of collection. Add a scheduled deletion job that purges expired child data. COPPA 2.0 requires deletion when data is no longer reasonably necessary.
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation (FTC Final Rule effective April 22, 2026)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when a child's personal information is retained indefinitely or lacks a deletion mechanism. COPPA 2.0 requires operators to delete children's data when no longer reasonably necessary for the stated collection purpose, with documented retention policies.
tp_criteria: Code stores children's personal information without a deletion or expiration mechanism
Application lacks documented data retention policy or deletion schedule for child accounts
System archives or retains children's data indefinitely even after account deletion or collection purpose ends
fp_criteria: Code implements automated deletion or data expiration for children's records after a defined retention period
Application documents clear retention policies aligned with data purpose (e.g., delete after 2 years post-account closure)
System implements parental or child requests for data deletion with working deletion logic
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS automatic deletion or time-based expiration for children's data, it's FP
If retention policy is documented and deletion mechanisms are in place, it's FP
If the code is a data archival or backup function (not the primary retention), verify the primary deletion logic exists elsewhere

TP: LevelSession stores per-user gameplay data (playtime, code, completion) with created/changed timestamps linked to a user, but no expiration, TTL, or cleanup policy. Child activity data is retained indefinitely in violation of COPPA's data minimization requirement under 16 CFR 312.10.

fp_examples.explanation: FP: Moodle implements a comprehensive GDPR/privacy data deletion system with delete_data_for_user(), delete_data_for_users(), and delete_data_for_all_users_in_context() methods. This satisfies COPPA's data retention requirements because user data can be systematically purged on request.

FP: Moodle's privacy provider implements data export alongside deletion, providing full data portability and lifecycle management. The system tracks exactly what user data exists and provides structured methods to export and delete it, satisfying COPPA retention requirements.

FP: Moodle's user privacy provider tracks a 'deleted' field in user metadata and implements the full privacy API (metadata, export, deletion). The 'deleted' flag enables soft-delete functionality, and the structured privacy interfaces ensure data lifecycle compliance with COPPA retention rules.

rules.name: Consent Mechanism Not Meeting VPC Standard
rules.description: COPPA 2.0 requires Verifiable Parental Consent (VPC) via methods that provide a greater level of assurance: signed consent forms, credit card transactions, video calls, government ID, or knowledge-based authentication. Simple email-based consent ('email plus') is only valid for internal use.
rules.fix_suggestion: Upgrade consent mechanism to meet COPPA 2.0 VPC standards. For external data sharing, use credit card verification, video calls, government ID, or knowledge-based authentication. Simple checkboxes and email confirmations do not meet the VPC standard for external use of children's data.
rules.penalty: $53,088 per violation (FTC Final Rule effective April 22, 2026)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when parental consent mechanisms don't meet COPPA 2.0's Verifiable Parental Consent standard. Valid VPC methods include signed consent forms, credit card verification, video calls, government ID, or knowledge-based authentication. Simple email ('email plus') is only valid for internal uses, not external service access.
tp_criteria: Code implements parental consent via email-only or email confirmation for external service access (ads, analytics, third-party APIs)
Consent mechanism uses simple email verification without secondary identity verification (no card, ID, or call requirement)
Application collects personal information from minors with email-based 'opt-in' consent that does not meet VPC assurance standards
fp_criteria: Code implements VPC via credit card, government ID, video call, or knowledge-based authentication
Email-based consent is used only for internal account management, not external data sharing or services
Application implements a signed digital consent form with identity verification before data collection
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS credit card verification, government ID verification, video call, or KBA before consent is granted, it's FP
If email consent is only used for password resets or account notifications (internal), it's FP
If the consent mechanism includes secondary identity checks or higher assurance verification, it's FP

rules.name: Default Privacy Set to Public
rules.description: AADC Standard 7 requires settings to be 'high privacy' by default. Children's data should only be visible to others if the child actively changes the setting. Default-public profiles, content, or activity violate this standard.
rules.fix_suggestion: Set all privacy defaults to the most restrictive option. Profiles, activity, and content should be private by default. Users (especially children) should actively opt in to share data with others. See ICO AADC Standard 7.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when a child's profile, content, or activity data is publicly visible by default. AADC Standard 7 requires 'high privacy by default'—children's data should only be visible if they actively change privacy settings, protecting them from unwanted exposure.
tp_criteria: Code sets default profile visibility to 'public' or 'everyone' for child accounts without requiring explicit opt-in
User content (posts, photos, activity) is public by default for underage users
Application allows default discovery of child profiles in public search or recommendation systems
fp_criteria: Code defaults all child account visibility to 'private' or 'friends-only'
Privacy settings require child (or parent) to explicitly select 'public' to enable wider visibility
Application restricts child account discoverability by default and requires opt-in for public listing
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code SETS default privacy to 'private', 'friends-only', or restricted access for minors, it's FP
If visibility is public by default but child must actively opt-in to that setting, it's FP
If the application restricts child account indexing/discovery by default, it's FP
If the code IMPLEMENTS privacy-protective defaults (e.g., profile set to private, tracking disabled by default), it's FP — the rule flags missing high-privacy defaults.

rules.name: Opt-Out Tracking Enabled by Default
rules.description: AADC Standard 7 requires optional data uses to be individually selected and activated. Tracking, analytics, or personalization enabled by default with an opt-out mechanism violates this standard.
rules.fix_suggestion: Switch from opt-out to opt-in for all tracking, analytics, and personalization. These features must be off by default and require active user consent before activation. See ICO AADC Standard 7.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when tracking, analytics, or personalization features are enabled by default with only opt-out available. AADC Standard 7 requires optional data uses to be individually selected—children should actively choose to enable tracking, not passively have it enabled.
tp_criteria: Code enables analytics tracking, ad targeting, or personalization for child accounts by default without parental/child consent
Tracking cookie or analytics script automatically fires for minors without prior opt-in
Application collects behavioral data or usage patterns by default with only opt-out mechanism available
fp_criteria: Code implements opt-in requirement: tracking/analytics only enable after explicit child or parental selection
Personalization and tracking are disabled by default and require active user/parent choice to enable
Application provides clear, easy opt-out for tracking and respects opt-out status before data collection
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code REQUIRES opt-in before enabling tracking/analytics for children, it's FP
If personalization features are disabled by default and require explicit activation, it's FP
If the application implements a control that allows children/parents to disable all tracking before data flows to analytics/ad systems, it's FP

rules.name: Excessive Personal Data Collection
rules.description: AADC Standard 8 requires collecting only the minimum personal data needed to provide the service. Requiring fields like phone, address, school, gender, or ethnicity beyond what is necessary violates data minimisation.
rules.fix_suggestion: Review which personal data fields are truly required for your service. Make non-essential fields optional. Give children choices over which elements of data they wish to provide. See ICO AADC Standard 8.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when apps collect personal data fields (phone, address, school, gender, ethnicity) that aren't necessary for core functionality. Over-collecting personal data from children increases privacy risks and violates AADC Standard 8's data minimisation principle.
tp_criteria: Code requests and stores personal fields (phone number, home address, school name, gender, ethnicity) without demonstrable functional necessity to the service
Form submission logic accepts and persists these fields without conditional logic that would limit collection to specific use cases
API endpoints or database schemas explicitly define these fields as required (non-nullable) rather than optional for users under 13
fp_criteria: The app implements conditional field collection that only requests personal data when genuinely needed for a specific service (e.g., shipping address only for delivery orders)
Fields are defined in code but marked as optional, deprecated, or explicitly skipped during child user registration flows
Code shows these fields are collected only for adult user accounts or in admin/parental control panels, not for children's direct use
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS optional field logic or conditional collection based on user age or service type, it's FP.
If collection is restricted to specific, documented use cases (delivery, emergency contact) rather than broad profiling, it's FP.
If fields are collected but immediately discarded or not persisted, it's FP—focus on what data is actually STORED, not just requested.

rules.name: Third-Party Data Sharing Without Child Safety Check
rules.description: AADC Standard 9 prohibits disclosing children's data unless there is a compelling reason. Analytics and advertising SDKs that share data with third parties require child-safety checks before initialization.
rules.fix_suggestion: Before initializing third-party SDKs, check user age and disable data sharing for children. Use child-directed SDK configurations (e.g., tag_for_child_directed_treatment). Do not share children's data with data brokers or ad networks. See ICO AADC Standard 9.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when analytics, advertising, or tracking SDKs share children's data with third parties without safety checks. AADC Standard 9 requires demonstrating a compelling reason for data disclosure and implementing child-safety controls before initializing third-party integrations.
tp_criteria: Third-party SDK (analytics, ad network, tracking library) is initialized unconditionally without checks for child age, parental consent, or child-safety status
SDK initialization code lacks conditional guards such as age verification, child-safety mode flags, or consent validation before data transmission
Documentation or code comments indicate the SDK collects behavioral/identifiable data (user ID, events, location) and shares with external parties without safeguards
fp_criteria: The app implements age-checking logic that conditionally disables or limits the SDK's data collection and sharing for users under 13
SDK is initialized only after explicit parental consent or child-safety mode verification, not by default
The SDK is imported but intentionally not instantiated, or only used in adult-only features with clear code paths preventing child access
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS child-safety checks before SDK initialization (e.g., 'if !isChild then initAnalytics()'), it's FP.
If the SDK is configured with child-safe settings (anonymization, no tracking, no third-party sharing) or user consent gates, it's FP.
Unconditional or default-enabled SDKs that lack child-age checks are TP, regardless of privacy policy claims.

rules.name: Geolocation Enabled by Default
rules.description: AADC Standard 10 requires geolocation options to be switched off by default. Location tracking, sharing, and high-accuracy positioning must not be activated without explicit user action.
rules.fix_suggestion: Set geolocation to off by default. Require explicit user action to enable location services. When location is active, provide a prominent visible indicator. Location sharing with others should reset to off at end of session. See ICO AADC Standard 10.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when location services (GPS, WiFi positioning, high-accuracy geolocation) are enabled by default or activated without explicit user action. AADC Standard 10 requires geolocation to be off by default and require affirmative opt-in.
tp_criteria: Geolocation API calls (e.g., requestLocationUpdates, getCurrentPosition, startLocationTracking) are invoked automatically on app launch or user login without explicit user action
Location permission is requested with default 'allow' or 'always allow' logic, or location collection starts before user consent is confirmed
High-accuracy location mode (GPS-based, not coarse cell/WiFi approximation) is the default setting, not a user-selected option
fp_criteria: Location services are only requested after explicit user action (button tap, feature selection) and require affirmative consent before any collection starts
Code shows location is disabled or null by default, with user-facing toggle or setting to enable it
Location permission is only requested for map, navigation, or safety features that genuinely require it, with alternative coarse options available
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS default-disabled location (e.g., 'locationEnabled = false' or location only after consent check), it's FP.
If location collection requires explicit user action (button press, menu selection) before any API call, it's FP.
Automatic or background location collection, even if permission was previously granted, is TP if not explicitly re-confirmed by the user.

rules.name: Continuous Background Location Tracking
rules.description: AADC Standard 10 requires using minimum granularity for geolocation. Continuous background location tracking or watch-based location monitoring collects excessive positional data from children.
rules.fix_suggestion: Use single-point location requests instead of continuous monitoring. Avoid background location tracking. Use the minimum granularity needed (e.g., city-level rather than precise coordinates). See ICO AADC Standard 10.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects continuous background location tracking or high-frequency location updates that collect excessive positional data from children. AADC Standard 10 requires minimum granularity—coarse location or infrequent point sampling, not constant tracking.
tp_criteria: Code uses background location tracking with requestLocationUpdates or similar APIs running continuously while app is minimized or locked
Location is sampled or logged at high frequency (e.g., every second, every minute) or stored in a location history database without aggregation
Geofencing or location watch features are set to track movement in real-time or continuously sync location to a server
fp_criteria: Location is sampled only at coarse intervals (e.g., once per hour or on-demand) and not stored as a continuous history
Geolocation is used only for one-time point-in-time features (e.g., 'find nearby friends now') and not for background tracking
Background location is disabled by default, and continuous tracking only occurs after explicit user opt-in with clear consent language
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS coarse-grained location (WiFi/cell-based approximation) or one-time sampling instead of continuous GPS, it's FP.
If background location requests are gated behind explicit user toggles with clear warnings about battery/privacy impact, it's FP.
Any continuous or background location collection without user re-confirmation in the app UI is TP, even if system permissions were previously granted.

rules.name: Profiling or Algorithmic Feed Enabled by Default
rules.description: AADC Standard 12 requires profiling to be switched off by default for children. Algorithmic content feeds, behavioral profiling, and personalization engines must not be active without explicit opt-in.
rules.fix_suggestion: Switch profiling off by default. Provide a chronological or non-personalized feed as the default experience. Only enable algorithmic personalization if the child actively opts in. See ICO AADC Standard 12.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when algorithmic content feeds, recommendation engines, or behavioral profiling are enabled by default for child users. AADC Standard 12 requires profiling to be switched off by default and require explicit opt-in.
tp_criteria: Algorithmic feed or recommendation engine is active by default on app launch or user login without explicit user choice or toggle
Personalization features (content ranking, feed curation, 'for you' algorithms) run automatically based on behavioral profiling without opt-in
No user-accessible toggle or setting exists to disable profiling; it is always on or can only be disabled through buried settings
fp_criteria: Profiling and algorithmic feeds are disabled by default, and users must explicitly enable them through a visible, in-app toggle or consent screen
The app shows a non-algorithmic, static, or chronological feed by default, with algorithmic options available only after user opt-in
Code shows profiling logic is only executed after checking a user preference flag or consent record that defaults to false
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS default-disabled profiling (e.g., 'profilingEnabled = false unless user opts in'), it's FP.
If algorithmic feeds require explicit user action (button toggle, consent dialog) before activation, it's FP.
Any automatic or default-enabled recommendation engine or behavioral profiling without explicit in-app opt-in is TP.

rules.name: Behavioral Data Collection for Recommendation Engine
rules.description: AADC Standard 12 restricts profiling children. Collecting behavioral data (interests, habits, browsing patterns) to feed recommendation algorithms requires safeguards to protect children from harmful content amplification.
rules.fix_suggestion: If using recommendation algorithms, implement age-appropriate content filtering. Do not amplify harmful, addictive, or age-inappropriate content to children. Provide transparency about why content is recommended. See ICO AADC Standard 12.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects collection of behavioral data (interests, habits, browsing patterns, watch history) to feed recommendation algorithms. AADC Standard 12 restricts profiling of children and requires safeguards to prevent harmful content amplification.
tp_criteria: Code collects and stores behavioral data (browsing history, watch time, search queries, click patterns, 'likes', interaction timestamps) in a user profile or analytics database
Behavioral data is explicitly fed to a recommendation or ranking algorithm without content-safety filtering or diversity constraints
No documentation or code indicates content filtering or safety checks prevent recommendation of harmful, age-inappropriate, or extreme content based on child's behavior
fp_criteria: Behavioral data collection is disabled by default or only occurs after explicit opt-in with clear consent language
Recommendation algorithms include documented safety filters or curators that prevent promotion of harmful content categories
The app collects behavioral data only for non-profiling purposes (e.g., analytics, fraud detection) and explicitly separates it from recommendation logic
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS content-safety filtering or restricted recommendation categories (e.g., 'no mature content' even if user engaged with it), it's FP.
If behavioral data collection is separate from recommendation logic or only used for aggregated, non-personalized features, it's FP.
If behavioral profiling is required to use core features and lacks safety filters, it's TP regardless of parental controls in settings.

rules.name: Pre-Checked Consent or Privacy Boxes
rules.description: AADC Standard 13 prohibits nudge techniques that lead children to weaken or turn off privacy protections. Pre-checked consent, marketing, or data-sharing boxes are a nudge that defaults to less privacy.
rules.fix_suggestion: Remove all pre-checked consent and data-sharing boxes. Consent inputs should start unchecked, requiring active selection by the user. This applies to marketing consent, newsletter signups, data sharing agreements, and privacy preferences. See ICO AADC Standard 13.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects pre-checked consent boxes, marketing checkboxes, or privacy-weakening defaults that use nudge techniques to lead children toward sharing more data. AADC Standard 13 prohibits pre-ticked boxes or defaults that reduce privacy protection.
tp_criteria: Consent, marketing, or data-sharing checkboxes are pre-checked ('checked=true') by default, requiring the user to uncheck them to opt out
Form or settings show privacy-reducing options (e.g., 'share profile with friends', 'allow analytics') as the default state, with children required to actively change settings to reduce sharing
UI code initializes privacy settings to weaker defaults (e.g., isPublic=true, sharingEnabled=true) instead of stronger privacy (private profile, no sharing)
fp_criteria: All consent and data-sharing checkboxes are unchecked by default, requiring active checking to enable sharing or reduce privacy
Privacy settings default to the strongest protection (private profile, no sharing, no tracking), with opt-in required to weaken them
The app uses radio buttons or explicit 'Private by Default' framing rather than checkboxes, preventing accidental opt-in through inattention
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS unchecked-by-default checkboxes or private-by-default settings, it's FP.
If privacy settings use explicit opt-in (require user action to enable sharing), it's FP.
Any pre-checked box for consent, marketing, or data sharing is TP, regardless of whether it's technically 'easy' to uncheck.

rules.name: Confirmshaming or Guilt-Based Privacy Nudge
rules.description: AADC Standard 13 prohibits exploiting psychological processes to weaken children's privacy. Confirmshaming uses guilt, shame, or fear-of-missing-out language to pressure users into sharing more data or accepting weaker privacy settings.
rules.fix_suggestion: Present privacy choices neutrally without emotional manipulation. Avoid language that makes children feel bad for choosing privacy. Do not imply social exclusion or loss for choosing restrictive settings. See ICO AADC Standard 13.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects confirmshaming, guilt-based messaging, or fear-of-missing-out language that exploits children's psychology to weaken privacy settings. AADC Standard 13 prohibits such manipulative nudges.
tp_criteria: Decline buttons or privacy-protective choices use guilt-inducing language (e.g., 'No thanks, keep me out of the fun', 'I don't want friends to find me')
Accept buttons use positive framing (e.g., 'Yes, let's connect!') while decline buttons use negative framing, creating emotional asymmetry
Dialog or message copy uses shame, FOMO, or social exclusion language (e.g., 'Your friends are sharing their location. You sure?', 'Everyone else allows this.')
fp_criteria: Decline and accept buttons use neutral, symmetrical language (e.g., 'Allow' / 'Don't Allow', 'Share' / 'Keep Private') without emotional framing
Confirmation dialogs do not reference social pressure, missing out, or peer behavior
No messaging links privacy choices to social exclusion, loneliness, or missing experiences
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS symmetrical button labels and neutral language for both options, it's FP.
If messages avoid FOMO language, social pressure references, or emotional manipulation, it's FP.
Any asymmetrical emotional framing or shame-based language in decline buttons is TP, even if the choice remains technically available.

rules.name: Privacy-Weakening Reward Mechanism
rules.description: AADC Standard 13 prohibits nudges that lead children to provide unnecessary personal data. Offering rewards, unlocks, or premium features in exchange for sharing more data or making profiles public incentivizes weaker privacy.
rules.fix_suggestion: Do not gate features or rewards behind data sharing or public profile requirements. Core service features should be available regardless of privacy settings. See ICO AADC Standard 13.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects reward mechanisms that incentivize children to share more data, make profiles public, or weaken privacy settings. AADC Standard 13 prohibits nudges that trade privacy for benefits.
tp_criteria: App offers rewards, premium features, unlocks, badges, or currency for actions that increase data sharing (e.g., 'Share your location to earn 100 coins')
Profile visibility or public/private status is tied to game progression, feature access, or rewards (e.g., 'Make your profile public to unlock multiplayer')
Behavioral data collection or profiling opt-in is incentivized with exclusive content, cosmetics, or status benefits
fp_criteria: Rewards and premium features are available without requiring privacy-weakening actions or additional data sharing
Public profile features are optional and come with no gameplay, feature, or social advantages over private profiles
Data collection is never tied to rewards, unlocks, or progression—children can fully play the game with minimal data collection and maximum privacy
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS reward systems that do not depend on or incentivize data sharing, it's FP.
If privacy choices (public/private profile, location sharing, tracking opt-in) carry no gameplay or reward consequences, it's FP.
Any direct or indirect link between privacy choices and in-game rewards, unlocks, or progression is TP.

rules.name: Weak Age Gate Using Self-Declaration Only
rules.description: AADC Standard 3 requires a risk-based approach to recognizing user age. Simple self-declaration checkboxes or dropdowns ('Are you over 13?') are easily bypassed and provide inadequate age assurance for high-risk services.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement a risk-based age assurance approach. For high-risk services, use age estimation technology, identity verification, or neutral age estimation rather than simple self-declaration. If unable to verify age, apply the code's standards to all users. See ICO AADC Standard 3.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects weak age-gating mechanisms that rely solely on self-declaration (e.g., 'Are you over 13?' checkbox) without additional verification. AADC Standard 3 requires risk-based age assurance that is harder to bypass for high-risk services.
tp_criteria: Age gate uses only a checkbox, radio button, or text input where user self-declares age (e.g., 'I confirm I am 13 or older') with no verification
Age verification logic accepts any input without cross-validation (e.g., date picker allows obviously false dates like year 1900 or future dates)
No secondary verification, parental consent, ID check, or other safeguard is used to confirm age before granting access to the service
fp_criteria: App implements additional age verification beyond self-declaration (ID verification, parental consent, email domain validation, third-party age-check service)
For low-risk services, simple self-declaration is appropriate and documented as compliant with risk-based age assurance
Age gate includes server-side validation, logical date-range checks, or cross-references to prevent obvious age falsification
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS multi-factor age verification (ID check, parental consent, email validation), it's FP.
For services with low data-collection or behavioral-targeting risk, self-declaration alone may be acceptable—check service classification.
Pure client-side self-declaration checkboxes with no validation or secondary safeguards are TP for high-risk services (social, video, behavioral data collection).

rules.name: Targeted Advertising to Minors
rules.description: AADC Standard 5 prohibits using children's personal data in ways detrimental to their wellbeing. Targeted advertising using children's behavioral data, profiles, or personal information is a detrimental use under the code.
rules.fix_suggestion: Do not serve targeted or personalized advertising to children. Use only contextual advertising (based on page content, not user data) if advertising is necessary. See ICO AADC Standard 5.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when an app uses children's personal data (behavioral profiles, browsing history, location, interests) to serve targeted advertisements. Targeted advertising exploits children's developmental vulnerabilities and is considered detrimental to their wellbeing under AADC Standard 5.
tp_criteria: Code actively constructs or uses a behavioral profile of a child user (age < 18) to select which ads to display
Ad targeting logic references user behavioral data, interaction history, or inferred preferences to serve personalized advertisements
Ad network integration passes child user data or identifiers to third-party ad networks known to use profiling (e.g., Google Ad Manager with user data, Facebook Audience Network with behavioral data)
fp_criteria: App serves contextual ads (ads matched only to current page content, not user history or profile) with no behavioral data sharing
Ad code exists only in documentation, comments, or disabled/commented-out sections
App is clearly an adult-only service (age-gated at sign-up, terms explicitly restrict to 18+) and code serves targeted ads only to verified adults
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS contextual-only ad serving (matching ads to page content without user profile or behavioral data), it is FP.
If child age is known in the app context AND targeted ad logic fires for that child user, it is TP. If age-gating logic prevents ad targeting to children, it is FP.
If ad targeting references only real-time content context (article topic, search query) and not stored user data, interaction history, or inferred interests, it is FP.

rules.name: Covert Child Monitoring Without Notification
rules.description: AADC Standard 11 requires that if parental monitoring or tracking features are active, the child must be given an obvious sign. Covert surveillance features that hide monitoring from the child violate this standard.
rules.fix_suggestion: When parental monitoring or tracking is active, display a clear, prominent indicator visible to the child. Provide age-appropriate explanations of what monitoring is active. Respect the child's growing autonomy. See ICO AADC Standard 11.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects parental monitoring or child tracking features that operate without the child's knowledge. AADC Standard 11 requires that if a child's location, activity, or communications are being monitored, the child must receive a clear, obvious indicator (e.g., icon, notification, banner). Covert monitoring violates children's right to autonomy and privacy.
tp_criteria: Code implements location tracking, activity logging, or message/call monitoring of a child user without displaying any in-app indicator, notification, or status icon to the child
Monitoring feature is explicitly designed to be hidden from the child (e.g., backgrounded without notification, silent logging, non-disclosed data collection)
Parental control or monitoring functionality actively suppresses or disables any user-facing disclosure of the monitoring activity
fp_criteria: Code implements monitoring but displays a clear, always-visible indicator to the child (e.g., 'Parental Monitoring Active' icon, persistent banner, notification in child's activity feed)
Monitoring code exists only in parental/admin-only interfaces and is not applied to child-facing flows
Feature is test code, documentation, or a feature flag that is disabled by default
rule_logic: If monitoring functionality EXISTS and a clear user-facing indicator or notification to the child is IMPLEMENTED, it is FP.
If monitoring is active for a child user AND no indicator code exists in the child-facing UI, it is TP.
If the feature is administrative-only (accessible only to parent accounts, not shown in child UI), it is FP.

questions.text: We detected a monitoring/tracking feature ({pattern}) in {filePath}. Is this feature visible to the child being monitored?

yes.reason: Monitoring feature is visible to the child — transparent operation per AADC

I'm not sure.reason: Developer uncertain about monitoring visibility. Recommend UX review.

questions.text: Does the child receive a notification or visual indicator when monitoring is active?

yes.reason: Child notified during monitoring — meets AADC transparency requirement

I'm not sure.reason: Developer uncertain about notification mechanism. Recommend UX audit.

questions.text: Can the child disable or opt out of monitoring?

yes.reason: Child can opt out of monitoring — respects autonomy per AADC

no.reason: No opt-out from monitoring — AADC requires child control proportionate to age

I'm not sure.reason: Developer uncertain about opt-out mechanism. Recommend feature review.

rules.name: User Content Without Report or Block Mechanism
rules.description: AADC Standard 15 requires prominent tools to help children report concerns. AADC Standard 6 requires active content moderation. User-generated content (comments, messages, posts) without report, flag, or block mechanisms fails both standards.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add prominent report, flag, and block mechanisms alongside all user-generated content features. Implement content moderation for user communications. Provide children with easy ways to report harmful content. See ICO AADC Standards 6 and 15.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects user-generated content (comments, posts, messages, reviews) features without built-in tools for children to report concerns or block unwanted content. AADC Standards 6 and 15 require active moderation and prominent reporting/blocking tools to protect children from harmful content and interactions.
tp_criteria: Code enables children to post, comment, or message publicly or semi-publicly, but does not implement a report/flag mechanism accessible in the UI where such content appears
User-generated content is displayed to children without an associated 'block user', 'mute', or 'hide content' button readily available next to or near the content
Content moderation logic exists but is not triggered by child user reports (automated moderation alone without child-accessible reporting tools does not satisfy the standard)
fp_criteria: Report/flag and block mechanisms are prominently implemented in the UI for all user-generated content visible to children
User-generated content feature exists only in admin interfaces or is disabled for child users
Content is curated/moderated only by moderators or algorithms, not user-submitted (e.g., app-published content only, no comments or user posts)
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If user-generated content is displayed to children AND both report and block tools are accessible in the UI, it is FP.
If UGC exists in child-facing flows but report/block mechanisms are missing or hidden behind multiple taps, it is TP.
If content moderation is admin-only with no child-accessible reporting interface, it is TP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS reporting or blocking tools for user-generated content (e.g., report button, block user function), it's FP — the rule flags missing safety tools.

rules.name: Monetization Override Without Child Safety Check
rules.description: AADC Standard 1 requires the best interests of the child to be a primary consideration. In-app purchase prompts, subscription upsells, or premium feature gates in child-facing flows without age-gated suppression prioritize revenue over child wellbeing.
rules.fix_suggestion: Before showing monetization prompts (in-app purchases, upsells, premium gates), check if the user is a child and suppress or gate these flows accordingly. The best interests of the child must take priority over commercial interests. See ICO AADC Standard 1.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects in-app purchase prompts, subscription upsells, or premium feature gates that are shown in child-facing user flows without age-gated suppression logic. AADC Standard 1 requires the best interests of the child to be a primary consideration; monetization tactics that pressure children to spend override this principle.
tp_criteria: Code implements in-app purchase prompts, 'upgrade to premium', or paywall dialogs that are displayed to child users (age < 18) without conditional logic to suppress or tone down the pressure
Monetization prompts appear at high-friction moments (after game loss, notification dismissal, forced gatewalls) designed to drive conversion without age-gating suppression
Premium feature upsells, subscription requests, or purchase dialogs lack age-aware messaging (e.g., no parental consent requirement for children, no warnings about spending)
fp_criteria: App implements age-gating that suppresses or significantly tones down monetization prompts for child users (e.g., fewer prompts, higher friction, parental consent gates)
In-app purchases and subscription offers are only shown to verified adult users (age-gated at sign-up or feature-level)
Monetization code is test-only, admin-only, or intentionally disabled for production child accounts
rule_logic: If in-app purchase/subscription prompts are displayed in child user flows AND age-gating logic suppresses or moderates these prompts for minors, it is FP.
If monetization prompts fire without any age-aware conditional logic (always show to all users), it is TP.
If the app implements parental consent gating or reduced-frequency prompts for children, it is FP.

rules.name: Child Data Processing Without DPIA Reference
rules.description: AADC Standard 2 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for services likely to be accessed by children. Code that processes child data (user profiles with age, student records, child accounts) should reference or link to DPIA documentation.
rules.fix_suggestion: Conduct a DPIA before processing children's data and reference it in your codebase. Add DPIA completion checks or documentation links where child data is processed. See ICO AADC Standard 2 and ICO DPIA guidance.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects code that processes child data (user profiles with age fields, student/minor account records, children's personal information) without evidence of or reference to a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). AADC Standard 2 requires a DPIA for services accessed by children to assess and mitigate privacy risks.
tp_criteria: Code processes data fields explicitly tied to children (e.g., age < 18, 'is_minor' flag, student_id, parental_email, child_profile) without any comment, documentation, or reference linking to a DPIA
Child data processing logic exists (storage, transmission, analytics) but contains no DPIA reference, compliance note, or data protection assessment metadata
Service is explicitly documented as child-accessible but code contains no DPIA URI, document reference, or compliance tracking
fp_criteria: Code includes DPIA reference, URL, or document ID in comments or compliance metadata (e.g., 'DPIA-2024-001 assessed', 'See privacy-assessment.md')
Child data processing is handled through a third-party service that documents its own DPIA (code delegates responsibility with clear audit trail)
Child data is not actually processed (only parental/guardian data is stored; child accounts are proxied through parent accounts)
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If child data fields are processed AND any DPIA reference or compliance documentation link is present in code/comments, it is FP.
If child data processing occurs without any DPIA mention or compliance metadata, it is TP.
If a DPIA requirement is documented elsewhere and the code is part of an assessed service, it is FP (requires evidence of assessment, not evidence in code itself).

rules.name: Privacy Notice Without Child-Friendly Version
rules.description: AADC Standard 4 requires privacy information to be concise, prominent, and in clear language suited to the age of the child. Services must provide 'bite-sized' explanations at the point of data use, not just adult-facing legal privacy policies.
rules.fix_suggestion: Provide age-appropriate, bite-sized privacy notices alongside standard privacy policies. At the point of data collection, show concise explanations a child can understand. Consider using icons, animations, or short sentences instead of legal language. See ICO AADC Standard 4.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects privacy notices and data collection disclosures that are written only for adults (complex legal language, lengthy policies) without child-friendly alternatives. AADC Standard 4 requires privacy information to be presented in 'bite-sized' language and prominently displayed at the point of data collection, tailored to the child's age.
tp_criteria: App collects personal data from children but only displays a standard adult-level privacy policy (dense legal text, >500 words, passive voice) without a separate age-appropriate version
Data collection prompts lack clear, simple language explaining what data is collected and why (e.g., 'We collect your location to improve your experience' reduced to 'Location access required')
Privacy information is buried in settings, separate screens, or requires navigation away from the data collection point, rather than shown inline at moment of collection
fp_criteria: App provides a separate, child-friendly privacy explanation (using simple vocabulary, active voice, <100 words per data type) in addition to full policy
Data collection prompts include clear, age-appropriate explanations at the point of collection (e.g., inline notices, modal dialogs with plain language)
App is adult-only (age-gated at entry) and only shows standard adult privacy policies
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If child data collection occurs AND child-friendly privacy information is displayed at the point of collection, it is FP.
If the app collects child data but only a complex, adult-level privacy policy is available (no simplified version), it is TP.
If privacy info is presented at data collection time in simple language, it is FP; if relegated to a separate settings screen, it is TP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS a clear, child-friendly privacy notice or policy page, it's FP — the rule flags missing child-appropriate privacy information.

rules.name: Connected Toy/Device Without Privacy Mode
rules.description: AADC Standard 14 requires connected toys and devices to include effective tools to enable conformance with the Code. IoT devices that communicate with children's data must have hardware/software privacy modes, mute capabilities, and clear data collection indicators.
rules.fix_suggestion: Connected toys and IoT devices must include privacy modes that limit data collection, hardware mute capabilities for microphones/cameras, and clear indicators when data is being collected. Ensure parental controls are built into the device software. See ICO AADC Standard 14.
rules.penalty: Up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover (UK GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects connected toys and IoT devices that collect children's data without providing privacy controls such as mute buttons, data collection indicators (lights/sounds), or privacy mode toggles. AADC Standard 14 requires hardware and software safeguards that give children and parents tools to manage data collection from connected devices.
tp_criteria: Connected toy or device firmware/software initiates data collection (audio, video, location, biometrics) without a hardware mute button, microphone kill switch, or camera cover mechanism
Device has no visual or audible indicator (LED, sound) that signals when data collection is active, making it impossible for children to know when they're being recorded
Code does not implement a privacy mode or data collection disable feature accessible via hardware button or app interface
fp_criteria: Device includes a physical mute button, camera shutter, or microphone kill switch that directly disables data collection
Active data collection is indicated by a persistent LED light, sound cue, or app notification visible to the child
App provides a privacy mode toggle that disables data collection for the connected device
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If connected device collects data AND has no hardware or software privacy controls (mute, indicator, privacy mode), it is TP.
If device firmware includes a data collection indicator or mute mechanism, it is FP.
If the app-side code implements a privacy mode that disables or limits device data collection, it is FP.

rules.name: Profiling-Based Ad Targeting Without Minor Exclusion
rules.description: DSA Article 28(2) strictly prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data when the platform is aware with reasonable certainty that the recipient is a minor. This ban cannot be overridden by parental consent.
rules.fix_suggestion: Before serving ads, check if the user is a minor. If so, disable all profiling-based ad targeting. Only contextual advertising (based on page content, not user data) is permitted for minors under DSA Article 28(2). This restriction cannot be waived by parental consent.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects ad targeting systems that use profiling (behavioral analysis, interest categories, inferred demographics) to show ads to minors. DSA Article 28(2) strictly prohibits this practice when a platform is aware or reasonably certain the user is a minor, regardless of parental consent. This is a critical violation with no exceptions.
tp_criteria: Ad targeting logic creates or uses a user profile (behavioral, interest-based, demographic) for a user known or reasonably believed to be a minor (<18 years)
Code passes minor user data (age, user_id, interests, behavior vectors) to ad networks or DSPs with instructions to use it for targeting
Profiling-based ad selection occurs for minor users even if parental consent flags or premium settings are enabled
fp_criteria: Ad targeting is context-only (matched to page/search content) with no user profiling, behavioral data, or history reference
Age-gating logic confirms user is 18+ before any profiling-based ad selection is permitted
Ad system excludes or explicitly filters out minor users from profiling-based ad delivery pipelines
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-gating that prevents profiling-based ad targeting for confirmed minors, it is FP.
If minor user profiling for ad targeting occurs without explicit age-gating exclusion, it is TP (no exceptions for parental consent).
If ad targeting relies only on contextual signals (page content, search terms) and not user history or profiles, it is FP.

rules.name: Media Autoplay Without Minor-Conditional Default
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require autoplay of video/audio content to be disabled by default for minor users. Autoplay drives extended engagement and undermines minors' ability to control their usage.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable autoplay by default for minor users. Require explicit user action to play media content. If autoplay is needed, gate it behind an age check and provide prominent controls to pause or stop playback. See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects video or audio autoplay features that are enabled by default for minor users. DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require autoplay to be disabled by default for minors because autoplay drives extended engagement and reduces minors' control over their consumption. Autoplay increases session times beyond user intent.
tp_criteria: Video or audio content automatically plays when a page loads or content is displayed to a user identified as a minor, without requiring a user tap/click
Autoplay is enabled by default for minor users with no toggle or setting to disable it (or toggle exists but autoplay is pre-selected)
Autoplay triggers on feed scrolls, navigation, or other passive interactions without explicit user intent
fp_criteria: Autoplay is disabled by default for minor users (setting is off, requires explicit user enable)
Code includes conditional logic that disables autoplay specifically for users under 18
Autoplay exists only in adult-gated sections or requires explicit parental/user opt-in before activation
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If minor user is detected AND autoplay is on by default, it is TP.
If autoplay is disabled by default for minors (setting defaults to off), it is FP.
If code IMPLEMENTS age-gating that turns off autoplay for minors, it is FP.

rules.name: Infinite Scroll Without Minor Gating
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require continuous content delivery mechanisms (infinite scroll) to be disabled by default for minors. Infinite scroll exploits psychological mechanisms to extend session times beyond user intent.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable infinite scroll by default for minor users. Provide pagination or a 'Load More' button that requires deliberate action. Include session time awareness features (e.g., 'You've been scrolling for X minutes'). See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects continuous content delivery mechanisms (infinite scroll) that are enabled by default for minor users. DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require infinite scroll to be disabled by default for minors because it exploits psychological mechanisms to extend session times beyond user intent and undermines minors' ability to self-regulate.
tp_criteria: Feed or content list automatically loads and appends new content as user scrolls to the bottom, for users identified as minors, with no natural stopping point
Infinite scroll is enabled by default for minor users with no toggle to enable pagination or 'load more' buttons
Content feeds do not implement a scroll depth limit, session time warning, or user-controlled stopping mechanism for minors
fp_criteria: Infinite scroll is disabled by default for minor users (pagination or 'load more' button is default)
Code includes conditional logic that disables infinite scroll for users under 18
Infinite scroll exists only in adult-gated sections or requires explicit minor/parent opt-in
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If minor user is detected AND infinite scroll is on by default, it is TP.
If infinite scroll is disabled by default for minors (pagination or manual 'load more' is default), it is FP.
If code IMPLEMENTS age-gating that disables infinite scroll for minors, it is FP.

rules.name: Push Notification Registration Without Minor Checks
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require push notifications to be disabled by default for minors, with additional restrictions during core sleep hours. Notification registration without age-gating or time-of-day restrictions violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable push notifications by default for minor users. If notifications are enabled, restrict them during sleep hours (typically 10pm-7am based on age). Require explicit opt-in and provide granular notification controls. See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects push notification registration systems that don't verify the user's age or implement quiet hours for minors. Push notifications can drive compulsive checking behavior, so DSA requires them to be off by default for anyone under 18 and silent during sleep hours (typically 9 PM to 8 AM).
tp_criteria: Code initializes push notification registration without calling an age-verification function or checking a minor flag before enrollment
Push notification sending logic has no time-of-day restrictions or quiet-hours enforcement for users identified as minors
Registration flow accepts push notification opt-in without age-gating or shows the same notification UI/defaults to minor and adult users
fp_criteria: Code is in a test suite, mock, or example documentation file showing how NOT to implement notifications
Push notification logic explicitly checks user age and disables notifications for minors or enforces quiet hours
Code is an import statement, type definition, or vendor SDK initialization that does not itself control notification defaults
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-verification checks before registering push notifications, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS quiet-hours logic (e.g., no notifications between 21:00-08:00 for minors), classify as FP.
A registration call that does not reference age or minor status and sets notifications to enabled by default is TP.

rules.name: Streak or Engagement Loop Mechanics
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require streak mechanics and daily engagement reward loops to be disabled by default for minors. These patterns create compulsive usage through loss aversion and variable reward schedules.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable streak mechanics by default for minor users. If streaks are offered, ensure they do not penalize users for breaks and do not create anxiety about losing progress. Consider replacing streaks with non-compulsive engagement features. See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule identifies streak mechanics and daily engagement reward loops that are active by default for minor users. Streaks exploit loss aversion (fear of losing a streak) and variable reward schedules to create compulsive usage, which DSA forbids for minors without explicit opt-in.
tp_criteria: Code increments or tracks a streak counter without checking user age, or applies streak logic uniformly to minors and adults
Daily reward or bonus system is triggered automatically without an age-gate or explicit opt-in for minors
Streak-related notifications or reminders are sent to minors without evidence of opt-in consent or age verification
fp_criteria: Streak logic is disabled, commented out, or wrapped in a condition that prevents it from running for minors
Code is test data, mock, or documentation illustrating streak mechanics as a negative example
Streak feature is behind an explicit opt-in gate that requires minor users to affirmatively enable it and includes age verification
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a feature flag or age-check that disables streaks for minors, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS an explicit consent flow requiring minors to opt-in before streak tracking begins, classify as FP.
Automatic streak increment or daily bonus logic without age-gating or opt-in control is TP.

rules.name: Behavioral Recommendation Without Non-Profiled Alternative
rules.description: DSA Articles 27 and 28 require platforms to offer at least one recommendation option that is not based on profiling and to make it the default for minors. Engagement-based signals (watch time, dwell time, scroll depth) in recommender systems without a non-profiled fallback violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Provide a chronological or editorial feed as the default experience for minor users. If using algorithmic recommendations, ensure a non-profiled alternative is easily accessible and set as default. Prioritize explicit user preferences over implicit behavioral signals. See DSA Articles 27 and 28.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects recommendation systems that rely solely on engagement-based profiling (watch time, clicks, dwell time) without offering a non-profiled alternative as the default. DSA Article 27 and 28 require minors to have access to at least one recommendation option that does not use behavioral profiling, and it must be the default choice.
tp_criteria: Recommender system uses only engagement signals (watch time, click-through rate, dwell time, scroll depth) without a separate non-profiled ranking option
Code path for minor users routes all recommendations through a profiling-based algorithm with no fallback to randomized, chronological, or category-based sorting
API or configuration shows a single recommendation strategy that is engagement-optimized, with no toggle or alternative available for minors
fp_criteria: Code implements a non-profiled recommendation option (random, chronological, category-sorted) that is selectable or default for minors
Recommender logic checks user age and applies a separate, non-profiled algorithm specifically for minors
Code is documentation, research, or vendor SDK reference that does not itself execute recommendation logic
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a non-profiled recommendation path for minors (e.g., random, chronological, trending without engagement data), classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS a user-selectable toggle between profiled and non-profiled recommendations that defaults to non-profiled for minors, classify as FP.
A recommender that uses only engagement metrics without an alternative non-profiled option is TP.

rules.name: Cross-Platform Tracking of Minors
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines restrict using minors' activity across or beyond the platform unless it serves the best interests of the minor. Cross-site tracking, device fingerprinting, and cross-app identifiers used for profiling minors violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Do not use cross-platform tracking identifiers for minors. Disable third-party cookies, device fingerprinting, and advertising identifiers for users known to be under 18. Activity tracking must be limited to the current platform and session. See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects cross-platform tracking of minors through cookies, device fingerprints, advertising IDs, or cross-app identifiers used to build behavioral profiles across multiple sites or apps. DSA restricts such tracking unless it serves the minor's best interests, which commercial profiling does not.
tp_criteria: Code initializes third-party tracking pixels, ad networks, or analytics that transmit user device identifiers (IDFA, GAID, fingerprint) without age verification
Cookie or local-storage logic stores persistent identifiers that are shared with external partners or ad networks, with no age-gate or opt-out for minors
Cross-app or cross-site profiling logic (e.g., unified ID, pixel matching) is enabled by default without checking minor status
fp_criteria: Code implements age verification and disables third-party tracking, cookies, and cross-site identifiers for minors
Tracking initialization code is conditional on an explicit opt-in or consent gate that is not pre-checked for minors
Code is an import statement, vendor library declaration, or documentation; it does not itself execute tracking initialization
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-verification before enabling third-party tracking or identifiers, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS opt-in consent that must be explicitly granted before cross-site identifiers are used for minors, classify as FP.
Initialization of third-party tracking, device fingerprinting, or cross-app identifiers without age-gating is TP.

rules.name: AI or Chatbot Interaction Without Disclosure
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require clear, persistent signals when minors are interacting with AI rather than humans. AI features (chatbots, AI-generated responses, AI-powered filters) must be opt-in for minors, not automatically enabled.
rules.fix_suggestion: Display a clear, persistent, child-friendly indicator when a minor is interacting with AI rather than a human. AI chatbots, AI-generated content, and AI-powered features must require explicit opt-in for minor users. See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects AI chatbots, AI-generated content, or AI-powered features that interact with minors without clear, persistent disclosure that they are communicating with AI rather than humans. DSA requires such features to be opt-in for minors and never presented as human interaction.
tp_criteria: Chatbot or AI response handler is triggered without displaying a persistent 'AI' or 'Bot' label, badge, or disclosure visible to the minor user
AI-powered features (filters, content generation, recommendations labeled as AI) are enabled by default without an age-check or opt-in gate
Code routes minor user interactions to AI endpoints without any UI affordance, disclaimer, or toggle to disable AI interaction
fp_criteria: Code displays a persistent, clear disclosure (badge, label, or header) indicating AI interaction on every AI-generated response
AI features are gated behind an explicit opt-in that requires minor users to affirmatively enable AI interaction
Code is test data, documentation, or vendor library that does not itself render UI or handle user interaction
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS persistent AI disclosure (badge, label) visible on every AI response, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS an opt-in gate for minors before AI features are enabled, classify as FP.
AI-generated responses or interactions sent to minors without a UI disclosure label or opt-in control is TP.

rules.name: Ephemeral or Disappearing Content Feature
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require disappearing/ephemeral content features (Stories-style) to be disabled by default for minors. These features create urgency and FOMO, driving compulsive checking behavior.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable disappearing/ephemeral content features by default for minor users. If offered, ensure content expiration does not create artificial urgency. Allow minors to review content without time pressure. See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects disappearing or ephemeral content features (such as Stories-style posts that vanish after viewing) that are enabled by default for minors. These features create artificial urgency and FOMO (fear of missing out), driving compulsive checking behavior that DSA forbids without explicit opt-in.
tp_criteria: Ephemeral content UI (Stories, Snaps, temporary posts) is visible and functional by default for users without age verification or opt-in
Content expiration logic is active for minors without an age-check or explicit opt-in control
Notifications or reminders about disappearing content are sent to minors to create urgency, without age-gating or opt-out controls
fp_criteria: Ephemeral features are disabled, hidden, or non-functional for minor user accounts
Access to ephemeral content requires an explicit opt-in that is not pre-checked for minors, and age verification is performed before opt-in
Code is test, documentation, or vendor library that does not control content expiration or UI visibility
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-verification and disables ephemeral content for minors, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS an explicit, unchecked opt-in gate for ephemeral content that minors must affirmatively enable, classify as FP.
Ephemeral content features that are active by default without age-gating or opt-in is TP.

rules.name: Read Receipts or Typing Indicators Enabled by Default
rules.description: DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines require read receipts and typing indicators to be disabled by default for minor users. These features create social pressure to respond immediately and can enable monitoring and bullying.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable read receipts and typing indicators by default for minor users. Allow minors to choose whether to share their read status and typing activity. These features should require explicit opt-in. See DSA Article 28(1) Guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 6% of annual global turnover (DSA Article 52)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects read receipts and typing indicators that are enabled by default for minor users. These features create social pressure to respond immediately and enable monitoring and harassment, so DSA requires them to be disabled by default for minors.
tp_criteria: Read receipt or typing indicator feature is initialized as enabled without checking user age or requiring opt-in
Message metadata (delivery status, read status, typing status) is sent to other users by default for minor accounts
Settings or preferences show read receipts and typing indicators toggled on by default for minors without explicit opt-in
fp_criteria: Code implements age verification and disables read receipts and typing indicators for minor accounts
Read receipt and typing indicator features require an explicit opt-in that is not pre-checked for minors
Code is configuration, documentation, or test data that does not itself enable or transmit read receipt signals
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-verification and sets read receipts/typing indicators to disabled by default for minors, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS an unchecked opt-in gate that requires minors to explicitly enable read receipts before they function, classify as FP.
