Read receipt or typing indicator logic that transmits these signals to other users by default without age-gating is TP.

rules.name: Default Tracking Enabled
rules.description: CAADCA requires default high-privacy settings for children. Tracking, analytics, or telemetry must be OFF by default. Code that initializes tracking as enabled without explicit consent violates CAADCA Section 31(b)(7).
rules.fix_suggestion: Set tracking, analytics, and telemetry to OFF by default. Require explicit opt-in consent before enabling any data collection. Children should not be tracked by default under CAADCA.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects tracking, analytics, or telemetry that is initialized in an enabled state by default for child users. CAADCA requires high-privacy settings by default, meaning tracking must be explicitly opted-in by parents or disabled entirely for children under 13 unless legally required.
tp_criteria: Tracking SDK, analytics library, or telemetry service is initialized with tracking enabled and no age verification before initialization
Code sets tracking to enabled by default and relies on end-user opt-out rather than requiring affirmative opt-in for child accounts
Configuration enables data collection, event logging, or user identifier transmission without a child-safety flag or age-gate
fp_criteria: Tracking initialization includes age verification logic and skips or disables tracking if the user is under 13
Code initializes tracking in a disabled state and requires explicit parent consent or opt-in before data collection begins
Code is an import statement, SDK reference, or documentation that does not itself control initialization or data transmission
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age verification and disables or skips tracking initialization for children under 13, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS a parent-consent gate that must be affirmatively completed before tracking is enabled, classify as FP.
Tracking initialization with enabled=true or default enabled state without age verification or child-safety checks is TP.

rules.name: Analytics Without Privacy Mode
rules.description: CAADCA requires privacy-protective defaults. Analytics SDKs must be initialized with privacy mode, anonymization, or child-safe configuration. Code that initializes analytics without privacy protections may violate CAADCA.
rules.fix_suggestion: Initialize analytics with privacy mode enabled: anonymize IPs, disable user-level tracking, enable child-safe mode. Consider using privacy-preserving analytics alternatives.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects analytics SDKs or services that are initialized without privacy-protective defaults such as anonymization, data minimization, or child-safe mode. CAADCA requires analytics for children to be configured to minimize personal data collection and protect privacy by default.
tp_criteria: Analytics SDK is initialized without a privacy mode, anonymization flag, or child-safe configuration option set
Code initializes analytics with default settings that transmit personally identifiable information, device IDs, or IP addresses without anonymization
Analytics configuration does not disable marketing tracking, cross-site analytics, or user profiling features for child users
fp_criteria: Analytics initialization includes age verification and enables privacy mode or anonymization for users under 13
Code initializes analytics with explicit privacy-protective parameters (e.g., anonymize_ip=true, child_mode=true, marketing_tracking=false)
Code is documentation, vendor SDK reference, or test data that does not itself control analytics initialization settings
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS privacy-mode or anonymization flags during analytics initialization, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS age verification and applies child-safe analytics settings for users under 13, classify as FP.
Analytics initialization with default settings without privacy protections or child-mode flags is TP.

rules.name: Missing Age Estimation or Verification
rules.description: CAADCA Section 31(b)(1) requires businesses to estimate the age of child users with a reasonable level of certainty. Registration or signup flows that collect no age indicator violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add age estimation to your registration flow: collect date of birth, use an age estimation API, or implement neutral age screening. CAADCA requires 'reasonable certainty' that users are not children.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects registration, signup, or onboarding flows that do not collect or verify any age indicator. CAADCA Section 31(b)(1) requires businesses to estimate or verify the age of child users with reasonable certainty; flows that skip age collection entirely cannot demonstrate age compliance.
tp_criteria: Registration or signup form does not include any age-related question, date-of-birth field, or age estimation mechanism
Onboarding flow allows account creation without requesting birth date, age category, or parental consent indicator
Code path creates a user account without executing any age verification or age estimation function
fp_criteria: Registration flow includes a date-of-birth field, age slider, or age category selection that users must complete
Signup logic calls an age-verification function or service before account creation is finalized
Code is test data, mock, or vendor library that does not itself control account creation or user registration
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a date-of-birth or age field in the registration flow, classify as FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS an age-verification or age-estimation function call during signup, classify as FP.
A registration or signup flow that creates an account without requesting or verifying age is TP.

rules.name: Behavioral Profiling Without Safeguards
rules.description: CAADCA Section 31(b)(4) prohibits profiling children by default. Code that builds behavioral profiles, interest graphs, or user segments without age-checking or child safeguards violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable behavioral profiling by default for users who may be children. If profiling is necessary, implement age verification first and apply heightened protections for children under 18.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects code that builds behavioral profiles, interest graphs, or user segments from children's activity without age-checking or safeguards. Profiling children by default is prohibited under CAADCA Section 31(b)(4) because it enables targeted manipulation and privacy invasion.
tp_criteria: Code actively constructs user behavior profiles (e.g., interest_graph, behavior_cluster, user_segment) and passes them to personalization/targeting systems without checking user age
Tracking system collects sequential behavioral events and aggregates them into a profile that is used for downstream personalization without age gating
Code explicitly calls profiling functions or builds segment lists and applies them to content/ad delivery with no age verification guard
fp_criteria: Code is in a test suite or mock data generator that simulates profiling for testing purposes only
Profiling logic exists but is wrapped in a conditional that checks age and only executes for age >= 18 (adult mode)
Code imports profiling libraries or declares profiling classes/types without actually instantiating or executing profiling logic
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-checking before profile creation or personalization (e.g., `if (user.age >= 18) { createProfile() }`), it is FP.
If profiling is detected but explicitly disabled for children (feature flag or conditional), it is FP.
If code is within a test file, vendor library, or documentation example, it is FP.

rules.name: Content Recommendation Without Age Filter
rules.description: CAADCA requires transparent, age-appropriate content recommendations. Recommendation engines that lack age-based filtering or content rating checks may expose children to harmful content.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add age-based filtering to content recommendations. Implement content rating checks and exclude age-inappropriate material for child users. Make recommendation logic transparent per CAADCA requirements.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects recommendation engines that lack age-based filtering or content rating checks, which may expose children to harmful content. CAADCA requires recommendations to be transparent and age-appropriate.
tp_criteria: Recommendation algorithm fetches or ranks content without checking content_rating, maturity_level, or age_appropriate_flag before serving to user
Code calls a recommendation/suggestion function and returns results directly to children without filtering by age suitability
Recommendation ranking function explicitly ignores or bypasses content rating parameters when generating suggestions
fp_criteria: Recommendation system includes explicit age-based content filtering logic that validates content_rating against user age before display
Code is documentation or example showing how recommendations should NOT be implemented
Recommendation library is imported but not used, or recommendations are only shown to age >= 18 users via conditional gate
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS content filtering by age or maturity rating before recommendations are returned, it is FP.
If recommendations exist but are guarded by a user age check (e.g., `if (user.age >= 16) { recommendContent() }`), it is FP.
If code is in a test file or vendor library without active recommendation logic, it is FP.

rules.name: Manipulative Consent UI
rules.description: CAADCA Section 31(b)(7) prohibits dark patterns that lead children to provide unnecessary personal information, weaken privacy settings, or extend use. UI patterns like 'skip' or 'continue without' on consent screens are manipulative.

patterns.pattern: >\s*(?:Skip|No thanks|Not now|Maybe later|Continue without|I don't care)\s*<

rules.fix_suggestion: Present consent choices with equal visual weight. Don't make privacy-protective options harder to find or smaller than privacy-invasive options. Avoid manipulative language that pressures children to share data.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects manipulative consent UI patterns that trick children into providing unnecessary personal information or weakening privacy settings. CAADCA Section 31(b)(7) prohibits dark patterns like deceptive 'skip' or 'continue without' buttons that circumvent consent.
tp_criteria: Code renders a consent or permission dialog with a visually prominent 'skip', 'continue without', 'maybe later', or 'not now' button that bypasses data collection requirements
UI logic allows users to proceed without granting requested permissions by providing an easy non-consent path that is more prominent or easier than the consent button
Consent flow implements conditional logic where declining consent still allows data collection or still advances user through flow without friction
fp_criteria: Code implements a consent dialog where all buttons (accept/decline/skip) are equally sized and styled, and declining has equivalent friction to accepting
Dialog is only shown to users age >= 18 or in non-child mode
Code is in a documentation file, design spec, or negative example labeled as 'anti-pattern' or 'do not implement'
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS equal or greater friction for declining consent vs. accepting, it is FP.
If the UI includes a prominent decline/skip button but it triggers a clear, frictionless rejection (no data collection proceeds), it is FP.
If the consent flow is age-gated to exclude children, it is FP.

rules.name: Urgency-Creating Countdown Timer
rules.description: CAADCA prohibits dark patterns that exploit children. Countdown timers on offers, limited-time promotions, or fear-of-missing-out (FOMO) mechanics are manipulative design patterns targeting children.
rules.fix_suggestion: Remove urgency-creating countdown timers, FOMO mechanics, and limited-time pressure from child-facing interfaces. CAADCA prohibits manipulative design that exploits children's vulnerability to pressure tactics.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects countdown timers and FOMO mechanics (fear-of-missing-out) that exploit children into taking actions urgently. CAADCA prohibits such manipulative dark patterns that create artificial scarcity or urgency.
tp_criteria: Code implements a countdown timer displayed to children on an offer, promotion, or limited-time action with no genuine supply or time constraint
UI renders a timer that triggers urgency language ('offer expires in', 'limited spots', 'only X left') to pressure children into immediate action
Logic resets or restarts the countdown timer after expiration, creating a fake scarcity loop designed to re-engage children repeatedly
fp_criteria: Countdown timer is tied to a genuine system constraint (e.g., real inventory depletion, actual server maintenance window, or verifiable appointment slot availability)
Timer feature is only shown to users age >= 18 or is behind a 'disable_fomo_mechanics' toggle for child accounts
Code is in a test file, design documentation, or example labeled as anti-pattern or 'what not to do'
rule_logic: If the countdown timer is linked to a real, verifiable system event or supply constraint, it is FP.
If the timer is only active for adult users or is age-gated, it is FP.
If the code is in a test suite or documentation context, it is FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS timers for legitimate purposes (game mechanics, session timeout) without urgency language targeting children, it's FP — the rule flags manipulative countdown timers.

rules.name: Confirmshaming Pattern
rules.description: CAADCA prohibits manipulative design patterns that shame children into making privacy-invasive choices. Confirmshaming uses guilt-inducing language on opt-out or decline buttons.

patterns.pattern: >\s*(?:No,? I don't want|I prefer not to|I'll miss out|No,? I hate saving|I don't like)\s*

rules.fix_suggestion: Use neutral, non-manipulative language for all opt-out and decline options. Replace confirmshaming copy with straightforward alternatives like 'No thanks' or 'Decline'.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects confirmshaming patterns where guilt-inducing or shame language on decline buttons manipulates children into making privacy-invasive choices. CAADCA prohibits such manipulative design.
tp_criteria: Decline or opt-out button uses guilt-inducing language (e.g., 'No, I don't want to be safe', 'Reject and receive worse recommendations', 'Decline to lower your privacy')
Opt-out button is labeled with negative self-referential language that implies shame or poor judgment by declining (e.g., 'I prefer spyware')
UI presents asymmetric button language where accept button is positive ('Yes, protect me') while decline is shaming ('No, leave me vulnerable')
fp_criteria: Decline button uses neutral, non-emotional language (e.g., 'No thanks', 'Skip', 'Decline') without shame or guilt framing
Both accept and decline buttons use equivalent, non-manipulative language without emotional loading
Code is in a design specification or example explicitly labeled as anti-pattern or negative example
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the decline button uses neutral language without emotional manipulation, it is FP.
If both buttons are framed symmetrically without guilt or shame language, it is FP.
If the code is documentation or anti-pattern example, it is FP.
If the code IMPLEMENTS clear opt-out options without manipulative or guilt-inducing language, it's FP — the rule flags confirmshaming patterns.

rules.name: Precise Geolocation Without Purpose
rules.description: CAADCA Section 31(b)(3) restricts collecting children's precise geolocation. Code that requests fine-grained location (GPS) without a clear, necessary purpose violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Use coarse/approximate location (city-level) instead of precise GPS coordinates. Only request fine-grained location when strictly necessary for core functionality. Never persistently track a child's location.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects code that requests fine-grained geolocation (GPS) from children without a clear, necessary purpose. CAADCA Section 31(b)(3) restricts collecting precise location data due to safety and tracking risks.
tp_criteria: Code calls a GPS/precise location API (e.g., requestLocationPermission, getLatitude/getLongitude) without a documented safety-critical or service-essential use case
Fine-grained location is collected and stored or transmitted without a clear mapping to a necessary feature (e.g., location requested but not used by any service logic)
Location data is collected at high frequency (e.g., continuous tracking) without explicit purpose or user control, and no age verification prevents collection from minors
fp_criteria: Code requests location but is wrapped in age-check that only executes for users age >= 18
Location collection is tied to a genuine, documented safety feature (e.g., 'lost child' alert, emergency service) or core service requirement with parental consent
Code is requesting coarse location (country/region level) rather than precise GPS coordinates
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-gating or age verification before requesting fine-grained location, it is FP.
If precise location is collected for a documented safety-critical feature with parental consent, it is FP.
If code is requesting coarse location or is in a test/documentation context, it is FP.

rules.name: Excessive Data Collection
rules.description: CAADCA Section 31(b)(3) requires data minimization — only collect personal information that is reasonably necessary. Code that collects extensive personal data fields beyond what the service needs may violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Only collect data that is strictly necessary for the service's core functionality. Remove collection of non-essential fields. Implement data minimization by design per CAADCA requirements.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects excessive data collection beyond what is reasonably necessary for the service. CAADCA Section 31(b)(3) requires data minimization; collecting extensive personal information fields (e.g., health, biometrics, SSN) without necessity violates this principle.
tp_criteria: Code collects personal data fields (e.g., SSN, biometric data, health status, religious affiliation) that are not used by any documented service feature
Data collection form requests 10+ personal information fields when the service only needs 2-3 fields to function
Code stores or transmits sensitive personal categories (financial account details, family structure, medical history) without a clear functional requirement for them
fp_criteria: Data fields collected are each tied to explicit, documented service features that require them
Data collection is age-gated to exclude children (e.g., only collected from age >= 18 users)
Code is in a test file, documentation, or example showing how NOT to collect data
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS purpose-limited data collection with each field mapped to a necessary feature, it is FP.
If data collection is age-restricted to adults only, it is FP.
If code is in a test or documentation context, it is FP.

rules.name: One-Click Purchase Without Confirmation
rules.description: CAADCA requires friction in purchase flows for children. One-click or instant purchases without a confirmation step can lead to unauthorized spending by minors.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add a confirmation step before any purchase. Require explicit confirmation (e.g., 'Are you sure?' dialog) before processing payments. For children, require parental authentication for purchases.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects one-click or instant in-app purchases without confirmation steps. CAADCA requires friction in purchase flows for children to prevent unauthorized spending by minors who may not understand financial consequences.
tp_criteria: Purchase code executes a transaction immediately upon button click without displaying a confirmation dialog, PIN entry, or second verification step
Purchase function skips confirmation logic and directly charges or debits without requiring explicit confirmation from the user
Code implements 'one-tap checkout' or 'instant buy' without any confirmation UI layer between purchase intent and transaction execution
fp_criteria: Code implements a confirmation dialog or verification step (e.g., 'Are you sure you want to purchase?', PIN entry, biometric confirmation) before transaction executes
Purchase flow is age-gated to only allow one-click purchases for users age >= 18
Code is in a test file, documentation, or negative example labeled 'do not implement'
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a confirmation step between purchase intent and execution, it is FP.
If one-click purchase is only enabled for age >= 18 users, it is FP.
If code is in a test or documentation context, it is FP.

rules.name: In-App Purchase Without Parental Gate
rules.description: CAADCA requires parental consent for financial transactions involving children. In-app purchase flows that don't check for age or parental authorization expose children to unauthorized spending.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add parental authentication or consent before allowing in-app purchases for users who may be children. Implement age-gating and require parental approval for virtual currency purchases.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects in-app purchase flows that don't check for age or parental authorization. CAADCA requires parental consent for financial transactions involving children to prevent unauthorized spending.
tp_criteria: In-app purchase function executes without calling an age-verification check or parental consent validation function
Code allows purchase completion for any user without confirming age >= 18 or validating parental authorization token/PIN
Purchase flow skips all authentication/authorization steps and proceeds directly from product selection to payment
fp_criteria: Code implements age-verification before purchase (e.g., `if (user.age < 18) { requestParentalConsent() }`)
Purchase requires parental PIN, biometric, or explicit consent token before transaction executes
Code is in a test file, vendor SDK documentation, or example showing required controls
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-checking and parental consent validation before purchase, it is FP.
If purchase is guarded by parental authentication/authorization, it is FP.
If code is in test or documentation context, it is FP.

rules.name: Push Notifications Without Frequency Limit
rules.description: CAADCA prohibits features that encourage excessive use by children. Push notifications without frequency limits or quiet hours can manipulate children into compulsive engagement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement notification frequency limits and quiet hours for child users. Disable streak-based and FOMO notifications. Allow children to control notification settings easily.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects push notification systems without frequency limits or quiet hours, which can manipulate children into compulsive engagement. CAADCA prohibits features that encourage excessive use.
tp_criteria: Push notification code sends notifications without checking daily or hourly frequency limits, allowing unlimited notifications to children
Notification system lacks quiet hours configuration and can send notifications during typical sleep hours (e.g., 10 PM - 8 AM)
Notification logic includes engagement-maximizing patterns (e.g., staggered reminders, repeated notifications for same action, high-priority flags on low-urgency items)
fp_criteria: Code implements notification frequency limits (e.g., max 5 per day) and respects quiet hours configuration
Notification system is age-gated to exclude children or is only fully enabled for age >= 18 users
Code is in a test file or documentation example
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS frequency caps or quiet hours for notifications, it is FP.
If notification system is age-restricted to adults, it is FP.
If code is in test or documentation context, it is FP.

rules.name: Missing Child-Friendly Privacy Notice
rules.description: CAADCA Section 31(b)(6) requires privacy information to be provided in clear, age-appropriate language. Registration forms and data collection points must include prominent, child-friendly privacy disclosures.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add a clear, child-friendly privacy notice to all data collection points. Use simple language explaining what data is collected, why, and who has access. Include a prominent link to your privacy policy.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects registration forms and data collection points that lack child-friendly privacy notices required by CAADCA. Clear, age-appropriate privacy disclosures are essential for children's apps to comply with transparency requirements and build trust with young users and parents.
tp_criteria: Code implements a registration or signup form that collects personal data (name, email, location, device ID) without displaying a privacy notice or disclosure modal to the user
Privacy notice exists but uses adult-level legal language (e.g., 'Processing of personal data pursuant to GDPR Article 6') rather than plain language suitable for children
Data collection occurs (e.g., location tracking, camera access, contact list sync) without any corresponding disclosure step visible to the child user before or immediately after collection
fp_criteria: Code is located in a test suite, mock implementation, or staging-only module not deployed to production
Privacy notice is implemented in a parent/guardian consent flow or admin dashboard, not in the child-facing user interface
Code imports or references a third-party privacy notice library (e.g., privacy notice component from shared design system) that is documented as CAADCA-compliant
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a child-friendly privacy disclosure or notice component (plain language, visual design, age-appropriate tone), it's FP regardless of detection heuristics.
Privacy notices displayed only in terms-of-service documents or footer links do not satisfy the 'prominent' requirement—they must appear at or before the point of data collection.

rules.name: Targeted Advertising to Children
rules.description: CAADCA Section 31(b)(4) prohibits profiling children for targeted advertising. Code that serves behavioral or targeted ads without age verification violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disable targeted and behavioral advertising for users who may be children. Use only contextual (non-personalized) ads. Implement age verification before serving personalized advertising.
rules.penalty: $2,500-$7,500 per affected child

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects code that serves targeted or behavioral advertisements to children without age verification. CAADCA prohibits profiling minors for advertising purposes to prevent manipulation and exploitation of children through personalized ad targeting.
tp_criteria: Code implements ad selection or personalization logic that uses behavioral data (user activity, session history, interaction patterns, inferred interests) to choose which ads to display, without preceding age verification
Ad serving code conditionally targets users based on demographic inferences (e.g., 'if age < 18, use generic ads') but the age determination relies on unverified self-declaration or device heuristics
Code loads or initializes advertising SDKs (e.g., Google Ads, Facebook Audience Network) that are configured to enable behavioral targeting on user segments that include children
fp_criteria: Code implements age-gated ad delivery: behavioral targeting is blocked or disabled for users who fail age verification, with fallback to non-targeted (contextual) ads
Ads are served based only on page context or content category (contextual advertising), not on user behavioral data or profile
Code is in an admin panel, configuration file, or documentation describing ad policies, not in the runtime ad-serving path
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age verification before ad personalization, it's FP even if ad serving code is present elsewhere.
Contextual ads (ads selected based on current page content, not user history) do not constitute targeted advertising and are compliant—only behavioral/profile-based ad selection triggers this rule.

rules.name: Missing Age Verification at Registration
rules.description: Account creation or signup flow detected without age verification. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 (as amended 2024) s.63B requires social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify that users are aged 16 or over before allowing account creation. Registration flows must include age assurance mechanisms — not just self-declaration.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add an age verification step before account creation. Under AU OSA s.63B, social media services must use reasonably effective age assurance to prevent under-16s from creating accounts. Implement identity-based verification (document check, biometric estimation, or digital ID) — not just self-declaration.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects signup or account creation flows that allow users to register without age verification. The AU Online Safety Act requires social media platforms to verify users are 16+ before creating accounts, not merely collect a self-declared age. Simple checkboxes or unverified date fields do not satisfy this requirement.
tp_criteria: Registration endpoint or form accepts account creation requests without calling an age verification service or technology (e.g., API call to age assurance provider, ID document verification, or cryptographic proof)
Signup flow only collects a date-of-birth field or 'I am 16+' checkbox without backend validation, verification API call, or confirmation logic
Account creation completes and is marked as 'active' or 'verified' immediately upon form submission, with no age verification step in the workflow before the account can be used
fp_criteria: Code implements integration with a documented age assurance provider (e.g., Yoti, Aware3D, or similar service with cryptographic verification)
Signup flow includes a backend age verification step: database lookup, third-party API call, or cryptographic validation occurs before account activation
Code is in a test environment, staging API, or admin-only registration endpoint, not in the public-facing signup flow
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age verification technology (calls to age assurance APIs, ID verification, or cryptographic proof validation), it's FP.

Self-declaration alone (user provides DOB and form checks if calculated age >= 16 client-side or server-side) is a violation—'reasonable steps' requires technology-based assurance, not math on unverified input.

rules.name: Self-Declaration Age Check
rules.description: Reliance on self-declared age (checkbox, simple DOB field without verification) detected. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 (as amended 2024) s.63C requires 'reasonably effective' age assurance — simple self-declaration (e.g., 'I am over 16' checkbox or unverified date-of-birth entry) does not meet this threshold. Platforms must use technology-based age assurance methods.
rules.fix_suggestion: Replace self-declaration age checks with a reasonably effective age assurance method. AU OSA s.63C requires technology-based verification such as biometric age estimation, digital identity document checks, or government-issued digital ID verification. A simple checkbox or unverified DOB field is insufficient.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects age verification that relies solely on self-declared information such as checkboxes or unverified date-of-birth entry. The AU Online Safety Act requires 'reasonably effective' age assurance, which prohibits simple self-declaration and mandates technology-based verification methods.
tp_criteria: Code implements age checking logic that only validates: if (parsedDOB.getFullYear() >= currentYear - 16) or similar birthday arithmetic, without calling an external age verification API or service
Registration form includes only a checkbox (e.g., 'I confirm I am 16 or older') or a date input field, with no backend verification call or third-party validation
Age verification is performed on the client-side (JavaScript age calculation) or via a simple database lookup without external age assurance service integration
fp_criteria: Code calls an external age verification service API (Yoti, Aware, government ID verification, etc.) to validate age before account approval
Age verification includes document upload, ID scanning, biometric checks, or other technology-based methods beyond date entry
Code is in documentation, comments, or a configuration file describing what age verification should be, not in the actual runtime implementation
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a call to an external age assurance technology provider, it's FP regardless of whether self-declaration code also exists elsewhere.
Client-side age calculation from unverified date input is always a violation—the platform cannot trust user-provided DOB without external verification.

rules.name: Missing Under-16 Account Purge
rules.description: Underage user detection without corresponding account deletion or data purge mechanism. When a social media platform determines a user is under 16, the AU Online Safety Act 2021 (as amended 2024) s.63D requires the platform to close the account and delete associated personal data. Failing to purge underage accounts exposes the platform to enforcement action by the eSafety Commissioner.
rules.fix_suggestion: When a user is determined to be under 16, immediately close the account and delete all associated personal data. Implement an automated purge pipeline triggered by underage detection. AU OSA s.63D requires platforms to take reasonable steps to close accounts and remove data of users found to be under the minimum age.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects logic that identifies underage users but fails to automatically delete their accounts and associated data. The AU Online Safety Act requires platforms to purge underage accounts and personal data upon detection to prevent ongoing harm and regulatory violation.
tp_criteria: Code detects a user is under 16 (via age verification failure, underage account discovery, or manual admin action) but does not trigger account deletion, data purge, or deactivation within the same workflow
Logging, alert, or notification code identifies an underage user but subsequent code only flags the account for manual review without automatic deletion or immediate data purge
Age re-verification or compliance check detects a user registered with false age information, but the codebase contains no automatic account closure or data deletion routine
fp_criteria: Code implements automatic account deletion or data purge workflow triggered by underage detection (account marked for deletion, all personal data cleared from primary and backup storage)
Underage account handling is delegated to a documented external service or compliance tool that handles deletion (e.g., third-party data purge service with contract verification)
Code is in a test module, staging environment, or documentation describing the intended deletion process, not in production account management
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS automatic account deletion and data purge upon underage detection, it's FP regardless of other account management logic.
Manual review flags or alerts without automatic deletion are violations—'close the account and delete' (s.63D) requires automated execution, not manual intervention.

rules.name: Class 1/Class 2 Content Without Moderation
rules.description: User-generated content upload or submission detected without content moderation, classification, or safety scanning. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 Schedule 2 classifies illegal content as Class 1 (e.g., CSAM, terrorism) and harmful content as Class 2 (e.g., violence, self-harm). Platforms must proactively detect and prevent distribution of such material under s.109 (BOSE determination).
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement content moderation before or immediately after content upload. Use automated scanning for Class 1 material (CSAM hash matching via PhotoDNA or similar), and classification/filtering for Class 2 material (violence, self-harm). AU OSA Schedule 2 and BOSE s.109 require proactive detection and rapid removal.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects user-generated content upload or submission flows that lack content moderation, classification, or safety scanning. The AU Online Safety Act requires platforms to proactively detect and prevent distribution of Class 1 (illegal, e.g., CSAM) and Class 2 (harmful, e.g., violence, self-harm) content.
tp_criteria: Content upload endpoint accepts and publishes user-generated content (images, video, text) without calling a content moderation API, classifier, or scanning service
Code validates only file type and size (e.g., 'if file.size < 100MB && file.type in [jpg, png]') without semantic content analysis or moderation check
Submitted content is immediately stored, indexed, and made visible to other users without a moderation queue, scanning delay, or safety check
fp_criteria: Code implements integration with a content moderation service (e.g., AWS Rekognition, Google Vision, Crisp Thinking, or similar) and blocks/quarantines flagged content
Upload flow includes automatic virus/malware scanning and policy classification before content is published
Code is in a documentation file, configuration template, or test stub, not in the actual content ingestion pipeline
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS content moderation, classification, or scanning before publishing user-generated content, it's FP.
File type/size validation alone is not content moderation—semantic analysis or external moderation service calls are required to detect harmful content.

rules.name: Content Removal SLA Non-Compliance
rules.description: Content reporting or flagging mechanism detected without time-bound removal or escalation workflow. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 s.88 empowers the eSafety Commissioner to issue removal notices requiring compliance within 24 hours. Platforms must have automated escalation and removal pipelines to meet this SLA.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement a time-bound content removal pipeline. AU OSA s.88 removal notices require compliance within 24 hours. Add SLA tracking, automated escalation for unresolved reports, and priority queuing for eSafety Commissioner notices. Ensure removal timestamps are logged for compliance auditing.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects content reporting mechanisms without time-bound removal or escalation workflows. The AU Online Safety Act empowers the eSafety Commissioner to issue removal notices requiring compliance within 24 hours; platforms must have automated pipelines to meet this SLA.
tp_criteria: Code implements a 'Report' or 'Flag Content' button/API endpoint that records the report but does not trigger any automated escalation, review queue, or removal workflow
Reported content handling stores the report in a database with no associated timeout, escalation logic, or SLA tracking for removal
Content report workflow requires manual admin review without automated priority queuing, timeout escalation, or status tracking tied to a 24-hour deadline
fp_criteria: Code implements automated escalation: reports trigger immediate content quarantine, move to a review queue with SLA tracking, or initiate a timed removal workflow
Removal logic includes time-bound checks (e.g., 'if report.age > 24 hours, auto-remove') or integration with a ticket system that enforces SLA timers
Code is in documentation or a policy file describing reporting procedures, not in the report handling implementation
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS time-bound escalation or automatic removal triggered by reported content age, it's FP.
Manual review without SLA enforcement is a violation—the 24-hour removal requirement needs automated timing and escalation logic.

rules.name: Minor Data Retention Without TTL
rules.description: Storage of child or minor user data without time-to-live, retention policy, or automatic deletion mechanism. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE determination (s.109) and Privacy Act 1988 APP 11.2 require data minimization and defined retention limits for personal information, particularly for minors. Data must not be kept longer than necessary.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add retention limits (TTL, expiresAt, or retention policy) to all data stores containing minor user information. Implement automated purge mechanisms. AU OSA BOSE (s.109) expects data minimization, and Privacy Act 1988 APP 11.2 requires deletion when data is no longer needed for its collected purpose.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects storage of child or minor user data without defined retention policies, time-to-live (TTL), or automatic deletion mechanisms. The AU Online Safety Act and Privacy Act require data minimization and automatic purging of personal information, especially for minors, to prevent unnecessary retention.
tp_criteria: Code stores personal data (name, email, location, activity logs, session records) for underage users without setting a TTL, deletion timestamp, or retention policy in the database schema
Data retention configuration has no defined maximum retention period: user records persist indefinitely or are only deleted via manual intervention
Database schema for minor user accounts contains no automatic cleanup, no scheduled deletion job, and no timestamp field tracking when the record should be purged
fp_criteria: Code implements automatic deletion: database records include a TTL field, or a scheduled job (cron, Lambda, etc.) periodically deletes minor data older than a defined retention period
Data retention policy is explicitly configured: code comments or schema migrations document maximum retention (e.g., 'delete after 90 days' or 'purge on account closure')
Code is in a configuration file or policy document, not in the actual data storage or cleanup implementation
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS automatic TTL-based deletion or scheduled purging of minor user data, it's FP.
Indefinite retention of personal data for minors violates APP 11.2 and Privacy Act principles—even if retention is 'for business purposes,' no mechanism for automatic deletion is non-compliant.

rules.name: Missing Safety Impact Assessment Hook
rules.description: Feature launch, deployment, or rollout code detected without a safety assessment or risk evaluation step. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE determination (s.109) expects platforms to proactively assess the safety impact of new features before deployment, particularly features that affect minors or user-generated content.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add a safety impact assessment gate before feature launches. Create a safetyReview() or impactAssessment() hook that evaluates potential harms to minors, content moderation implications, and regulatory compliance before enabling new features. AU OSA BOSE (s.109) expects proactive safety evaluation.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects feature launches, deployments, or rollout code that lacks a safety assessment or risk evaluation step. The AU Online Safety Act BOSE determination expects platforms to proactively assess safety impact before deploying new features, particularly those affecting minors or user-generated content.
tp_criteria: Feature flag, deployment, or release code path does not call or reference a safety assessment function, checklist, or approval workflow before enabling the feature
New feature affecting user-generated content, messaging, or child safety rolls out without documented risk assessment or approval from a safety/compliance team
Code enables a feature for all users (or all minors) without a prior safety review gate or deployment condition checking for assessment completion
fp_criteria: Code implements a safety assessment hook: feature deployment is conditioned on a safety_assessment_completed flag, or calls a review_safety_impact() function
Feature launch includes documentation linking to a safety impact assessment or risk review performed before deployment
Code is a feature toggle or configuration that explicitly gates deployment pending safety review (e.g., 'deploy_if(safety_approved == true)')
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a conditional deployment gate or safety assessment hook, it's FP.
Assessment documentation alone (comments, linked tickets) without a code-level deployment gate is insufficient—the rule checks for execution-time safety checks.

rules.name: Missing Transparency Report Generation
rules.description: Platform analytics, metrics, or reporting infrastructure detected without transparency report generation for safety compliance. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE determination (s.109) requires platforms to publish transparency reports covering content removal statistics, complaint resolution rates, and safety enforcement actions.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement transparency report generation that publishes safety statistics including: content removal counts by category, average removal time, complaint resolution rates, and eSafety Commissioner notice compliance. AU OSA BOSE (s.109) requires platforms to be transparent about their safety practices.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects platform analytics, metrics, or reporting infrastructure that lacks transparency report generation for safety compliance. The AU Online Safety Act BOSE determination requires platforms to publish transparency reports covering content removal statistics, complaint resolution rates, and enforcement actions.
tp_criteria: Code implements metrics collection or logging for content moderation, complaints, and enforcement actions but does not aggregate, summarize, or export data for transparency reporting
Analytics events are logged (e.g., 'content_removed', 'complaint_received', 'account_suspended') without corresponding report generation, export, or publication pipeline
Reporting infrastructure exists for internal dashboards but no public-facing or external report generation functionality is present
fp_criteria: Code implements a transparency report generator: function aggregates moderation metrics, complaint data, or enforcement statistics into a structured report format
Reporting pipeline exports transparency data to a file, API endpoint, or publishing system with scheduled updates
Code is in documentation or a roadmap file describing planned transparency reporting, not in the actual implementation
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS transparency report generation (aggregation, export, or publication of safety metrics), it's FP.
Internal metrics and dashboards alone do not satisfy transparency requirements—public-facing report generation or export is required.

rules.name: Third-Party SDK Without Safety Vetting
rules.description: Third-party SDK, script, or external library loading detected without safety vetting or allowlisting. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE determination (s.109) requires platforms to ensure third-party services integrated into their products also comply with online safety requirements. Unvetted third-party code may introduce content safety, data handling, or age-verification gaps.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement a third-party SDK vetting process. Maintain an allowlist of approved SDKs and verify each third-party integration for AU OSA compliance before deployment. Ensure third-party services handle minor data appropriately and support content moderation requirements. AU OSA BOSE (s.109) extends safety expectations to third-party integrations.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when third-party SDKs, scripts, or external libraries are loaded into the application without evidence of safety vetting or being on an approved allowlist. Unvetted third-party code can introduce content safety gaps, improper data handling, or missing age-verification controls that violate the AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE requirements.
tp_criteria: Code dynamically loads or imports an external SDK/library from a remote URL without any local allowlist lookup or vetting check
Third-party service is initialized with full permissions without any safety validation, data filtering, or compliance checks before use
Application integrates with third-party analytics, advertising, or content delivery service without evidence of vendor safety certification or contractual compliance clauses
fp_criteria: SDK is loaded within a test file, mock setup, or development-only conditional block
Third-party library is a well-known, industry-standard package from a major vendor (e.g., React, jQuery, Firebase) with standard npm/package manager installation
Code contains explicit allowlist checking logic that validates the SDK source against a maintained approved vendors list before initialization
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a vetting mechanism (allowlist check, vendor validation function, or compliance certificate verification), it's FP
If the SDK is loaded with explicit safety controls such as content filtering, data sanitization, or limited permission scopes, consider whether vetting evidence exists; missing evidence = TP

rules.name: Missing Complaint Mechanism
rules.description: User-facing feature, dashboard, or settings page detected without an accessible complaint or safety reporting mechanism. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 s.46 requires platforms to provide users (including parents and guardians) with a clear and accessible way to report online safety concerns, including cyberbullying, harmful content, and image-based abuse.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add an accessible complaint and safety reporting mechanism to all user-facing pages. Users must be able to report cyberbullying, harmful content, and image-based abuse. AU OSA s.46 requires platforms to provide clear reporting pathways and respond to complaints in a timely manner.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects user-facing features, dashboards, or settings pages that lack an accessible mechanism for users (including parents and guardians) to report safety concerns such as cyberbullying, harmful content, or abuse. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 s.46 mandates that platforms provide clear, accessible reporting pathways.
tp_criteria: User dashboard or settings page is rendered without any visible report button, complaint form, or safety reporting link
Code explicitly handles user interactions on a content page or messaging interface but contains no event handler or function call to trigger a complaint submission workflow
Application has community features (comments, user profiles, messaging) but the code shows no routing, modal, or UI component dedicated to safety reporting
fp_criteria: Code is part of the complaint/reporting mechanism itself (e.g., the form handler, submission endpoint, or thank-you confirmation page)
Report feature is implemented but located in an admin-only or backend settings area not accessible to regular users
Documentation, comments, or type definitions describe the reporting feature (proof of design intention), even if UI implementation is incomplete
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a complaint submission form, report handler, or safety reporting API endpoint, it's FP
If the code renders a user-facing page or feature but contains no reference to reporting mechanisms, it's TP
If a feature is marked as 'coming soon' or conditionally disabled in the UI but the infrastructure exists, it's FP

rules.name: Cross-Border Minor Data Transfer
rules.description: Transfer of child or minor user data to overseas servers, regions, or third-party international endpoints detected without adequate protection controls. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE (s.109) and Privacy Act 1988 APP 8 require that personal information transferred overseas receives equivalent protection. For minors' data, additional safeguards are expected.
rules.fix_suggestion: Ensure minor data transferred internationally has equivalent protection. Implement encryption in transit, verify the receiving jurisdiction's data protection adequacy, and document safeguards. AU Privacy Act 1988 APP 8 requires reasonable steps to ensure overseas recipients handle data consistently with Australian Privacy Principles. BOSE (s.109) heightens expectations for minors.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when child or minor user data is transferred to overseas servers, regions, or international third-party endpoints without adequate protection controls. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE and Privacy Act 1988 APP 8 require that personal information transferred overseas receives equivalent protection, with minors' data requiring additional safeguards.
tp_criteria: Code identifies a user as a minor or child and then sends their personal data (name, contact info, behavioral data, device ID) to an international API endpoint or cloud region without encryption, anonymization, or contractual safeguards
API call or data upload function contains no age-gating, data minimization, or regional routing logic — minor user data flows to overseas servers by default
Application transfers minor user profile data to international third-party services (analytics, advertising, CDN) without evidence of Data Processing Agreements or equivalent protection clauses
fp_criteria: Data transfer occurs only after explicit user/parental consent is verified and logged, with clear disclosure of the overseas destination
Transfer is of anonymized, hashed, or pseudonymized data that cannot be linked back to individual minors
Code implements regional data routing that ensures minor data remains within Australian jurisdiction or approved partner regions with contractual equivalence
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-based data routing (e.g., 'if minor, store locally; if adult, allow overseas'), it's FP
If the code IMPLEMENTS data minimization for overseas transfers (e.g., stripping PII before international API calls), assess whether minors' data is still exposed; if yes, it's TP
If overseas transfer is conditional on explicit parental consent with proof of verification, it's FP

rules.name: Age-Restricted Content Without Re-Authentication
rules.description: Access to age-restricted, mature, or harmful content categories detected without re-authentication or age re-verification. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 s.109 BOSE expectations and the Restricted Access System Declaration require platforms to implement stepped access controls — users must re-verify their age or identity before viewing restricted content, even if previously authenticated.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement re-authentication or age re-verification before serving age-restricted content. Even if a user is already logged in, access to R18+ or MA15+ classified content should require a step-up verification (biometric, PIN, or identity re-check). AU OSA Restricted Access System Declaration and BOSE (s.109) require robust access controls for restricted material.
rules.penalty: Up to AUD $49.5M (body corporate) or AUD $2.475M (individual)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when age-restricted, mature, or harmful content is accessible without re-authentication or age re-verification at the point of access. The AU Online Safety Act 2021 BOSE expects platforms to implement stepped access controls — users must re-verify age or identity before viewing restricted content, even after initial authentication.
tp_criteria: Code renders a content page marked as age-restricted or mature but does not call an age-verification or re-authentication check function before displaying that content
Application checks user age only at initial signup but allows full access to restricted content categories later without prompting for re-verification
Content filtering or access control logic relies solely on a cached age flag from the user session without requesting fresh age verification at restricted content access time
fp_criteria: Code implements a re-authentication or age re-verification modal/form that triggers before restricted content is displayed
Restricted content rendering is behind a function that calls an age-verification API and blocks display until verification succeeds
Code is part of an admin or parent control interface where stepped verification is implemented to override child access
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age re-verification (e.g., modal request, re-auth check) at the restricted content access point, it's FP
If restricted content is rendered without any re-verification call in the display logic, it's TP
If a content access function checks `isAgeVerified` flag from cache without calling a fresh verification, it's TP

rules.name: Unconsented Behavioral Profiling
rules.description: Behavioral profiling of children without explicit opt-in consent violates EU AI Act Art. 9. Analytics platforms must gate identify() calls behind verified consent.
rules.fix_suggestion: Gate user identification behind explicit consent: if (hasParentalConsent) { analytics.identify(...) }
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects behavioral profiling of children without explicit opt-in consent, which violates EU AI Act Article 9. Analytics platforms must gate identify() calls and profiling operations behind verified, documented consent mechanisms to ensure children's behavioral data is not collected without parental/user agreement.
tp_criteria: Code calls analytics.identify() or similar profiling function with child user data without checking a consent flag or requiring explicit consent verification first
Behavioral tracking, feature usage logging, or user profiling is enabled by default for all users, including identified minors, with no opt-in gate
Application collects child behavioral data (interaction patterns, preferences, engagement metrics) for profiling without storing proof of parental or child consent
fp_criteria: Code contains a consent gate that checks `hasProfileConsent` or similar flag before any identify() or profiling call is executed
Profiling calls are wrapped in a conditional that confirms child age and enforces parental consent verification before execution
Code is in a testing/mock environment or is part of the consent management UI itself (not the profiling enforcement point)
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a consent check before identify() (e.g., 'if (hasConsent) analytics.identify()'), it's FP
If identify() or behavioral profiling is called without a preceding consent verification, it's TP
If profiling is conditional on age and parental consent is verified before execution, it's FP

rules.name: Algorithmic Manipulation Without Audit
rules.description: Content recommendation algorithms targeting children must have audit trails per EU AI Act Art. 9. Ranking and recommendation functions need logging hooks.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add audit logging to recommendation functions: log input features, output ranking, and model version for each recommendation served.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects content recommendation algorithms targeting children without audit trails or logging hooks. The EU AI Act Article 9 requires that ranking and recommendation functions targeting children have documented audit mechanisms to track algorithmic decisions and enable oversight of potential manipulation.
tp_criteria: Code implements a recommendation or ranking algorithm that selects content for display to minors but contains no logging function call that records the algorithm's decision, inputs, or reasoning
Recommendation function returns ranked content without calling any audit log, event tracking, or decision record function
Application personalizes content feeds for child users through algorithmic ranking but has no hooks for external audit, inspection, or decision transparency
fp_criteria: Recommendation function calls a logging or audit function (e.g., logAlgorithmicDecision(), auditTrail.record()) that captures the algorithm's inputs, outputs, and decision factors
Code contains instrumentation that records ranking decisions, scores, and reasoning to an audit log accessible for compliance review
Recommendation logic is wrapped in a function that emits audit events or structured logs for each algorithmic decision
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS audit logging for algorithmic decisions (e.g., log calls after recommendation selection), it's FP
If a recommendation function runs without any audit trail instrumentation, it's TP
If recommendation decisions are logged to a tamper-evident audit system, it's FP

rules.name: ML Model Without Fairness Testing
rules.description: ML models processing children's data must undergo bias and fairness testing per EU AI Act Art. 9. Training pipelines need documented fairness checks.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add fairness testing to ML pipeline: run bias audits (demographic parity, equalized odds) before deploying models that affect children.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects ML models processing children's data without documented bias and fairness testing. The EU AI Act Article 9 requires that training pipelines for models handling child data include documented fairness checks and bias mitigation to prevent discriminatory outcomes.
tp_criteria: Code trains or deploys an ML model using child user data without any fairness_check(), bias_test(), or validation function call in the training pipeline
Model training script processes child data but contains no documented fairness metrics, bias detection logic, or test assertions for equitable outcomes
ML model is validated only on accuracy metrics without any fairness evaluation, demographic parity checks, or bias audit functions
fp_criteria: Model training pipeline includes explicit fairness_check() or bias_mitigation() function calls with documented test results
Training code contains assertions or validation checks for fairness metrics (e.g., demographic parity, calibration) specific to child data cohorts
Documentation or comments in the training code reference completed fairness testing and bias mitigation steps with test coverage
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS fairness testing or bias detection functions in the ML pipeline, it's FP
If ML training processes child data without any fairness test or bias check function calls, it's TP
If fairness testing is documented in comments but not implemented as code, it's FP (design intention); if no mention exists, it's TP

rules.name: Synthetic Content Without Labeling
rules.description: AI-generated images, text, or audio must be clearly labeled per EU AI Act Art. 50. Children especially need visible disclosure of synthetic content.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add visible AI-generated content labels: include 'AI Generated' badge/watermark on all synthetic media shown to children.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects AI-generated images, text, or audio displayed to children without clear labeling disclosing their synthetic nature. The EU AI Act Article 50 requires visible disclosure of synthetic or AI-generated content, especially to children who may be vulnerable to confusion or misinformation.
tp_criteria: Code renders an AI-generated image, text, or audio asset to a user identified as a child without displaying a label, badge, or disclosure stating it is synthetic or AI-created
Application retrieves content from an AI generation API and displays it in a child-facing interface without adding a 'synthetic,' 'AI-generated,' or 'created by AI' indicator
Content rendering logic shows no conditional logic that adds disclosure metadata or visible labels to synthetic content before presentation to minors
fp_criteria: Code adds a visible label, badge, watermark, or disclaimer (e.g., 'This image was created by AI') before displaying generated content to children
AI-generated content is wrapped in a component or function that enforces disclosure labeling before rendering
Content is generated and labeled only in non-child contexts or admin interfaces, or is explicitly excluded from child display
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a disclosure label or synthetic content badge before child-facing content display, it's FP
If AI-generated content is displayed to children without a visible disclosure function being called, it's TP
If synthetic content carries metadata but no visible label is rendered, assess child visibility; if child can see it unlabeled, it's TP

rules.name: Automated Decision Without Human Appeal
rules.description: Automated decisions affecting children (bans, suspensions, access denial) must have a human appeal mechanism per EU AI Act Art. 14.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add human appeal mechanism: implement an appeal/review endpoint and surface it in the moderation notification to the user.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects automated decisions affecting children (account suspensions, bans, access denials) without a human appeal mechanism. The EU AI Act Article 14 requires that automated decisions impacting children have a documented human review and appeal process to ensure fairness and prevent irreversible harm.
tp_criteria: Code implements an automated decision (ban, suspension, content removal, access denial) triggered by an algorithm without providing a user-accessible appeal function or human review request pathway
Automated enforcement action is executed directly without storing or exposing a way for affected users to request human review
Application logs show automated decisions affecting minors but no appeal mechanism, escalation process, or human review queue is triggered
fp_criteria: Code implements an appeal or human review request function that affected users can call to challenge an automated decision
Automated decision execution includes a mandatory escalation to human review queue or appeal workflow before the action becomes final
Code contains conditional logic that routes automated decisions affecting children to a human moderator for confirmation before enforcement
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a user-facing appeal function or human review request mechanism tied to automated decisions, it's FP
If an automated decision is executed without calling or offering an appeal workflow, it's TP
If an automated decision for a child user is conditional on human approval or includes mandatory escalation, it's FP

rules.name: Missing AI Disclosure
rules.description: AI systems interacting with children must disclose they are AI per EU AI Act Art. 13. Chatbots, tutors, and assistants need visible AI disclosure.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add AI disclosure: show 'You are chatting with an AI' before first interaction and in the UI header.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects AI systems (chatbots, tutors, assistants) interacting with children without visible disclosure that they are AI. The EU AI Act Article 13 requires that AI systems clearly disclose their AI nature to users, especially children, to prevent deception and ensure informed interaction.
tp_criteria: Code renders a chatbot, tutor, or assistant interface interacting with child users without displaying a visible disclosure that the system is AI-powered
AI assistant responds to child user messages without including or displaying a system message, badge, or interface indicator that identifies it as artificial intelligence
Application loads an AI interaction component for child users with no ai_disclosure_label, disclosure_text, or visible identifier that signals AI operation
fp_criteria: Code displays a visible label, header, or badge (e.g., 'AI Assistant,' 'Powered by AI,' 'I'm an AI') before or during AI interaction with children
AI assistant is wrapped in a component that enforces disclosure UI rendering before user interaction begins
Code is part of an admin, testing, or non-child interface where disclosure may not be required
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a visible AI disclosure label or badge shown to child users before or during interaction, it's FP
If an AI assistant or chatbot interface is rendered to children without a disclosure function being called, it's TP
If disclosure is in documentation or comments but not rendered visibly to the user, it's TP

rules.name: No Training Data Disclosure
rules.description: High-risk AI systems must disclose training data sources per EU AI Act Art. 13. Children's AI products need model cards or equivalent documentation.
rules.fix_suggestion: Create a model card documenting training data sources, intended use, limitations, and bias considerations.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: High-risk AI systems must disclose where their training data came from, as required by the EU AI Act. For children's apps, this means providing model cards or similar documentation explaining what data trained the AI system and any relevant limitations.
tp_criteria: Code implements an AI/ML model in production but contains no documentation, comments, or disclosure mechanism about training data sources
Children's app uses personalized AI features without providing any model card, technical documentation, or user-facing explanation of training data scope
AI system documentation exists but omits critical training data details (dataset names, sources, time periods, or data composition)
fp_criteria: Code contains training data disclosure in documentation, README files, or in-app help sections accessible to users
Model card or equivalent technical documentation file exists in the repository with training data source details
Code is test code, example code, or proof-of-concept that doesn't run in production serving children
Documentation is present in type declarations, docstrings, or comments describing the model's training data origins
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS AI/ML model training or uses a pre-trained model, check for corresponding user-facing or technical documentation of training data sources. Absence of any disclosure = TP.

For children's apps: if personalization or algorithmic decisions exist, disclosure must be child-accessible (not just in technical terms of service). Dense technical documentation without child-readable summaries may still be TP.

rules.name: Algorithmic Decision Blackbox
rules.description: High-stakes decisions (content removal, access control) must have explainability mechanisms per EU AI Act Art. 13. Opaque automated decisions violate transparency requirements.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add explainability: include a 'reason' parameter in automated decisions and surface it to affected users.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: High-stakes decisions made by AI systems—such as removing user content, blocking access, or moderating behavior—must be explainable to users. Hidden algorithmic decision-making without transparency violates EU AI Act requirements and undermines user trust.
tp_criteria: Code implements automated content moderation, access control, or account suspension logic without any explainability mechanism (no explanation logging, no feedback to user, no appeal process)
Decision-making algorithm lacks both: (1) internal documentation of decision factors, and (2) user-facing explanation of why a specific decision was made
High-stakes automated decision is made via opaque neural network or black-box model with no counterfactual explanation, feature importance tracking, or fallback to human review
fp_criteria: Code implements explainability mechanism such as decision reason logging, user-facing explanations, appeal workflows, or human review queues
Automated decision uses transparent, rule-based logic with documented decision trees or clear conditional statements that are self-explanatory
Code is documentation, comments, or type definitions describing how decisions are made but not the actual decision-making implementation
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: For every high-stakes automated decision (content removal, access denial, recommendation blocking), verify existence of explainability output. If decision is made but explanation is never generated or shown to user = TP.

If code uses a black-box model (neural network without interpretation layer), check for compensating controls: decision logging, user notification, or mandatory human review. Absence of all three = TP.

rules.name: Age-Based Personalization Not Disclosed
rules.description: Personalized content that varies by age must disclose this to users per EU AI Act Art. 13. Children should know their experience is age-adapted.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disclose age-based personalization: add a visible notice that 'Content is adapted for your age group' when age-specific filtering is active.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: When AI systems personalize content differently based on a child's age (e.g., easier language for younger users, different content recommendations), this age-based adaptation must be disclosed to the child. Children have the right to know their experience is being customized.
tp_criteria: Code implements age-based personalization logic (branching on age variable, age-segmented content serving, or age-adapted algorithms) without any user-facing disclosure that personalization is occurring
Content recommendations, language complexity, or feature availability varies by age but no explanation is provided to the child about why their experience differs
Age is used in algorithmic decision-making for children but no transparency control or disclosure mechanism allows the child to understand the role of age in their personalized experience
fp_criteria: Code discloses age-based personalization to the user in app settings, help section, or onboarding flow
Age-based logic is only in documentation, comments, or type declarations and not actually executed for content personalization
Code is test code or admin-only feature control that does not reach end-user children
Personalization is explained in terms of service, privacy policy, or in-app tooltip visible to users about the child's age
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-based content adaptation or recommendation filtering, it MUST have corresponding disclosure to the child. Absence of disclosure = TP. Disclosure in adult-only privacy policy (not child-readable) = TP.
Check for user-facing transparency controls: If code branches on age but never shows the child why their content differs = TP.

rules.name: Missing AI Terms of Service
