rules.description: AI-powered services for children need dedicated AI terms explaining capabilities, limitations, and data practices per EU AI Act Art. 13.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add dedicated AI terms of service: create an /ai-terms page explaining how AI features work, their limitations, and child-specific protections.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: AI-powered services designed for children must have dedicated terms of service or documentation explaining what the AI can and cannot do, how it uses data, and what its limitations are. Generic AI disclaimers in adult terms don't meet children's transparency needs.
tp_criteria: App contains AI-powered features (personalization, recommendations, chatbot, content moderation) but no dedicated AI-specific terms or documentation accessible to children
AI capabilities and limitations are described only in dense technical documentation or adult-focused privacy policy, not in child-comprehensible format
AI terms of service file, in-app help section, or documentation does not address children specifically: fails to explain AI decisions, data use, or capability limits in age-appropriate language
fp_criteria: Dedicated AI terms of service or child-readable documentation exists explaining AI capabilities, limitations, data practices, and decision-making in accessible language
Code includes child-friendly AI explainer, onboarding flow, or help section that covers AI functionality and data usage
AI terms are present in documentation files, README, or in-app help accessible to the user
Code is test code, vendor code, or proof-of-concept not deployed to children
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS AI features, check for dedicated child-facing documentation. If only generic terms exist = TP. If terms exist but are not child-readable (use technical jargon, assume adult literacy) = TP.
Disclosure must be in-app or easily discoverable, not buried in multi-page adult terms. Accessibility and age-appropriateness are required, not just presence of disclosure.

rules.name: AI Tutor Bypass (Auto-Answering)
rules.description: Educational AI must scaffold learning, not provide direct answers. Auto-answering bypasses critical thinking development (Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development).
rules.fix_suggestion: Replace auto-answering with scaffolded hints: provide progressive clues instead of complete solutions.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Scaffolding Rule

knowledge.plain_description: Educational AI systems designed for children must scaffold learning—guiding students through problems rather than providing direct answers. Auto-answering bypasses critical thinking and violates sound pedagogical principles (Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development).
tp_criteria: Educational AI tutor implements a direct-answer response mode where users ask a question and receive the complete, final answer without intermediate hints or guided steps
Code includes a 'show answer' button or auto-answer feature that returns the solution directly, allowing students to bypass problem-solving scaffolding
AI response logic skips hint generation, step-by-step guidance, or Socratic questioning—jumping directly to the answer when queried
fp_criteria: Code implements scaffolded learning: hints before answers, step-by-step guidance, guided questioning, or progressive difficulty that requires student engagement before solution reveal
Auto-answer feature exists but is gated behind admin/teacher controls, not available to students, or requires explicit disabling of educational mode
Code is documentation or comments describing pedagogical approach; actual response logic implements scaffolding
Code is test tutor or proof-of-concept, not deployed in production to children
rule_logic: Check for answer delivery path: if student query leads directly to answer without intermediate guidance steps = TP. If query triggers hint generation first = FP.
If code IMPLEMENTS scaffolded learning (hints, step-by-step, guided discovery), it's FP even if auto-answer feature exists elsewhere in codebase.

rules.name: Emotional Over-Reliance Risk
rules.description: AI companions/tutors must detect and mitigate emotional dependency in children. Extended interactions without disengagement prompts risk unhealthy attachment (IEEE 2089-2021).
rules.fix_suggestion: Add disengagement prompts: remind users to take breaks after extended sessions and suggest real-world activities.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Anti-Dependency Clause (IEEE 2089-2021)

knowledge.plain_description: AI companions and educational tutors interacting with children must detect signs of unhealthy emotional dependency and actively encourage disengagement. Extended interactions without breaks or wellness checks risk fostering over-reliance and emotional attachment (IEEE 2089-2021).
tp_criteria: AI companion or tutor allows unlimited continuous interaction without implementing session time limits, engagement breaks, or periodic disengagement prompts
Code lacks detection logic for dependency risk signals (excessive interaction frequency, emotional language escalation, expressed loneliness, addiction indicators) and does not trigger intervention
System does not offer or encourage disengagement: no 'take a break' suggestions, no wellness mode, no recommendations to interact with peers or offline activities
fp_criteria: Code implements session limits, mandatory breaks, or periodic 'take a break' prompts that pause AI interaction
Dependency detection logic exists: monitors for excessive use patterns, emotional language cues, or interaction frequency and triggers intervention or user notification
Wellness mode or offline activity recommendations are offered periodically or when engagement thresholds are exceeded
Code is documentation or test code not deployed to children
rule_logic: For every AI companion or tutor targeting children, check for: (1) interaction limits or break prompts, AND (2) dependency detection logic. Absence of both = TP.
If code IMPLEMENTS dependency mitigation (breaks, wellness mode, offline suggestions), it's FP even if interaction is otherwise unlimited.

rules.name: Synthetic Content Without Child-Readable Labels
rules.description: AI-generated content shown to children must have labels comprehensible to the child's age group. Abstract disclaimers are insufficient — use visual indicators.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add child-comprehensible AI labels: use emoji or visual badges (e.g., sparkle icon) instead of text-only 'AI Generated' disclaimers.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Truth in Synthesis

knowledge.plain_description: Content generated by AI and shown to children must be labeled as AI-generated with labels that children can actually understand. Abstract legal disclaimers or hidden metadata don't suffice—visual, age-appropriate indicators are required.
tp_criteria: Code serves AI-generated content (images, text, video) to children without any label, badge, or visual indicator marking it as synthetic
AI-generated content is labeled but the label uses abstract language ('synthetic', 'machine-generated') or is buried in metadata/footer, not visually salient to child readers
Label exists but uses age-inappropriate vocabulary or assumes literacy levels beyond the app's target age group (e.g., 'neural network synthesis' for 6-year-olds)
fp_criteria: Code attaches visual, prominent badge or label to AI-generated content (e.g., colored icon, 'AI made this' label in plain language, clear visual separation)
Label is age-appropriate: uses vocabulary and reading level matching the target child age group
Code embeds accessibility features: alt-text, clear icon labels, or dynamic tooltips explaining what the label means
Code is documentation or test code not deployed to children
rule_logic: If code IMPLEMENTS visual, age-appropriate labeling of synthetic content, it's FP. If label is present but not visual or uses complex terminology = TP.
Check: is the label (1) visually prominent (not in footer), (2) in plain language for the age group, and (3) applied to every instance of synthetic content? If any missing = TP.

rules.name: Engagement Optimization Without Disclosure
rules.description: Algorithms optimizing for engagement/time-on-device in children's apps violate No-Nudge principles (IEEE 2089-2021). Must disclose engagement optimization and offer wellbeing modes.
rules.fix_suggestion: Disclose engagement optimization and add wellbeing features: implement screen time limits, usage dashboards, and 'take a break' reminders.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: No-Nudge Mandate (IEEE 2089-2021)

knowledge.plain_description: Algorithms that optimize for engagement, session length, or time-on-device in children's apps violate no-nudge principles and exploit behavioral vulnerabilities. These engagement-maximizing algorithms must be disclosed and a wellbeing mode must be available (IEEE 2089-2021).
tp_criteria: Code implements engagement optimization algorithm (maximizing session time, reward loops, notification triggers, algorithmic infinite scroll) without disclosing this practice to the child or parent
Engagement-optimized content ranking or recommendation system is deployed without any wellbeing mode, time limit option, or child-controlled engagement settings
Algorithm uses known dark patterns (variable rewards, FOMO triggers, streak counters) to drive child engagement without any transparency or opt-out mechanism
fp_criteria: Code discloses engagement optimization in settings, help section, or privacy policy accessible to children and parents
Wellbeing mode or time management features are offered: session limits, break reminders, engagement transparency dashboard, or child-controlled content ranking
Code implements engagement transparency: shows engagement metrics, allows disabling of notifications/rewards, or lets child control recommendation algorithm
Code is test code, admin feature, or not deployed to children
rule_logic: If code IMPLEMENTS engagement optimization, verify: (1) disclosure to user, AND (2) wellbeing mode exists. Absence of either = TP.
If code IMPLEMENTS wellbeing features (time limits, transparency, mode toggle), it's FP even if underlying optimization algorithm exists.

rules.name: No User Identity Reset Mechanism
rules.description: AI systems learning child preferences must offer periodic identity/preference reset capability. Children's interests change rapidly — stale profiles can create filter bubbles.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add identity reset capability: implement 'Reset My Preferences' option and offer periodic 'Would you like to refresh your interests?' prompts.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Right to Reset

knowledge.plain_description: AI systems that learn and adapt to children's preferences must allow periodic reset of user identity and preference profiles. Children's interests change rapidly, and stale or outdated AI profiles can create filter bubbles and limit exposure to new ideas.
tp_criteria: Code implements user preference learning and personalization but provides no mechanism for users to reset or clear their preference profile
AI system tracks and stores child behavior/preferences with no option to start fresh; user preferences are persistent and cannot be cleared without deleting entire account
Preference reset functionality does not exist or is only available to administrators, not to the child or parent
fp_criteria: Code implements user-accessible reset feature: button to clear preferences, reset recommendation history, or start with fresh profile
Reset mechanism is available in user settings, privacy controls, or account management accessible to the child or parent
Code is documentation or test code not deployed to children
Code does not implement personalization or preference learning, so reset is not applicable
rule_logic: For every AI system that learns child preferences, check for user-accessible reset option. Absence = TP.
If code IMPLEMENTS preference learning, reset capability MUST be user-triggered (not automatic, not admin-only). If reset is available but requires admin action = TP.

rules.name: Excessive Data Collection in AI Pipeline
rules.description: AI systems processing children's data must implement data minimization — collecting only what is strictly necessary. Broad collection scopes, wildcard field selection, or indefinite retention violate the data minimization principle (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), IEEE 7010-2020).
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement data minimization: specify exact fields needed, set finite retention periods (e.g., 30 days), and document the purpose for each data field collected.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Data Minimization (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), IEEE 7010-2020)

knowledge.plain_description: AI systems processing children's data must strictly follow data minimization principles—collecting only the minimum data necessary for their stated purpose. Broad data collection, wildcard field selection, indefinite retention, or collection scope creep violates GDPR and IEEE principles designed to protect children.
tp_criteria: Code collects data fields or categories not strictly necessary for the AI system's documented purpose (e.g., collecting biometric data for simple recommendations, collecting location for non-location-based feature)
Data collection uses wildcard patterns, broad scopes, or undefined field selection ('collect all user interactions', 'store all sensor data') without justification or limitation
Children's data is retained indefinitely, or retention policy is undefined; no automatic deletion, purge, or age-out mechanism exists for collected data
fp_criteria: Code implements strict data scope: collects only named, documented fields required for the specific AI function (e.g., reading level and quiz responses for tutor, not location/contacts)
Retention policy is defined and enforced: automatic deletion after X days/months, per-user deletion requests honored, or data purge on account deletion
Data minimization is documented: code comments, configuration files, or privacy policy specify exactly what data is collected and why
Code includes data access controls limiting collection to necessary fields: schemas with explicit field lists, allowlist-based collection, or API contracts specifying required data only
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: Audit data collection scope: list all fields/categories collected for AI pipeline. Each must have documented justification tied to a specific AI function. Unjustified fields = TP.
Check retention: if any collected data lacks deletion policy or is stored indefinitely = TP. If retention is tied to account lifetime but should expire sooner per minimization = TP.
If code IMPLEMENTS minimized collection (named fields, justified scope, retention limits) with documented policy, it's FP.

rules.name: AI Interface Without Neurodivergent Accommodations
rules.description: AI systems for children must accommodate neurodivergent users (ADHD, autism, dyslexia). Timed interactions, rapid UI transitions, and sensory-heavy content without alternatives violate accessibility principles (WCAG 2.2, IEEE 2089-2021 Section 7.3).
rules.fix_suggestion: Add neurodivergent accommodations: offer extended time options, reduce-motion mode, pause/resume controls, and adjustable pacing for all timed AI interactions.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Neurodivergent Accessibility (IEEE 2089-2021 Section 7.3)

knowledge.plain_description: AI interfaces for children must provide accommodations for neurodivergent users (ADHD, autism, dyslexia) such as adjustable pacing, reduced sensory stimulation, and alternative interaction modes. Without these features, children with neurodivergence cannot use the system safely and equitably.
tp_criteria: Code implements timed interactions (countdown timers, rate-limited responses) with no pause, slow-down, or disable option
UI transitions happen rapidly (animations <300ms, auto-advance without user control) without accessibility toggles for motion sensitivity
System displays sensory-heavy content (flashing, rapid color changes, loud audio) without alternative low-stimulation modes or content filtering
fp_criteria: Code implements configurable interaction speeds, pause mechanisms, or 'focus mode' settings that reduce cognitive load
Accessibility settings exist for motion reduction, extended timeouts, or simplified UI presentation
Code is in test suite, documentation, or type definitions only (not production interface code)
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS neurodivergent accommodation features (adjustable timing, reduced animations, sensory toggles), classify as FP
Only flag actual runtime UI/interaction code; accessibility imports, configuration schemas, or feature flags that ENABLE accommodations are FP
Judge severity by whether accommodations are actual implementation (FP) vs. documented but missing from code (TP)

rules.name: AI Decision Affecting Child Without Parent Involvement
rules.description: High-impact AI decisions about children (content restrictions, learning path changes, behavioral assessments) must include a parental co-regulation mechanism — parents must be notified and given override capability (IEEE 2089-2021 Section 6.4, UN CRC Art. 5).
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement parental co-regulation: notify parents of high-impact AI decisions, provide override controls, and require parent-child joint confirmation for significant changes.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Parental Co-Regulation (IEEE 2089-2021 Section 6.4)

knowledge.plain_description: AI systems making high-impact decisions about children (content filtering, learning path changes, behavioral assessments) must notify parents and give them ability to override the decision. Without parental co-regulation, children have no adult advocate when AI decisions affect their safety or development.
tp_criteria: Code detects a high-impact decision event (content block, learning curriculum change, behavioral flag) but makes the change without notifying parent/guardian
System implements parental notification but provides no mechanism for parent override or veto of the AI decision
Parent notification is sent only after decision is already locked in and executed with no rollback option
fp_criteria: Code implements parental notification AND override/appeal mechanism where parent can reverse AI decisions
Decision event is low-impact (e.g., UI theme selection, session logging) that does not affect child safety or development
Code is in documentation, schema definitions, or permission models that describe the co-regulation feature
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS both notification AND parental override capability, classify as FP even if implementation is partial
Only flag systems that make substantive decisions about child's content access, learning, or behavior — cosmetic UI decisions are FP
Parental co-regulation requires both notification AND override; notification-only is TP

rules.name: AI Chatbot Without Crisis Escalation Protocol
rules.description: AI systems interacting with children must detect crisis signals (self-harm, suicidal ideation, abuse disclosure) and immediately escalate to human professionals. Chatbots and AI companions without crisis detection in child-facing contexts violate duty of care (IEEE 2089-2021 Section 8, Surgeon General Advisory 2023).
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement crisis escalation: add keyword detection for self-harm/suicide/abuse signals, immediately route to crisis hotline (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), notify a designated adult, and halt AI-only interaction.
rules.penalty: Constitutional AI Principle: Crisis Escalation Protocol (IEEE 2089-2021 Section 8)

knowledge.plain_description: AI chatbots and companions interacting with children must detect crisis signals (self-harm, suicidal thoughts, abuse disclosure) and immediately escalate to human professionals. Without crisis detection and escalation, AI systems put children in danger by responding to emergencies with only AI judgment.
tp_criteria: Chatbot accepts child user input but has no crisis signal detection (keywords, severity scoring, intent classification for self-harm/abuse/suicidal content)
Code detects crisis signals but does not escalate to human professional (no alert sent to counselor, crisis line, or care provider)
Escalation mechanism exists but is asynchronous, batched, or delayed rather than immediate real-time routing to available human responder
fp_criteria: Code implements crisis detection (keyword matching, ML classifier, safety thresholds) AND immediate escalation to qualified human professional
System is not a child-facing chatbot (e.g., internal admin tool, developer API, adult mental health bot)
Code is in test suite mock, documentation, or specification for escalation procedure
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS both crisis detection AND immediate human escalation, classify as FP
Judge 'child-facing' strictly: any system where children are known users requires crisis protocol; adult-only systems are FP
Escalation must be real-time and to qualified humans (not auto-reply, not just logging, not delayed queue)

rules.name: Training Data Without Quality Documentation
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 10(2) requires training data sets to be subject to data governance practices — including documentation of data sources, collection methodology, and quality metrics. ML pipelines without data provenance tracking violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add data governance documentation: create a data card for each training dataset documenting source, collection method, size, demographics, known biases, and quality metrics.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: Training data governance requires documentation of data sources, collection methodology, and quality metrics throughout the ML pipeline. Systems that use training data without provenance tracking or source documentation cannot prove compliance with data protection and bias mitigation requirements.
tp_criteria: ML training pipeline loads data from sources but contains no metadata, lineage tracking, or documentation of where data came from or how it was collected
Data processing code has no quality metrics (missing-value rates, duplicate detection, outlier documentation) or data validation logs
Model training notebook or script has no comments, code, or configuration documenting collection methodology, sampling strategy, or data version info
fp_criteria: Code implements data lineage tracking (e.g., metadata tags, provenance DAG, dataset registry) with source and collection method documentation
Training script includes data quality validation (schema checks, summary statistics, data profiling reports)
Code is in type definitions, import statements, or mock/test data only
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS data governance practices (documented sources, quality metrics, lineage tracking), classify as FP
Look for evidence of documentation: comments, configuration, metadata fields, or separate documentation files linked to data loading code
Absence of governance is TP; even partial documentation of sources or methodology shows effort toward compliance

rules.name: Training Data Without Bias Testing
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f) requires examination of training data for possible biases, especially for children where demographic imbalances can cause disproportionate harm. Model training without bias audits violates this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add bias testing to the training pipeline: run demographic parity checks, compute equalized odds metrics, and document bias audit results before deployment.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: Training data must be examined for biases, especially for children where demographic imbalances can cause disproportionate harm (e.g., lower accuracy for certain age groups, ethnicities, or abilities). ML pipelines without bias testing and remediation are non-compliant.
tp_criteria: Training pipeline includes data from multiple demographic groups (age, gender, ethnicity, ability status) but has no bias audit code, fairness metrics, or disparity analysis
Model training completes without measuring performance disparities across demographic slices or fairness metrics (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds)
Code contains fairness-related features (demographic stratification) but no downstream testing or reporting of bias results
fp_criteria: Code implements bias testing (fairness metrics, demographic performance analysis, disparity thresholds) and documents results or remediation
Training data is demonstrably homogeneous (single demographic group) where bias testing is not applicable
Code is in documentation, research papers, or fairness library definitions
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS bias testing and fairness metrics evaluation, classify as FP
For children's AI, bias testing is mandatory if data includes multiple demographic groups; homogeneous data is FP
Testing must produce metrics or reports; test code that runs but discards results is weak evidence and may be TP

rules.name: No Data Representativeness Validation
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 10(3) requires training data to be representative of the deployment context. Children's AI systems must validate that training data represents age, cultural, and linguistic diversity of the target population.
rules.fix_suggestion: Validate data representativeness: use stratified sampling, verify demographic coverage across age groups, and document gaps between training data and target child population.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: Training data must be representative of the deployment context — for children's AI, this means data should reflect the age, cultural, and linguistic diversity of target users. Systems trained on non-representative data may fail or perform poorly for underrepresented groups.
tp_criteria: System is deployed to children across multiple ages (e.g., 5-12 year olds) but training data contains only one age group or no age validation of data
Target users include multiple languages or cultural contexts but training data is monolingual or from single cultural source with no representativeness check
Code makes no attempt to validate training data coverage across target user demographics or document any diversity analysis
fp_criteria: Code includes representativeness validation (age distribution analysis, language coverage checks, cultural diversity metrics) with documentation
Training data is intentionally scoped to single age, language, or cultural group matching actual deployment scope
Code is in configuration, documentation, or specification of data requirements
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS representativeness validation (demographic distribution checks, coverage analysis), classify as FP
Representativeness must match declared deployment context; if system targets diverse children but data is homogeneous, it's TP
Documentation or analysis of diversity is sufficient; no requirement for 100% perfect representation, only demonstrated validation effort

rules.name: Training Data Without Consent Verification
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 10(5) combined with GDPR Art. 6/9 requires that training data collection respects data protection law. Children's data used for training without verified parental consent is a severe violation.
rules.fix_suggestion: Verify consent before using children's data for training: implement opt-in parental consent for data use in ML training, maintain consent audit trail, and provide data deletion mechanisms.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover (combined with GDPR)

knowledge.plain_description: Children's data used for training must have verified parental consent under GDPR and EU AI Act. Using children's data to train AI models without documented parental consent is a severe violation affecting thousands of users' fundamental rights.
tp_criteria: Training dataset includes data known or suspected to be from children (age <18) with no consent verification process or consent documentation in pipeline
Code processes children's data for model training but consent records are not checked, validated, or enforced before data inclusion
Training data ingestion has no mechanism to filter out non-consented children's data or verify parental consent status
fp_criteria: Code implements consent verification (consent record lookup, age verification before data inclusion, documented consent audit trail)
Training data is documented as coming only from adults (age >=18) with no children's data
Code is in consent management infrastructure, GDPR audit utilities, or mock/test data
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS consent verification and enforcement before data inclusion, classify as FP
Assume data may include children unless explicitly proven otherwise; lack of age verification is TP
This is a compliance-determining rule: verified consent is non-negotiable; documentation of verification process is required

rules.name: AI System Without Human-in-the-Loop Mechanism
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 14(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed for effective human oversight. AI systems making consequential decisions for children without a human review checkpoint violate this requirement.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add human-in-the-loop: implement review queues for consequential AI decisions, add manual override capabilities, and require human approval for actions affecting child accounts.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: High-risk AI systems making consequential decisions about children must include a human-in-the-loop checkpoint where a qualified human reviews and approves or rejects AI decisions before they affect the child. Fully autonomous decisions without human review violate oversight requirements.
tp_criteria: AI system makes consequential decision (content restriction, learning intervention, safety flag) and executes it directly to child without human review queue or approval step
Code implements human review UI or workflow but review is optional, bypass-able, or routinely skipped without logging consequences
Decision execution code has no integration with human review system; human approval step is documented but not enforced in actual decision pipeline
fp_criteria: Code implements mandatory human-in-the-loop checkpoint where human must review and approve before decision affects child
Decision is low-risk (e.g., recommendation, preference logging) that does not restrict access or change child's experience
Code is in review interface templates, documentation, or configuration only
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS mandatory human review with enforcement before decision execution, classify as FP
Judge 'consequential' strictly for children: content filters, learning paths, behavioral alerts, and restrictions all require review
Human-in-the-loop must be in execution path (not optional); code that can bypass review is TP

rules.name: No Emergency Stop or Override Mechanism
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 14(4)(d) requires human overseers to be able to intervene or interrupt the AI system at any time. AI systems without kill switch, emergency stop, or override mechanism are non-compliant.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement emergency stop: add a kill switch endpoint (/api/ai/stop), monitoring alerts for anomalous behavior, and immediate halt capability accessible to human overseers.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: Human overseers must be able to stop or interrupt the AI system at any time via a kill switch or emergency stop mechanism. AI systems without this capability prevent humans from halting harmful behavior, making them non-compliant.
tp_criteria: System executes AI decisions in real-time (chatbot responses, content filtering, behavior modifications) with no emergency stop code, no interrupt handler, no manual kill switch
Override/stop mechanism exists in documentation or specification but is not implemented in actual code or is disabled/commented out
System accepts stop signals but continues processing background tasks or delayed actions after stop signal, not achieving full halt
fp_criteria: Code implements emergency stop mechanism (signal handler, stop flag, kill switch endpoint) that halts all active AI operations immediately
System is offline, test-only, or not actively executing AI logic against child users
Code is in documentation, specification, or emergency procedure guidelines
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS functional emergency stop mechanism that halts all AI operations, classify as FP
Emergency stop must be immediately effective, not queued or delayed; background tasks must also stop
This is compliance-determining: every production AI system for children must have functional kill switch in code

rules.name: AI Output Without Interpretability for Overseer
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 14(4)(b) requires that human overseers can correctly interpret the AI system's output. AI predictions, classifications, or recommendations served without explanation metadata are non-compliant.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add interpretability: attach explanation metadata (SHAP values, feature importance, confidence scores, or natural language reasoning) to every AI output served to overseers.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: AI predictions, classifications, and recommendations must include explanation metadata so human overseers can understand why the system made a decision. Black-box outputs that humans cannot interpret prevent effective oversight and violate interpretability requirements.
tp_criteria: Model produces predictions or classifications for child-affecting decisions (content recommendation, safety flag) but outputs contain only the decision/score with no feature importance, reasoning, or confidence threshold info
System logs AI decisions but explanation is limited to model name or version; no feature attribution, decision factors, or uncertainty quantification provided
Explanation interface or API exists in documentation but not integrated into actual decision output that human overseer receives
fp_criteria: Code includes explanation generation (feature importance, decision factors, confidence scores, reasoning summary) attached to every decision output
Decision output includes interpretability metadata (e.g., top factors, confidence, threshold comparison) that human can use to validate decision
Code is in documentation, explanation library, or configuration specifying interpretability requirements
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS explanation generation and attaches it to decision outputs, classify as FP
Explanation must be human-readable and linked to specific decision; model parameters alone are insufficient
Interpretability is required for overseer to validate decision; decisions without explanation prevent meaningful human review

rules.name: No Oversight Audit Trail
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 14(4) requires human oversight actions (reviews, overrides, approvals) to be logged. AI systems without audit trails for human oversight actions cannot demonstrate compliance.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add oversight audit trail: log every human review, override, and approval action with timestamp, reviewer ID, original AI output, and human decision rationale.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: The EU AI Act requires that human oversight actions (reviews, overrides, approvals) on AI system outputs must be logged in an audit trail. Systems without this logging cannot demonstrate compliance with transparency and accountability requirements.
tp_criteria: AI inference calls are processed and results returned to users/systems without any logging of human review, approval, or override actions
Code implements AI decision-making for high-risk scenarios (children's content moderation, safety decisions) but contains no audit trail, logging mechanism, or approval queue for human oversight
System allows AI outputs to be deployed or acted upon without storing evidence of human review decision, timestamp, reviewer identity, or rationale
fp_criteria: Code is test/mock code that simulates AI oversight without requiring production-grade audit trails
Logging and audit trail functionality is implemented elsewhere (e.g., in a separate compliance module, middleware, or external logging service not visible in scanned code)
Code is documentation, comments, or type definitions describing oversight requirements without being executable logic
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS audit logging of human actions (log statements with reviewer ID, timestamp, decision, rationale), it is FP regardless of AI presence.
If the code shows AI inference but delegates oversight to an external system (e.g., calls to 'approvalService.log()' or references to 'AuditTrail' classes), it is FP.
Human oversight is only satisfied if logging captures WHO reviewed/approved, WHEN, WHAT decision was made, and WHY — partial logging (e.g., only timestamps) is still TP.

rules.name: No Error Rate Monitoring
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 15(1) requires high-risk AI systems to achieve appropriate levels of accuracy and declare expected error rates. AI inference endpoints without accuracy monitoring or error rate tracking are non-compliant.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add accuracy monitoring: implement real-time error rate tracking, declare expected accuracy levels in model documentation, and set up alerts when accuracy degrades below thresholds.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: The EU AI Act mandates that high-risk AI systems must monitor their accuracy and declare expected error rates to users and regulators. AI inference endpoints without any accuracy or error rate monitoring mechanisms cannot meet this requirement.
tp_criteria: Code invokes an AI/ML inference endpoint (API call, model prediction, LLM completion) but contains no metrics collection, monitoring, or calculation of accuracy, precision, recall, or error rate
AI predictions are made on user inputs (especially children's data) and the system does not track or log prediction confidence, success rate, or comparison against ground truth
System processes AI outputs without any mechanism to measure, aggregate, or report expected vs. actual error rates to stakeholders
fp_criteria: Code is test/benchmark code that measures model accuracy offline or in CI/CD pipelines
Accuracy monitoring is delegated to an external ML monitoring platform (e.g., calls to 'MLOpsMonitor.trackAccuracy()' or references to observability libraries)
Code is documentation or configuration files describing accuracy requirements without being executable monitoring logic
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS accuracy metrics collection (accuracy calculation, confusion matrix, precision/recall computation, or logging of predictions vs. ground truth), it is FP.
If the code invokes AI inference but does not measure or log any metric about correctness or error, it is TP.
Monitoring deployed elsewhere (cloud monitoring services, separate metrics collectors) counts as implementation — flag only when AI calls exist with zero accuracy tracking visible.

rules.name: No Fallback for AI Failure
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 15(3) requires AI systems to be resilient against errors, faults, and inconsistencies. AI calls without error handling, timeouts, or fallback mechanisms expose children to unpredictable behavior.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add AI failure fallback: wrap all AI calls in try/catch with timeouts, implement graceful degradation (e.g., static content when AI unavailable), and log all failures for review.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: The EU AI Act requires AI systems to be resilient against errors and failures. AI inference calls without error handling, retry logic, timeouts, or fallback mechanisms leave children exposed to unpredictable or harmful behavior when the AI fails.
tp_criteria: Code makes AI API calls or inference requests with no try-catch, error handler, timeout mechanism, or fallback logic in the calling function
AI call failure (timeout, rate limit, invalid response) would propagate unhandled to the user or be passed to child users without safe defaults or human intervention
System processes children's requests through AI without defining fallback behavior (e.g., returning a default safe response, escalating to human review, or graceful degradation)
fp_criteria: Error handling and fallback logic is implemented in a wrapper function, middleware, or retry decorator that wraps the AI call
Code is test/mock code that intentionally bypasses error handling for testing purposes
AI call is wrapped in a try-catch block with defined fallback (return safe default, log error, escalate to human) or timeout is explicitly set
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS error handling (try-catch, if-error checks, timeout parameters, fallback responses), it is FP even if the fallback is simple.
If an AI call exists without any surrounding error handling in the same code block or referenced error handler, it is TP.
Timeouts, retry logic with backoff, and graceful degradation all count as resilience — absence of all three indicates TP.

rules.name: No Adversarial Robustness Testing
rules.description: EU AI Act Art. 15(4) requires high-risk AI systems to be resilient against attempts by unauthorized third parties to manipulate outputs (adversarial attacks). AI systems processing children's input without input validation or adversarial testing are vulnerable to prompt injection and manipulation.
rules.fix_suggestion: Add adversarial robustness: implement input sanitization for all user-provided text before passing to AI models, add prompt injection detection, and run periodic adversarial testing.
rules.penalty: EU AI Act Art. 99: Up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover

knowledge.plain_description: The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to be tested against adversarial attacks and manipulation attempts. AI systems that accept children's input without input validation or adversarial testing are vulnerable to prompt injection, jailbreaking, and malicious manipulation.
tp_criteria: Code passes user/child input directly to an AI model (LLM, text classifier, content filter) without sanitization, validation, or input filtering
System accepts children's input and uses it to construct AI prompts or model queries without escaping special characters, checking for prompt injection patterns, or validating input length/format
No evidence of adversarial testing, fuzzing, or robustness checks against malicious inputs designed to manipulate AI output
fp_criteria: Code implements input validation, sanitization, or filtering (regex checks, length limits, character whitelisting, prompt injection pattern detection) before passing to AI
Code is test/adversarial testing code that intentionally sends malicious inputs to measure system robustness
Input validation is delegated to a library or middleware (e.g., calls to 'InputValidator.sanitize()' or use of parameterized AI API calls)
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS input validation or sanitization (filtering, escaping, whitelisting, injection pattern detection), it is FP.
If user input is directly concatenated into an AI prompt or API call without any validation step, it is TP.
For children's services, the bar is strict — even basic validation (length checks, whitespace normalization) counts as partial mitigation; complete absence is TP.

rules.name: Hardcoded Age Threshold Without EU Geo-Routing
rules.description: GDPR Article 8 allows EU member states to set consent age between 13-16. A hardcoded age threshold (e.g., age < 13) without geo-routing fails to comply with member states that set the threshold at 14, 15, or 16. Ireland/Spain/UK = 13, France = 15, Germany/Netherlands = 16.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement geo-aware age gating that adjusts the consent threshold based on the user's EU member state. Use IP geolocation or user-declared country to route: DE/NL=16, FR=15, IE/ES/UK/DK/SE/PL/LV=13. Consider defaulting to 16 (strictest) for unknown EU origins.
rules.penalty: Up to 4% of global annual turnover (GDPR Art. 83)

knowledge.plain_description: GDPR Article 8 allows each EU member state to set the digital age of consent between 13-16. A hardcoded age threshold (like age < 13) without geographic routing fails to comply with countries that set higher thresholds (France=15, Germany/Netherlands=16). Services must dynamically adjust consent age based on user location.
tp_criteria: Code contains a hardcoded age check (e.g., 'if (age < 13)' or 'MIN_CONSENT_AGE = 13') with no conditional logic based on user location, IP geolocation, or country code
Age verification logic uses a single global threshold without branching or lookup tables for different EU member state requirements
Service routes all users through the same age gate regardless of whether they are in Ireland (13) or Germany (16)
fp_criteria: Code implements geo-routing or location-based age verification (checks user country and applies appropriate threshold, or queries a configuration service with location parameter)
Age threshold is retrieved from a configuration file, environment variable, or database lookup that varies by region
Code is documentation, comments, or type definitions describing age requirements without being executable logic
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS geo-routing (geolocation lookup, country-based conditional logic, location-aware threshold configuration), it is FP.
If age check is hardcoded to a single value (13, 14, 16) without location-based branching, it is TP even if the value is correct for some regions.
Dynamic thresholds retrieved from locale, user country, or regional config count as FP — static threshold in code is always TP.

rules.name: Legitimate Interest Basis for Minor's Data Processing
rules.description: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest cannot generally be used as a legal basis for processing children's data. The EDPB states that controllers should not rely on legitimate interest for children's data without a strict balancing test that heavily favors child rights.
rules.fix_suggestion: For children's data, use consent (GDPR Art. 6(1)(a)) or contract performance as the legal basis. Legitimate interest is generally inappropriate for processing children's data under EDPB guidelines.
rules.penalty: Up to 4% of global annual turnover (GDPR Art. 83)

knowledge.plain_description: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) prohibits using 'legitimate interest' as the legal basis for processing children's personal data. The EDPB states that controllers should use explicit consent, contract necessity, or legal obligation instead. Legitimate interest for children's data requires a strict balancing test favoring child rights, and is rarely justified.
tp_criteria: Code or configuration explicitly documents or declares 'legitimate_interest' as the legal basis for processing user data where the system services children or minors under 18
System collects or processes children's data and the only documented legal basis is 'legitimate interest' without evidence of parental consent, contract necessity, or legal obligation
Data processing logic (tracking, profiling, analytics, personalization) for children is justified in comments or documentation using 'legitimate interest' without consent or contract basis
fp_criteria: Code implements explicit consent collection (parental consent, child assent, consent UI) before processing children's data
Legal basis is documented as 'contract' (purchase, service delivery), 'consent' (explicit opt-in), or 'legal obligation' rather than 'legitimate interest'
Code is for adult users only, or legal basis for children is documented as requiring parental consent and consent is collected
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS explicit consent collection for children's data (consent UI, parental consent flow, legal basis set to 'consent'), it is FP.
If data processing is documented with 'legitimate_interest' as sole basis and no consent/contract/obligation mechanism is visible, it is TP.
Legitimate interest for children is FP only if accompanied by documented evidence of strict child-rights-favoring balancing test and consent or contract safeguards.

rules.name: Automated Decision-Making or Profiling of Minors
rules.description: GDPR Article 22 restricts automated individual decision-making, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects. For children, the EDPB recommends that profiling should not be permitted except where it is in the child's interest.
rules.fix_suggestion: Do not profile children or use their data for automated decision-making unless it is demonstrably in the child's best interest. Provide meaningful human oversight for any automated processing that affects children.
rules.penalty: Up to 4% of global annual turnover (GDPR Art. 83)

knowledge.plain_description: GDPR Article 22 restricts automated decision-making and profiling that produces legal or significant effects. For children, the EDPB advises that profiling should not be permitted unless it directly serves the child's interest. Automated targeting, behavioral segmentation, and recommendation systems for children without child-interest justification violate this rule.
tp_criteria: Code implements profiling of children (behavioral segmentation, interest classification, preference inference) to drive automated decisions (content targeting, ad targeting, feature personalization) without documented justification that the profiling serves the child's own interest

System uses automated decision-making on children's data (recommendation engine, content filter, access control) that produces significant effects (content visibility, feature access, interaction patterns) without human review or child consent
Profiling or automated decisions are applied to minor users without transparency (no explanation, no ability to contest, no human override option)
fp_criteria: Code implements profiling or automated decisions WITH documented child-interest justification (e.g., safety filtering, age-appropriate content recommendation, parental controls)
Automated decisions include human review, appeal, or override mechanisms for children or parents
Profiling is not applied to children or code explicitly excludes minors from profiling/automated decision systems
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS profiling/automated decisions AND documents that it serves child interest (safety, development, education) AND includes human review/appeal, it is FP.
If profiling or automated decision-making targets children without clear child-interest documentation, it is TP.
Transparent profiling with ability to contest or human oversight significantly reduces violation severity but does not eliminate TP if child interest is not documented.

rules.name: Excessive Data Collection from Minors
rules.description: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires data minimization — only collecting data that is adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary. For children's services, this standard is applied more strictly.
rules.fix_suggestion: Only collect data that is strictly necessary for the service. Make non-essential fields optional. Conduct a data minimization assessment for all fields collected from users who may be children.
rules.penalty: Up to 4% of global annual turnover (GDPR Art. 83)

knowledge.plain_description: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires data minimization — collecting only adequate, relevant, and necessary data. For children's services, this standard is applied more strictly. Excessive collection of personal data, behavioral data, biometric data, or location data from minors violates this principle.
tp_criteria: Code collects multiple categories of personal data from children (e.g., name, email, location, device ID, behavioral logs, biometric data, browsing history) where some categories are not directly necessary for the stated service purpose
Service requires collection of sensitive data (location, contacts, biometrics, detailed behavioral data) from minors for basic functionality that could be delivered with less data
Data collection logic includes optional or exploratory data gathering (e.g., 'nice to have' analytics, future profiling) from children without strict necessity justification
fp_criteria: Code collects only essential data directly necessary for the stated service (e.g., email for account creation, age for age verification, name for personalization)
Data collection is user-controlled with granular opt-in for optional data categories
Code implements data minimization by design (collects minimal fields, deletes unnecessary data, purpose limitation on collection)
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS granular consent for optional data categories or collects only necessary fields, it is FP.
If children's service collects multiple data types where at least one is not strictly necessary for core functionality, it is TP.
For children's services, the necessity bar is higher — behavioral tracking, location, device IDs beyond minimum session management, or biometric data without critical justification indicate TP.

rules.name: Missing Right to Erasure Implementation for Children
rules.description: GDPR Article 17(1)(f) specifically strengthens the right to erasure when data was collected from a child. Services must provide clear mechanisms for children (or their parents) to request deletion of all personal data.
rules.fix_suggestion: Implement a complete data erasure endpoint that deletes all personal data when requested, with special priority for data collected from children. Do not soft-delete or archive — GDPR Article 17 requires actual erasure unless a legal retention obligation applies.
rules.penalty: Up to 4% of global annual turnover (GDPR Art. 83)

knowledge.plain_description: GDPR Article 17(1)(f) strengthens the right to erasure specifically for data collected from children. Services must provide clear, accessible mechanisms for children (or their parents) to request deletion of all personal data. Missing erasure implementation violates this requirement.
tp_criteria: Service collects personal data from minors but provides no documented mechanism, UI, or API endpoint for children or parents to request data deletion or erasure
User account dashboard or settings for children's accounts lacks a 'delete my data', 'request erasure', or 'remove my information' option
Data retention policies exist but no process is documented or implemented to handle and fulfill right-to-erasure requests from children or legal guardians
fp_criteria: Code implements a data erasure or deletion mechanism (delete account button, erasure request form, API endpoint for deletion) accessible to children or parents
User interface includes clear option to request data deletion with confirmation and fulfillment process
Code is documentation or policy describing erasure rights without being executable functionality (but implementation is verified elsewhere)
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS erasure functionality (delete account, delete data button, erasure request form, fulfillment logic), it is FP.
If children's service stores personal data with no visible erasure mechanism or request process, it is TP.
Erasure implementation must be accessible to children/parents and must actually delete data (not just mark as deleted) — hidden or non-functional erasure is TP.

rules.name: Tracking SDK Active for Under-18 Users
rules.description: India DPDP Act Section 9(3) imposes a BLANKET BAN on tracking, behavioral monitoring, AND targeted advertising for anyone under 18. No consent override permitted. This is the strictest framework globally.
rules.fix_suggestion: Under India's DPDP Act Section 9(3), ANY tracking or behavioral monitoring for users under 18 is prohibited regardless of consent. Implement age-gating that completely disables all analytics, tracking, and ad SDKs for users under 18 in India.
rules.penalty: Up to ₹250 crore (~$30M USD)

knowledge.plain_description: India's DPDP Act Section 9(3) imposes a blanket ban on tracking, behavioral monitoring, and targeted advertising for anyone under 18. This is a strict prohibition with no consent override. Any tracking SDK, pixel, or behavioral monitoring active for users under 18 violates this requirement.
tp_criteria: Code initializes or activates a tracking SDK, analytics library, or pixel (Google Analytics, Facebook Pixel, Mixpanel, etc.) for users identified as under 18 or without age verification to exclude minors
System implements behavioral monitoring, behavioral advertising, or targeted ad delivery for users under 18 regardless of consent status
Tracking code runs for all users including minors without age-gating or exclusion logic to prevent tracking of under-18 users
fp_criteria: Code implements age verification and conditionally loads tracking only for users 18+ (IF age >= 18 THEN load tracker)
Tracking SDKs are initialized with explicit exclusion for minors or the system routes minors to a tracking-free experience
Code is test/development code or documentation that does not execute in production for real users
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age verification and age-gated tracking activation (load tracker only if age >= 18 verified), it is FP.
If tracking code is active without age verification or is active for all users including minors, it is TP — no consent override is permitted under DPDP.
Behavioral monitoring, profiling for ad targeting, and pixel tracking are all prohibited — any form of tracking targeting minors is TP.

rules.name: Data Processing Without Parental Consent for Under-18
rules.description: India DPDP Act Section 9(1) requires verifiable parental consent for ALL personal data processing of anyone under 18. Unlike COPPA (under 13), this extends to teenagers.
rules.fix_suggestion: Under India's DPDP Act, the age of majority for data processing is 18 (not 13). Implement verifiable parental consent for ALL users under 18 when processing personal data for Indian users.
rules.penalty: Up to ₹250 crore (~$30M USD)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects when an app or service processes personal data of anyone under 18 without obtaining verifiable parental consent first. India's DPDP Act requires this for all minors (not just under-13 like COPPA), making it critical for any service handling teenage users.
tp_criteria: Code actively collects personal data (name, location, contact info, device ID, behavioral data) from users identified or reasonably assumed to be under 18 without triggering a parental consent flow
Parental consent mechanism exists but is not 'verifiable' - e.g., parent can consent without identity verification, email confirmation, or documented proof of guardianship
The app processes personal data before parental consent is obtained, storing or transmitting it to backends, analytics, or third parties
fp_criteria: Code only processes data after a documented parental consent verification flow has been completed (e.g., verified guardian email, SMS challenge, government ID check)
Code is in test suite, sample data files, or documentation showing hypothetical flows but not used in production
Code path only executes for users age 18+ as determined by explicit age verification check prior to data collection
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS a verifiable parental consent mechanism (with identity verification of guardian before data processing), it's FP.
If personal data collection is conditional on passing an age-gating check that routes minors to a parental consent flow before any data processing, it's FP.
If the code collects personal data and the parental consent check is optional, happens after collection, or lacks verification steps, it's TP.

rules.name: Targeted Advertising to Under-18 Users
rules.description: India DPDP Act Section 9(3) imposes an absolute ban on targeted advertising directed at anyone under 18. This cannot be overridden by parental consent.
rules.fix_suggestion: Completely disable all targeted/personalized advertising for users under 18 in India. Only contextual (non-personalized) ads are permissible.
rules.penalty: Up to ₹250 crore (~$30M USD)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects targeted advertising directed at users under 18. Unlike parental consent requirements, India's DPDP Act has an absolute ban on targeted ads to minors that cannot be overridden by consent. This applies to any behavioral or interest-based ad serving.
tp_criteria: Code loads or initializes an ad network SDK (e.g., Google Ads, Facebook Audience Network, AppLovin) configured with behavioral targeting, interest categories, or audience segments
Code builds user profiles from behavioral data (clicks, purchases, session duration, content preferences) and passes them to ad serving systems, even if no ads are currently shown
Ad serving logic uses age-gating that is bypassable or unenforced, allowing minors to receive targeted ads intended for adults
fp_criteria: Ad network SDK is present but explicitly configured to disable behavioral targeting (e.g., `setPersonalizedAdsEnabled(false)`, non-personalized ad requests only)
Code is in documentation, comments, or example code showing what NOT to do in a children's app
Ad targeting uses only contextual signals (page content, time of day) with no behavioral profiling or interest-based segments
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS non-personalized ad serving or explicitly disables behavioral targeting for users under 18, it's FP.
If an ad network is initialized but age-gating ensures no ads are served to verified minors, it's FP.
If behavioral targeting is active (interest segments, audience lists, user profiles) and can reach users under 18, it's TP.

rules.name: Behavioral Monitoring of Under-18 Users
rules.description: India DPDP Act Section 9(3) prohibits behavioral monitoring of children under 18. This includes session recording, heatmaps, scroll tracking, and engagement analytics.
rules.fix_suggestion: Under India's DPDP Act, behavioral monitoring of anyone under 18 is prohibited. Disable session recording, heatmaps, and engagement analytics for users under 18 in India.
rules.penalty: Up to ₹250 crore (~$30M USD)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects behavioral monitoring systems that track minor users' in-app activity. India's DPDP Act prohibits session recording, heatmaps, scroll tracking, engagement analytics, and similar monitoring of anyone under 18, regardless of parental consent.
tp_criteria: Code initializes session recording SDKs (e.g., Smartlook, Fullstory, Hotjar, LogRocket) that capture screen recordings, clicks, scrolls, or keystroke data from users under 18
Analytics or tracking code sends engagement metrics (time on screen, scroll depth, interaction heatmaps, user journey funnels) to backends without age-gating that blocks minors
Device motion sensors, screen activity listeners, or frame-by-frame activity logging are used to monitor behavior and sent to third-party services without age verification
fp_criteria: Behavioral monitoring SDK is present but explicitly disabled for users identified as under 18 via age-gating before any data collection
Code only collects basic app performance metrics (crash logs, load times, API latency) with no user behavior tracking or session data
Code is test instrumentation, staging environment setup, or documentation example that is not used in production serving minors
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-gating that prevents behavioral monitoring SDKs from initializing or sending data for users under 18, it's FP.
If monitoring code only tracks non-behavioral signals (performance, errors) but not user interactions, it's FP.
If session recording, heatmap, engagement analytics, or interaction tracking is active without age-based disabling for minors, it's TP.

rules.name: Processing Detrimental to Child's Well-Being
rules.description: India DPDP Act Section 9(2) prohibits any processing of children's data that is 'likely to cause any detrimental effect on the well-being of a child.' This broad provision covers addictive design, manipulative interfaces, and harmful content personalization.
rules.fix_suggestion: Review all data processing that involves children for potential detrimental effects on well-being. This includes addictive design patterns, engagement loops, and excessive notifications.
rules.penalty: Up to ₹250 crore (~$30M USD)

knowledge.plain_description: This rule detects data processing practices that are likely to harm a child's well-being under India's DPDP Act. This includes addictive design patterns, manipulative dark UI/UX, and algorithmic content personalization that promotes harmful content to minors.
tp_criteria: Code implements engagement-maximizing features targeting minors (infinite scroll, auto-play, notification spam, streak counters, social comparison metrics, or variable rewards) designed to create compulsive use

Algorithmic recommendation or personalization logic learns from minor users' behavior to recommend increasingly extreme, age-inappropriate, or harmful content (violence, self-harm, eating disorder content, hate speech)

UI/UX patterns use dark patterns on minors (disguised exits, hard-to-find privacy controls, pre-checked data sharing, confirmation delays) that manipulate minors into behaviors counter to their interests
fp_criteria: Code implements well-being safeguards for minors (session time limits, auto-pause, content filtering, recommended break notifications, interaction rate limiting)
Algorithmic logic includes explicit well-being checks that prevent recommending harmful content categories to users under 18
Code examples or documentation describing discouraged practices that are not implemented in the actual app codebase
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS well-being safeguards (engagement limits, harmful content filtering, consent friction for addictive features), it's FP.
If dark patterns or addictive features are gated behind age verification that restricts them to users 18+, it's FP.
If code uses engagement manipulation, algorithmic recommendation of harmful content, or dark patterns without age-gating or well-being controls, it's TP.

rules.name: Non-Essential Data Collection from Children (Under 12)
rules.description: LGPD Article 14 requires processing of children's (under 12) data to be in their 'best interest.' Collecting non-essential data (location, behavioral tracking, device identifiers) even with consent violates this standard.
rules.fix_suggestion: Under LGPD Article 14, only collect data that is strictly necessary and in the child's best interest. Location data, device identifiers, and behavioral tracking are generally not in a child's best interest unless directly required for the service.
rules.penalty: Up to 2% of revenue, capped at R$50 million per violation

knowledge.plain_description: Brazil's LGPD Article 14 requires that any data collection from children under 12 must serve their 'best interest,' not the company's business interests. Collecting non-essential data like location, behavioral tracking, or device identifiers—even with parental consent—violates this standard.
tp_criteria: Code collects location data, device identifiers (IMEI, MAC address), or hardware sensor data from users under 12 with no functional purpose tied directly to core app features (e.g., collecting location for a photo editor, device ID for tracking)
Analytics or behavioral tracking code logs user activity, session data, or engagement metrics from children under 12 for business optimization or marketing purposes rather than service delivery
Code requests excessive permissions (camera, microphone, contacts, calendar) from under-12 users during onboarding or gameplay without clear necessity to the app's stated function
fp_criteria: Non-essential data collection is gated behind explicit 'best interest' justification UI where parents confirm the data serves the child's benefit, with alternatives provided
Code only collects data strictly necessary for core functionality (e.g., minimal user ID for save state, username for multiplayer, age for content filtering)
Data collection request includes clear, age-appropriate explanation of why the data improves the child's experience with the app
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS 'best interest' assessment or offers non-data alternatives to unlock features, it's FP.
If data collection is limited to what's functionally necessary (e.g., username, save state, age verification only), it's FP.
If code collects location, device IDs, behavioral analytics, or excessive permissions from under-12 users without clear functional necessity, it's TP.

rules.name: Data Collection Gated Behind Gameplay
rules.description: LGPD Article 14 §4 prohibits conditioning game/app participation on providing excess personal data. Children must not be required to share data beyond what is necessary to participate.
rules.fix_suggestion: Do not gate game features, levels, or content behind data collection requirements. Under LGPD Article 14 §4, children's participation cannot be conditioned on providing excess personal data.
rules.penalty: Up to 2% of revenue, capped at R$50 million per violation

knowledge.plain_description: LGPD prohibits conditioning game access or features on excessive data collection. Children under 12 must not be locked out of core gameplay, customization, or progression because they refuse to share unnecessary personal data.
tp_criteria: Core gameplay features (levels, characters, progression) are locked behind required data collection (full name, email, phone, location, birthday beyond age verification) that is not essential to the feature
Cosmetic or customization features are gated behind mandatory data requests (e.g., 'unlock skins by providing phone number')
Parental controls or safety features are presented as 'opt-in' data sharing, implying a child must give data to access protections
fp_criteria: Data collection requests are optional; gameplay and features remain fully accessible without providing unnecessary personal data
Required data is limited to what's functionally necessary (username for multiplayer, age for content filtering) and cannot be bypassed
Code implements graduated access where minimal data unlocks core features, with additional optional data for enhancement (e.g., nickname required to play, email optional for notifications)
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS optional data collection with full feature access regardless of consent, it's FP.
If data requests are framed as optional and features are accessible without them, it's FP.
If core or popular features require unnecessary data collection to unlock, it's TP.

rules.name: Missing Parental Consent for Under-12 Data Processing
rules.description: LGPD Article 14 §1 requires at least one parent or legal guardian to provide specific and highlighted consent for processing children's (under 12) personal data.
rules.fix_suggestion: For Brazilian users under 12, implement verifiable parental or guardian consent before processing any personal data. LGPD requires this consent to be 'specific and highlighted.'
rules.penalty: Up to 2% of revenue, capped at R$50 million per violation

knowledge.plain_description: LGPD Article 14 requires explicit, specific parental consent from at least one parent or guardian before processing any personal data from children under 12. The consent must be clearly highlighted and not bundled with other terms.
tp_criteria: Code collects personal data from users identified or reasonably assumed to be under 12 without requesting documented parental consent (email, verified phone, physical ID upload, or similar verification)
Parental consent is requested but bundled into a long privacy policy, terms of service, or general app terms without separate highlighting or emphasis
Consent flow allows data collection to proceed if parental consent is unclear, assumed, or obtained through non-specific language ('I agree to terms' covers all data use)
fp_criteria: Code implements explicit parental consent request before under-12 data collection, using separate, highlighted consent language distinct from other policies
Parental consent flow includes verification (parent email confirmation link, SMS challenge, guardianship ID check) ensuring the consenting person is an actual parent/guardian
Code blocks under-12 data processing until affirmative parental consent is documented and stored for audit trail
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS documented parental consent verification before under-12 data processing, it's FP.
If parental consent is obtained through a separate, highlighted process with guardian verification, it's FP.
If data is collected from under-12 users without explicit parental consent request or verification, it's TP.

rules.name: Adolescent Data Processing Without Rights Safeguards
rules.description: Brazil's LGPD and supplementary regulations distinguish between children (under 12) and adolescents (12-18). Adolescents have additional rights including being consulted about data processing and receiving age-appropriate explanations.
rules.fix_suggestion: For Brazilian adolescents (12-18), ensure data processing includes age-appropriate explanations and respects their right to be consulted. LGPD Article 14 §6 requires notices understandable by the child themselves.
rules.penalty: Up to 2% of revenue, capped at R$50 million per violation

knowledge.plain_description: Brazil's LGPD and supplementary regulations distinguish between children (under 12) and adolescents (12-18). Adolescents have rights to be consulted about data processing and to receive age-appropriate explanations of how their data is used, which code may not implement.
tp_criteria: Data processing explanations for adolescents (12-18) use adult-level legal language, technical jargon, or dense privacy policies without age-appropriate simplification
Code collects data from adolescents without providing them an opportunity to understand and assent to the processing, even when parental consent is obtained
Data sharing or processing changes are made without notifying or reconsulting adolescent users, treating them as passive subjects rather than rights-holders
fp_criteria: Code provides simplified, age-appropriate explanations of data processing in adolescent-facing UX, using plain language and visual aids
Adolescent users are presented with clear options to assent or object to data processing, with their input documented
Code implements notification mechanisms when data use changes, allowing adolescents to review and adjust settings
Code in test files, spec files, fixture files, or mock directories (__tests__/, test/, spec/, __mocks__/) — test code is never a real compliance violation.
rule_logic: If the code IMPLEMENTS age-appropriate explanations and adolescent assent/consultation mechanisms, it's FP.
If data processing is explained in plain language appropriate for 12-18 year olds, it's FP.
If explanations are complex, multi-step, or adolescents have no mechanism to understand or assent to processing, consider TP but note this has Compliance Determining: False.

rules.name: Behavioral Advertising Tracker in Minor-Facing Code
rules.description: OPC position: behavioral advertising to children may be deemed inherently inappropriate under PIPEDA Section 5(3) 'reasonable person' test, regardless of consent obtained.
rules.fix_suggestion: The OPC considers behavioral advertising to children inherently inappropriate. Remove behavioral ad trackers from code paths serving users under 13, and review for users 13-17.
rules.penalty: OPC compliance orders; Federal Court orders up to $100K CAD per violation

knowledge.plain_description: Canada's OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner) has stated that behavioral advertising to children may be inherently inappropriate under PIPEDA's 'reasonable person' test, regardless of whether consent was obtained. This rule flags behavioral ad targeting in minor-facing code.
tp_criteria: Code initializes or configures a behavioral advertising SDK (e.g., Google Ads with interest-based targeting, Facebook Audience Network, programmatic ad exchanges) that can serve interest-based or audience-targeted ads to identified or likely minor users
User behavior data (app usage patterns, content consumption, search history) is collected and sent to ad networks or DSPs for targeting purposes, even if ads aren't immediately shown
Ad serving logic selects ads based on behavioral profiles, interest segments, or contextual targeting patterns that assume behavioral tracking has occurred
